en: Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma (Shi Hu), Imperially Conferred Title of Dharma-Master, Purple Robe Awardee, and Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, during the Song Dynasty.
Chapter One: Comprehending the Characteristics of All Conditioned Phenomena (Saṃskāra-lakṣaṇa-parijñāna-varga). Part One of One.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. All were arhats—whose outflows were exhausted, who were free from all remaining afflictions, whose minds were well-liberated and whose wisdom was well-liberated; like great dragon kings, they were fully accomplished in all that needs to be done.

Having laid down their heavy burdens and attained great benefit, they had severed the fetters of existence and possessed unimpeded right knowledge. Their minds dwelt in tranquility and they had attained mastery—with the sole exception of the Venerable Ānanda, who remained as a person-in-training (pudgala).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"In accordance with your inclination, expound for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā as is appropriate."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra had this thought:
"Does the Venerable Subhūti now proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas by means of his own wisdom and eloquence?"
“Is it by means of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and sustaining grace that he speaks?
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, knew what Śāriputra was thinking and reflecting upon regarding such form and such mind.
Having understood this, he then addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"You should now know that whatever the World-Honored One’s śrāvaka disciples proclaim for themselves or explain to others regarding all phenomena, it is entirely through the Buddha's majestic spiritual power."
Why is this? If one is able to practice and study the Dharma taught by the Buddha, they will be able to realize the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena.
Because they have realized the Dharma, whatever they speak will not contradict the nature of all phenomena.
"Therefore, Śāriputra, the Dharma taught by the Buddha accords with the nature of all phenomena; sons of good family should understand it in this way.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha has spoken thus, commanding me to proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas according to my own inclinations and as is appropriate.”
World-Honored One!
By what meaning is one called a bodhisattva?
What dharma should be taught as the dharma of a bodhisattva?
"Bhagavān! I do not see any dharma named 'bodhisattva,' nor do I see any dharma named 'prajñāpāramitā.
For this reason, both the bodhisattva and the dharmas of a bodhisattva are non-existent; they cannot be seen and cannot be apprehended."
The perfection of wisdom is likewise non-existent, invisible, and unattainable.
For what kind of bodhisattva should I teach which perfection of wisdom?
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such an exposition, remains unmoved in mind, without alarm, without fear, and without falling back or sinking, this is precisely what is called teaching the prajñāpāramitā to a bodhisattva mahāsattva; this is precisely what is called understanding the prajñāpāramitā; this is precisely what is called abiding in the prajñāpāramitā.”
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and contemplates the perfection of wisdom, they should train in this manner."
Although that bodhisattva trains in this way, they should not give rise to the thought:
"I am training in this way. Why is that?
"That mind is no-mind, because the nature of the mind is pure.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying: "How is this so, Subhūti?"
"Is there that which is neither mind nor non-mind? Subhūti replied, "Śāriputra!..."
"What do you think, Śāriputra? Can that which is neither mind nor non-mind be apprehended as either existent or nonexistent?
Śāriputra replied, "No, Subhūti."
At that time, Subhūti addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"If the mind is not-mind and cannot be apprehended as either existent or non-existent, why do you now speak these words:
'Is there a mind that is not-mind?'"
Śāriputra asked, "What is meant by 'the nature of non-mind'? Subhūti replied:
"Because all things are indestructible and far removed from all conceptual discrimination, this is the non-mind nature.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Subhūti! It is just as the Buddha has said: you are the most supreme and foremost among those who practice the samādhi of non-contention (*araṇā*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they will attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. You should know that such a bodhisattva mahāsattva is never separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If there are those who wish to study the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, they should listen to, receive, read, recite, remember, contemplate, and practice according to the instructions of this Prajñāpāramitā; this is precisely what constitutes corresponding training in this Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to study the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas, one should listen to, receive, read, recite, memorize, contemplate, and practice according to the instructions of this Prajñāpāramitā; this is precisely what constitutes corresponding training in this Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to study the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas, one should listen to, receive, read, recite, memorize, contemplate, and practice according to the instructions of this Prajñāpāramitā; this is the skillful means within this Prajñāpāramitā by which one attains the complete assembly and correspondence of all the Bodhisattva Dharmas.

Why is this? Because this Prajñāpāramitā extensively expounds all the teachings of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; if a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they are then in accord with the dharma of the bodhisattvas.

If one wishes to study and practice the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one should listen to, receive, read, recite, memorize, contemplate, and practice according to the teachings of this Prajñāpāramitā; it is precisely through this Prajñāpāramitā that one becomes fully endowed with skillful means and gathers all the Buddha-dharmas.

Why is this? Because this Prajñāpāramitā extensively expounds all the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva trains in this manner, they will attain correspondence with the unsurpassed dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That which is called a ‘bodhisattva-mahāsattva’ cannot be seen by me, nor can it be apprehended; for a bodhisattva exists as nothing more than a name.”
World-Honored One!
Even this very name is invisible and unobtainable.
The *prajñāpāramitā* also exists as a mere name; it is invisible and unobtainable.
"What kind of bodhisattva should be taught which perfection of wisdom?
For this reason, World-Honored One, I have conceived a doubt."

When I seek the bodhisattva-mahāsattva within names, I ultimately cannot find it; yet those names have no place of abiding, nor are they without a place of abiding; they are neither determinate nor indeterminate.
Why is this? Because the nature of those names is non-existent.
Therefore, there is neither a place of abiding nor a place of non-abiding; there is neither determination nor non-determination.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, remains unmoved in mind, without alarm, without fear, and without falling back or sinking, one should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*; they abide on the bodhisattva stages without retrogression, being well-established in the correspondence with non-abiding.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and contemplates the perfection of wisdom, they do not abide in form, nor do they abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
Why is this? If one dwells in form, one is practicing the course of form and not practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If one dwells in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, one is practicing feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and not practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Why is this? Because one who dwells in [the apprehension of] phenomena is unable to receive the *prajñāpāramitā*, is not in accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*, cannot fulfill the *prajñāpāramitā*, and cannot achieve omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Why is this? Because the *prajñāpāramitā* does not grasp form, nor does it grasp feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

If one does not grasp form, it is not form; if one does not grasp feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, they are not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise without anything grasped.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice in this manner within the state of non-appropriation of phenomena; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s samādhi of non-appropriation of all phenomena.
Vast, perfect, immeasurable, and definitive, it cannot be destroyed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
World-Honored One!

That omniscience is without characteristics and without anything to be grasped; if there were characteristics that could be grasped, then people such as Śreṇika and Pūraṇa Kāśyapa would not have been able to give rise to faith in omniscience.

Why is this? Because such a person has given rise to faith and understanding in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and enters into such dharmas with a finite cognition (*pramita-jñāna*). They do not grasp form (*rūpa*); they do not grasp feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*). They do not take the dharma of joy as the object of their wisdom; they do not take internal form as the object of their wisdom; they do not take external form as the object of their wisdom; they do not take both internal and external form as the object of their wisdom; nor do they take that which is apart from internal and external form as the object of their wisdom.

In this way, one does not take internal feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as the object of wisdom; one does not take external feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as the object of wisdom; one does not take both internal and external feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as the object of wisdom; nor does one take [an object] apart from internal and external feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as the object of wisdom.

And those such as Śreṇika conceived deep faith and understanding in such dharmas and in the knowledge of all modes; they attained liberation through the nature of all dharmas, and furthermore, regarding all dharmas, they neither grasped nor rejected them, even unto nirvāṇa, which they likewise neither grasped nor rejected.
World-Honored One!

Although one who cultivates the Dharma of a bodhisattva has no grasping toward form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, they do not yet fulfill the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and eighteen unique qualities, nor do they realize nirvāṇa midway.
Therefore, World-Honored One,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand the perfection of wisdom in this way.
Furthermore, World-Honored One:
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and contemplates the perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate in this way:
"What dharma is the perfection of wisdom?"
What are the characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā*?
Since all phenomena are neither produced nor can they be apprehended, how could the *prajñāpāramitā* exist?

If, when a bodhisattva contemplates in this way, the mind remains unmoved, without alarm, without fear, and without retreating or sinking, one should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying: "If all form-dharmas are devoid of the intrinsic nature of form;

if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are devoid of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; if the perfection of wisdom is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom; if omniscience is further devoid of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom; if the perfection of wisdom is further devoid of the intrinsic nature of omniscience; and if omniscience is devoid of the intrinsic nature of omniscience—[then how can there be attainment?]"
"How is it that one says a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not depart from the perfection of wisdom? Subhūti replied, "Śāriputra!"

"So it is, so it is! All form-dharmas are devoid of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are devoid of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; even up to all-knowledge, which is devoid of the intrinsic nature of all-knowledge; the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā* is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*; all characteristics are devoid of the intrinsic nature of all characteristics; and even non-existence is devoid of intrinsic nature."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra again addressed Subhūti, saying: "How is it, Subhūti?
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this, will they be able to accomplish all-knowledge?"
Subhūti said: “So it is, so it is, Śāriputra!”
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva trains in this manner, they will be able to accomplish all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Why is this?
Because all phenomena are neither produced nor non-produced.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva can understand in this way and practice in this way, they are able to accord with and draw near to that omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). With body and mind purified, and all marks purified, they adorn and purify buddha-fields wherever they may be, bringing sentient beings to maturity and possessing all the Buddha-dharmas. This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as drawing near to omniscience.
Furthermore, the Venerable Subhūti said:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices with regard to the dharma of form, this is a mode of practice;
if he practices with regard to the characteristics of form, this is a mode of practice."
If formative activities arise, this is the characteristic of activity;
if formative activities cease, this is the characteristic of activity;
if formative activities disintegrate, this is the characteristic of activity.
If one practices with regard to emptiness or form, this is a mode of practice;
if I practice various practices, this too is a mode of practice;
if I practice the bodhisattva practices, this too is a mode of practice.
To have any attainment regarding the dharmas of a bodhisattva is itself a mode of activity.
Likewise, if one practices with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is a mode of activity;
if one practices with regard to the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is a mode of activity.
If there is the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, this is the mode of activity;
if there is the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, this is the mode of activity;
if there is the disintegration of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, this is the mode of activity.
If one perceives emptiness in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, this is a mode of practice;
to think "I am practicing various practices" is also a mode of practice;
to think "I am practicing the bodhisattva practices" is also a mode of practice.
To have the notion that "I have attained something regarding the bodhisattva-dharmas" is itself a mental sign; if one thinks,
"To practice in this way is what is called practicing the perfection of wisdom," [that too is a mental sign].
"This is also a mode of practice.
If one practices in such a manner, it should be known that this bodhisattva has not yet perfected skillful means.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying:
"How should one practice so as to be a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti replied, "Śāriputra!..."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice with respect to form, does not practice with respect to the characteristics of form, does not practice with respect to the arising of form, does not practice with respect to the cessation of form, does not practice with respect to the disintegration of form, does not practice with respect to the emptiness of form, and does not practice with respect to the notion of "I," nor give rise to the notion of "I" while practicing the bodhisattva path; and likewise does not practice with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; does not practice with respect to the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; does not practice with respect to the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; does not practice with respect to the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; does not practice with respect to the disintegration of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; does not practice with respect to the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;

does not practice with respect to the notion of "I," nor give rise to the notion of "I" while practicing the bodhisattva path—then they do not form this thought: "If one practices in this way, it is called practicing the perfection of wisdom."
"If it is thus, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Although that bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, he does not think, 'I am practicing,' nor does he think, 'I am not practicing,' nor does he think, 'I am both practicing and not practicing,' nor does he think, 'I am neither practicing nor not practicing.'"

Furthermore, one does not conceive of there being something practiced, nor does one conceive of there being nothing practiced; one does not conceive of both practicing and not practicing, nor does one conceive of neither practicing nor not practicing.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are without thought, without grasping, and without non-grasping; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s samādhi of non-appropriation of all phenomena.
Vast, perfect, immeasurable, and definitive, this samādhi cannot be destroyed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
It universally enters into the practices of all samādhis; if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this manner, they will swiftly attain the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke these words:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices innumerable samādhis yet has no perception of practice, and perceives innumerable samādhis yet has nothing perceived, that bodhisattva does not form such thoughts as:
‘I have entered this samādhi,’ ‘I shall enter this samādhi,’ or ‘I am now entering this samādhi.’”
"In this way, at all times, in all places, and in all modes, one is free from all marks and there is nothing produced.
If it is thus, one should know that this bodhisattva has already received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from a previous Buddha."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has no sign of activity within samādhi, and yet receives from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the prophecy of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment—does this samādhi have any object of observation?"
Subhūti said: “No, Śāriputra! Why is that?
"That samādhi is by nature non-existent, free from all conceptual discrimination and objects of cognition.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Subhūti! So it is, so it is! Subhūti!

Just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has proclaimed through his majestic power, eloquence, and sustaining grace, so should all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice and so should they train themselves.
"Why is this? If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, this constitutes training in the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, is he training in the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! It is so, it is so!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, this constitutes training in the perfection of wisdom.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, what dharmas should they train in?”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that dharmas do not exist and that there is likewise nothing to be learned, this constitutes training.”
"Why is this? Because all those phenomena are non-existent, yet foolish ordinary beings conceptually discriminate and cling to these non-existent phenomena.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If dharmas do not exist, how can they now exist?
The Buddha said:

“Śāriputra! All phenomena do not exist, yet they exist as they currently do; because those foolish ordinary beings do not understand this within the absence of phenomena, they call it ignorance (avidyā), and thus they cling to ignorance.”

Due to attachment, one gives rise to a discriminating mind; because of discrimination, one falls into the two extremes. Thus, through this successive process regarding all phenomena, various kinds of discrimination give rise to the appearance of what is attained.

Having made such conceptualizations, they give rise to attachment based on the two extremes; therefore, they conceptualize past phenomena, conceptualize future phenomena, and conceptualize present phenomena.
It is because of various conceptual constructions that they cling to name-and-form. Śāriputra,
those ordinary beings who give rise to conceptual constructions without understanding the non-existent nature of all phenomena are unable to understand or perceive the path of reality as it truly is.

Because they do not know or see, they do not emerge from the three realms; they are unable to abide in the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) nor give rise to faith therein, and for this reason they fall into the category of foolish ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*).
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, is he training in all-knowledge?”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this manner does not train in omniscience; yet a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this manner also trains in omniscience, and by training in this manner, they also train in all dharmas, drawing near to omniscience and accomplishing omniscience.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If a phantom person were to ask this question:..."
"How does one train in all-knowledge?
How does one draw near to all-knowledge?
How does one accomplish all-knowledge?"
“If he were to ask such a question, how should I answer? The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
"I now ask you; answer according to your own understanding.
Subhūti said, "Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy. The Buddha said, "Subhūti!"
What do you think: is illusion different from form, or is form different from illusion?
Likewise, is illusion different from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, or are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness different from illusion?
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One! That which is different from illusion is not form;
that which is different from form is not illusion. That illusion is itself form, and that form is itself illusion. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti, what do you think? Are all these five aggregates of clinging the bodhisattva?”
Subhūti said: “So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Sugata!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“You should know that the five aggregates of clinging are themselves illusory persons. Why is this?
It is said that form is like an illusion, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like illusions.

Since those [aggregates of] form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are precisely the six sense bases and the five aggregates, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise like an illusion.
"If one wishes to practice and study the Prajñāpāramitā, one should study it as being like an illusion; then one will attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"If there were bodhisattvas newly established in the Mahāyāna, upon hearing such a teaching, would they not be struck with alarm and fear? The Buddha said, "Subhūti!..."
If a bodhisattva newly established in the Mahāyāna follows an evil spiritual friend, they will experience alarm and fear upon hearing this Dharma;
however, if that bodhisattva follows a virtuous spiritual friend, they will not give rise to alarm or fear upon hearing this Dharma.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what is meant by a 'bad friend' (pāpamitra) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
The Buddha said:
"If there is one who instructs another to distance themselves from the *prajñāpāramitā*, this person is a bodhisattva’s bad friend (*akalyāṇamitra*).
What, then, is called a bodhisattva’s good friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)?"
The Buddha said:

“If, regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, one personally proclaims it and teaches it to others, and furthermore extensively demonstrates to others the deeds of Māra and the faults of Māra, urging them to awaken to them; having awakened, further causing them to distance themselves from them; and moreover urging them not to depart from the Buddhas.”

Subhūti! You should know that such a person has donned the armor of the Mahāyāna, is adorned with the Mahāyāna, and dwells securely in the Mahāyāna; this is a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
as the Buddha has said:”
"A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dons the armor of the Great Vehicle, adorns himself with the Great Vehicle, and dwells securely in the Great Vehicle.
World-Honored One, what is the meaning of the term "Bodhisattva"? Please explain it.
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti! You should know that the meaning of ‘non-sentence’ is the meaning of ‘bodhisattva.’”

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva encounters no obstruction regarding any phenomena; they understand all phenomena as they truly are, and even regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), they encounter no obstruction and know it as it truly is.
"This is explained as the meaning of 'bodhisattva.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
how is one named a 'mahāsattva'?"
The Buddha said,
“Because they are the most supreme among the multitudes of sentient beings, for this reason they are called ‘Mahāsattvas’ (Great Beings).
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I, too, would like to speak on the meaning of ‘mahāsattva.
The Buddha said:
"Speak as you wish; now is the very time. Śāriputra said:

"One who, having abandoned all views of a self, views of a sentient being, views of a life-force, views of a person, views of the various realms of existence, views of nihilism, views of eternalism, and views of a personal body (satkāyadṛṣṭi), teaches the Dharma to sentient beings—such a one is a mahāsattva."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I, too, would like to speak on the meaning of ‘mahāsattva.’”
The Buddha said, “Speak as you wish; now is the very time. Subhūti said:

"If one is without obstruction or attachment toward such minds—the mind of bodhi, the mind of omniscience, the untainted mind, the peerless mind, and the mind equal to the unequaled—and is not destroyed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, for this reason one is called a mahāsattva, and thereby enters the number of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying:
"In what way is that mind unobstructed and unattached? Subhūti replied:
"Because it is without mind, the mind has no obstructions and nothing to which it is attached.
Śāriputra asked: "What is the meaning of 'mind'?"
Subhūti said: “Śāriputra,
can the mind arise with respect to existence or non-existence?”
"Can it be apprehended? Śāriputra replied, "No, Subhūti."
At that time, Subhūti addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"If the mind cannot be apprehended in terms of existence or non-existence, for what reason is there any discourse concerning the mind?"
The Venerable Śāriputra praised Subhūti, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”
"It is exactly as the Buddha has said: you are the most supreme and foremost among those who practice the samādhi of non-contention.
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"I, too, delight in explaining the meaning of 'mahāsattva'.
The Buddha said, "Speak as you please; now is precisely the right time."
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:

"A mahāsattva is one who has donned the armor of the Great Vehicle, adorned himself with the Dharma of the Great Vehicle, and dwells securely in the Great Vehicle; for this reason, he is called by the meaning of 'mahāsattva'."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has donned the armor of the Great Vehicle—by what meaning is it named the 'armor of the Great Vehicle'?"
The Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva forms this thought:
'I should deliver immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, causing them to reach nirvāṇa.'"
"Although they have thus delivered such sentient beings, they harbor no notion of having delivered any sentient beings, and yet not a single sentient being has attained nirvāṇa. Why is this?"
Because the nature of all phenomena is fundamentally thus, they are free from all conditioned activity.
Subhūti, it is like a magician who, at a crossroads, uses his illusory arts to produce a great multitude of people, and having produced them, immediately makes them vanish.
Subhūti, what do you think?
Do these illusory persons have any place from which they come, or do they possess any reality?
“Is there anything that is extinguished or anything that is destroyed? Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

It is likewise for a bodhisattva mahāsattva: although they deliver immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, causing them to reach nirvāṇa, in reality there are no sentient beings who are delivered.”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this teaching, does not give rise to alarm or fear, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the armor of the Mahāyāna and adorned themselves with it.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes it in this way, they are one who has donned the armor of the Mahāyāna, being courageous, firm, and well-adorned.”
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, it is so, it is so!”
Why is this? That omniscience is unconditioned and non-conditioned; yet, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, it gives rise to various skillful means.
Furthermore, those sentient beings are likewise unconditioned and non-conditioned.
Subhūti said: “It is truly as the Buddha has spoken. Why is this? Because...”
Form is neither bound nor liberated; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither bound nor liberated.
World-Honored One!
The suchness of form is neither bound nor liberated; the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is likewise neither bound nor liberated.
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed Subhūti, saying:
"As the Venerable One has said:

'Form is neither bound nor liberated; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated. The suchness of form is neither bound nor liberated; the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither bound nor liberated.'"
In this context, what is form that is neither bound nor liberated?
What are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are neither bound nor liberated?
And what is the suchness of form that is neither bound nor liberated?
"What is the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that is neither bound nor liberated? Subhūti replied,
"Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!"

You should now know this: for an illusory person, form is neither bound nor liberated; for an illusory person, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated. For an illusory person, the suchness of form is neither bound nor liberated; for an illusory person, the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because there is nothing that exists, there is neither bondage nor liberation; because they are detached, there is neither bondage nor liberation; because they do not arise, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands in this way, he is one who dwells securely in the Great Vehicle, dons the armor of the Great Vehicle, and is adorned by the Great Vehicle.
At that moment, having heard these words, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra remained silent.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
As the Buddha has said:
"The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells securely in the Mahāyāna, dons the armor of the Mahāyāna, and is adorned by the Mahāyāna.
World-Honored One, for what reason is it named the Mahāyāna?
How does a bodhisattva thoroughly understand this?
From where does this vehicle emerge?
Having emerged, wherein does it abide?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The Great Vehicle is immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless; for this reason it is called the Great Vehicle.”
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva understands it in this way.
Furthermore, as for what you ask regarding from where the Great Vehicle emerges and where it abides:
this vehicle emerges from the triple world and abides in the *pāramitās*. Because it is without attachment, it abides in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and from this, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is born.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If dharmas neither emerge nor abide, then because they do not abide, they are associated with the non-abiding of all-knowledge."
Furthermore, this Mahāyāna is also non-existent; it has no emergence, and because there is no emergence, it emerges in this way. Why is this?

Whether there is something that emerges or nothing that emerges, these two dharmas are both unobtainable and non-arising. Thus, throughout all dharmas, there is no dharma that can emerge, nor is there any non-dharma that can emerge.
“Subhūti! It is in this way that the bodhisattva mahāsattva gives birth to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said:
‘That Mahāyāna Dharma is the most supreme among all the worlds of devas, humans, and asuras, and is equal to space.’”
Just as that space can accommodate immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, so too is this Mahāyāna Dharma; it can likewise accommodate immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.
"World-Honored One!
Regarding the Mahāyāna Dharma, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives no coming and perceives no going, nor is there any place of abiding.

The prior limit is unobtainable, the posterior limit is unobtainable, and the middle limit is unobtainable; the three periods of time are equal because nothing is produced. Therefore, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is explained in this way."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
"So it is, so it is! Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the Mahāyāna Dharma in this manner, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will then achieve the realization of all-knowledge."

The *Buddhamātṛ-janma-tripiṭaka-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Fascicle One, translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperial Envoy, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, and Purple-Robed Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree. Chapter One, Part Two: "Fully Understanding the Characteristics of All Conditioned Phenomena. At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The Buddha had commanded Subhūti to expound the *prajñāpāramitā*; why, then, does he now speak of the Mahāyāna?
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"In the Mahāyāna that I teach, will there not be a contradiction with that Prajñāpāramitā? The Buddha said, "No, Subhūti!"
"What you have said accords with the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Subhūti, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
I have sought for a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the past, the future, and the present, yet I cannot find one at all. Why is this?
Because form is limitless, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also limitless; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are limitless, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also limitless.
Form is unapprehendable because it does not exist for a bodhisattva; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unapprehendable because they do not exist for a bodhisattva.
“World-Honored One!
Thus, at all times, in all places, and in every manner, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is ultimately unobtainable.
The perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is likewise invisible and unobtainable; even up to omniscience (sarvajñatā), it is invisible and unobtainable.”
Thus, all phenomena (dharmas), at all times, in all places, and in all ways, are neither visible nor obtainable.
What, then, constitutes a phenomenon?
"What is that which is not the Dharma?
By what Dharma, O Bhagavān, should one be taught to enter the Prajñāpāramitā?"
"Bodhisattva" exists as a mere name, and "prajñāpāramitā" also exists as a mere name; yet even those names are without arising.
World-Honored One!
As it is said: "The self and the phenomena of the self are ultimately unarisen because the self has no intrinsic nature; all phenomena are likewise.
In this context, how is it that form is without attachment and without arising?
How are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness unattached and unarisen?
Because all dharmas lack intrinsic nature, they are unattached and unarisen; because dharmas lack intrinsic nature, all dharmas are unarisen; therefore, even non-arising is itself unarisen.
I now teach entry into the Prajñāpāramitā by means of the dharma of non-arising.
World-Honored One!
If one seeks all dharmas, even including the dharmas of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, apart from the dharma of non-arising, they are utterly unobtainable.
Why is this? World-Honored One, if one were apart from the dharma of non-arising, a bodhisattva mahāsattva would be unable to accomplish that practice of awakening.
World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this teaching, remains unmoved in mind, neither startled, nor terrified, nor retreating, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the perfection of wisdom and contemplating the perfection of wisdom.
“World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices or contemplates the perfection of wisdom, they do not grasp at form; they do not see the arising of form, nor do they see the cessation of form. In this same way, they do not grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they do not see the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor do they see their cessation.”
Why is this? If form is without arising, it is not form; if form is without cessation, it is not form.
This non-arising and form are non-dual and undifferentiated; this non-cessation and form are likewise non-dual and undifferentiated. To speak of form is, therefore, to speak of the non-dual dharma.

If feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without arising, they are not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without cessation, they are not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

This non-arising is non-dual and indistinguishable from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; this non-ceasing is likewise non-dual and indistinguishable from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. To speak of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is itself the non-dual dharma.
“World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has contemplated the perfection of wisdom in this way, they then have no apprehension, no arising, and no cessation regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
This applies even to all phenomena and all characteristics. Why is this?
If form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without arising and without ceasing, they are not, in fact, form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

This form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-dual and indistinguishable from non-arising and non-ceasing; if one speaks of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, they are themselves the non-dual dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Venerable Subhūti has said, a bodhisattva is precisely the dharma of non-arising."
"If this is so, how can it be that bodhisattvas, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, engage in difficult practices and have the perception of them as difficult? Subhūti said, "Śāriputra!"
I do not wish for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to have difficult practices or the perception of them as difficult.
Why is this? If they have the perception of difficulty, they will be unable to benefit immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.

If one conceives toward all sentient beings the notion of ease, the notion of joy, the notion of father, the notion of mother, and the notion of child, in this way one will be able to benefit immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should conceive this thought toward all sentient beings:
"At all times and in all places, I shall liberate them from all suffering."
All sentient beings are likewise so: at all times and in all places, they are liberated from all suffering.
Never abandoning sentient beings in any place, they cause all beings everywhere to be liberated from the aggregate of suffering, without giving rise to faults within their minds or intentions.
“Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a mind toward all sentient beings, there is no difficult practice, nor is there any perception of difficulty.”
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to this thought:
"Just as I am ultimately non-existent and unobtainable at all times, in all places, and in every respect."
"Those all dharmas, at all times, in all places, and in all ways, are likewise ultimately non-existent and unobtainable.
In this way, one gives rise to the perception of non-existence regarding all internal and external dharmas.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices with such a mind, there is no practice that is difficult to perform, nor is there any perception of it being difficult to perform.
"Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra!..."
As for what you previously said—
that "the Bodhisattva is non-arisen"— it is so, it is so!
"A Bodhisattva is truly non-arisen.
Śāriputra asked: "If the Bodhisattva is non-arisen, would not the qualities of that Bodhisattva also be non-arisen?"
Subhūti said: "The dharmas of a bodhisattva are likewise without arising. Śāriputra said:
“If the dharmas of a bodhisattva are non-arising, is that omniscience also non-arising?
Subhūti replied, “Omniscience is non-arising.”
Śāriputra asked: "Is the dharma of omniscience non-arisen? Subhūti replied:
"The dharma of omniscience is also unarisen. Śāriputra asked:
"If the dharma of omniscience is also unarisen, are those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) also unarisen?"
Subhūti said: "Ordinary beings, too, are likewise unarisen.
He further said:
“Are those dharmas of ordinary beings non-arisen?
Subhūti replied, “The dharmas of ordinary beings are also non-arisen.”
The Venerable Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying:

"If a bodhisattva and the qualities of a bodhisattva, omniscience and the qualities of omniscience, ordinary beings and the qualities of ordinary beings are all unarisen, then when that bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains omniscience—which is itself unarisen—does he attain the unarisen?"
The Venerable Subhūti said: “Śāriputra!
I do not wish for there to be anything to be attained within the dharma of non-arising.”
"Why is this? Because the dharma of non-arising cannot be apprehended. Śāriputra said:
“Is it that the dharma of non-arising does not attain non-arising? Subhūti replied, “So it is, so it is!”
"Non-arising dharmas do not attain non-arising.
Śāriputra said: "If those dharmas are non-arising, is non-arising itself also non-arising?"
Subhūti said: "The dharma of arising is non-arising, and non-arising is also non-arising. Śāriputra said:
“If there is neither arising nor one who arises, is that which you speak of and delight in speaking of arising or non-arising?
Subhūti replied, “That which is delighted in speaking of is also non-arising.”
Śāriputra said: "If one delights in speaking of non-arising, does that which is spoken of not itself arise? Subhūti replied:
"Whatever is spoken and whatever is delightfully expounded—all of it is unborn.
Venerable Śāriputra praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Subhūti! Among those who preach the Dharma, you are the most excellent and foremost. Why is this?
"Whatever questions are asked, he is able to answer them all, remaining unmoved and unimpaired regarding the characteristics of all phenomena. Subhūti said: "Śāriputra!"

Such is the fundamental nature of the Dharma: among the disciples of the Buddha, within this dharma that is without reliance, they are able to answer whatever questions are asked, remaining unmoved and unimpaired regarding the characteristics of all phenomena.
"Why is this? Because all dharmas have no basis upon which to rely.
Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying:
“If all phenomena have no basis, upon which perfection does the bodhisattva mahāsattva rely?
Subhūti replied, “Upon the perfection of wisdom.”
Śāriputra! You should know them as they truly are: because all those dharmas are without support, the pāramitās are likewise so.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this profound prajñāpāramitā, they should form this thought:
"There is no speaking, no showing, no hearing, and no attainment.

With the mind unmoved, having no characteristic of seeking and no characteristic of grasping—one should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the practice of the countless *prajñāpāramitā* without departing from this mindfulness.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom not depart from this mindfulness?"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not depart from this mindfulness, they will not depart from the practice of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not depart from the practice of the perfection of wisdom, they will not depart from this mindfulness.

Subhūti! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not depart from this practice and do not depart from this mindfulness, then all those sentient beings should likewise attain non-separation from the practice of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Why is this? Because all sentient beings do not depart from these practices, nor do they depart from these thoughts. Subhūti said:
“Śāriputra! What you have said accords with my meaning. Why is this?
Because sentient beings lack intrinsic nature, one should know that mindfulness also lacks intrinsic nature;
because sentient beings are detached, one should know that mindfulness is also detached;
because sentient beings have no mind, one should know that mindfulness also has no mind.
Because sentient beings lack awakening and comprehension, one should know that mindfulness also lacks awakening and comprehension;
because sentient beings know the meaning of reality as it is, mindfulness also knows the meaning of reality as it is.
"Śāriputra! I desire that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in this manner. **Chapter Two:

Śakra Devānām Indra** At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra came to the assembly together with forty thousand celestial beings; the Four Great Kings came with twenty thousand celestial beings; Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, came with ten thousand Brahma-beings; and the sons of the Śuddhāvāsa gods came with a thousand celestial beings. All such as these gathered for the assembly.
The light resulting from the karmic retribution of all those devaputras was completely eclipsed by the superior radiance of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:

"We gods, including the assembly of Brahmās, have all gathered here, desiring to hear the Venerable Subhūti proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, so as to instruct them on how they should abide."
"How should one practice and train?
How should one be in accord? Subhūti replied:

“Kauśika! Now, within this assembly of devaputras, by the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual sustenance (*adhiṣṭhāna*), those who have not yet resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should now give rise to that resolve.”

If one has already entered the stage of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma), they are incapable of generating the mind set on unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). Why is this?
Because such a person is bound by cyclic existence (saṃsāra).

If any among such people as these should be able to resolve their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall likewise rejoice in it and encourage them to generate that mind, so that their roots of goodness may never be severed.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
"You have skillfully exhorted and guided the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, causing them to attain correspondence with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The Buddha possesses great kindness and virtue toward sentient beings; it is for the sake of repaying this debt of gratitude to the Buddha that I now offer such exhortation. Why is this?

All the disciples of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past likewise exhorted the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in order to repay the Buddha’s kindness, causing those Bodhisattvas to abide in the true Dharma according to their pure conduct, and also teaching them to achieve the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Because of such practices, unsurpassed wisdom is generated.
World-Honored One!

I now likewise embrace and protect all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; by the power of the causes and conditions of my thus embracing and protecting them, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will swiftly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
“Listen attentively! Reflect upon this according to the truth.”

I shall now proclaim the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, which abides in the dharma of emptiness, so that all bodhisattvas may don the armor of the Great Vehicle and be adorned with the Great Vehicle.

One should know that the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) consists in not abiding in the five aggregates; not abiding in the eye faculty, nor in the objective field of forms; not abiding in eye-consciousness, nor in eye-contact; and furthermore, not abiding in any sensation produced by eye-contact.

In this way, one does not dwell in the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; one does not dwell in the objects of sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or mental phenomena; one does not dwell in the consciousnesses of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; one does not dwell in ear-contact through to mind-contact; nor does one dwell in the various sensations produced by ear-contact through to mind-contact. One does not dwell in the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness; one does not dwell in the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the path; one does not dwell in the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood, or the stage of Buddhahood.

Because they do not abide in the five aggregates, nor even in the stage of a Buddha, they do not abide in form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either permanent or impermanent;

they do not abide in form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either suffering or pleasure; they do not abide in form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as...
If emptiness were not empty, it would not abide in form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it would not abide in self or non-self;
it would not abide in form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being either pure or defiled;

and it would not abide in the emptiness of anything obtainable within the phenomena of form, nor in the emptiness of anything obtainable within sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
They do not abide in the unconditioned fruit of the srotāpanna; they do not abide in the unconditioned fruit of the sakṛdāgāmin;
they do not abide in the unconditioned fruit of the anāgāmin; they do not abide in the unconditioned fruit of the arhat;
they do not abide in the unconditioned fruit of the pratyekabuddha; and they do not abide in the Buddha-dharma.
He does not abide in the field of merit of a srotāpanna, nor does he abide in the seven rebirths of a srotāpanna;
he does not abide in the field of merit of a sakṛdāgāmin, nor does he abide in the sakṛdāgāmin’s ultimate return to this world to bring an end to suffering;
he does not abide in the field of merit of an anāgāmin, nor does he abide in the anāgāmin’s non-return to this world to attain nirvāṇa there.
They do not abide in the field of merit of an Arhat, nor do they abide in an Arhat’s entry into *nirvāṇa* without remainder in the present life;

they do not abide in the field of merit of a Pratyekabuddha, nor do they abide in a Pratyekabuddha’s passage beyond the stage of a Śrāvaka yet falling short of the Buddha-ground as they proceed toward *nirvāṇa*;

they do not abide in the supreme field of merit of the Buddhas, nor do they abide in the Buddha-dharma that transcends the stages of ordinary beings, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas. Rather, they benefit immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, and further cause immeasurable and incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings not to proceed toward the *nirvāṇa* without remainder of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but to resolutely proceed toward the realization of perfectly complete enlightenment and unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, thereby establishing the work of a Buddha.
"All such things as these do not abide at all.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra had this thought:

"If all Tathāgatas transcend the stages of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, benefiting immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, and further cause immeasurable, innumerable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings not to head toward the nirvana without remainder of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but to resolutely proceed toward the realization of the supreme nirvana of perfect, complete enlightenment, thereby establishing the Buddha-work."
"If one does not abide in any such dharmas, in what then should one abide?
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and knowing his thought, addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: "Śāriputra!..."
"What do you think?
Does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha have any dharma in which he abides? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti! A Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has no dharma in which to abide. Why is this?
"That non-abiding mind is called the Tathāgata; it does not abide in the realm of the conditioned, it does not abide in the realm of the unconditioned, because it does not abide therein.
Subhūti replied: "So it is, so it is!"
Śāriputra! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abide in the manner in which that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha abides.
Abiding in this way, they do not abide in anything, nor do they not abide; they are neither fixed nor unfixed.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they are well-established in the correspondence of non-abiding.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they are practicing the practice of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
At that time, there were among those in the assembly certain devaputras who thought to themselves:

"The speech, words, letters, and phrases of the various yakṣas can still be understood; yet, as for the dharmas spoken by the Venerable Subhūti, we members of the deva host are unable to comprehend them."
At that time, Subhūti, knowing the thoughts and intentions in the minds of those devaputras, addressed them, saying:

"You should know, O devaputras, that all those dharmas are without speech, without demonstration, without hearing, and without attainment; they are free from all conceptual discrimination and are without anything to be cognized."
At that time, the assembly of devaputras again had this thought:
"What the Venerable Subhūti has spoken is even more difficult to understand—vast, profound, supreme, and subtle; it is difficult for us, the host of devas, to enter into."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, having again understood the thoughts in the minds of the devaputras, immediately addressed them, saying:
"You should know this: those who wish to attain the fruit of a srotāpanna, and those who wish to abide in the fruit of a srotāpanna, should abide in this patience."

If one wishes to attain the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin and abide in the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin; if one wishes to attain the fruit of an Anāgāmin and abide in the fruit of an Anāgāmin; if one wishes to attain the fruit of an Arhat and abide in the fruit of an Arhat; if one wishes to attain the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha and abide in the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha; or if one wishes to attain the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and abide in the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—one should in all cases abide in this patience.
When the sons of the gods had heard this teaching, they further reflected:
"Who could there be who is able to listen to and receive the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti?"
At that time, Subhūti, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority and knowing their thoughts, spoke again:
"O assembly of devaputras!
You should know that those illusory persons are able to hear and receive the Dharma I preach."
"Why is this? Because they have neither heard nor realized any dharmas.
At that time, the assembly of devaputras addressed Subhūti, saying:
“How is it, Venerable One? Are all sentient beings like an illusion? Subhūti replied:
"All sentient beings are entirely like illusions and likewise like dreams.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings and these illusions and dreams are non-dual and without distinction."
For this reason, all those dharmas are also like illusions and dreams.

Whatever there is of the stream-enterer and the fruit of stream-entry, the once-returner and the fruit of once-returning, the non-returner and the fruit of non-returning, the arhat and the fruit of arhatship, the pratyekabuddha and the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood—all these are like illusions and like dreams; even that fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is like an illusion and like a dream.
At that time, the assembly of devaputras again addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"If unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) is said to be like an illusion or a dream, is the dharma of nirvāṇa also like an illusion or a dream?"
Subhūti said: "So it is!
Even nirvāṇa is like an illusion or a dream; how much more so other dharmas?"
The devaputras asked:
"For what reason is even that dharma of nirvāṇa said to be like an illusion or a dream? Subhūti replied:
"If there were any dharma that transcended nirvāṇa, I would likewise say it is like an illusion and like a dream.
Why is this? Because that illusion and dream are non-dual and indistinguishable from the dharma of nirvāṇa."

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, and other such great śrāvakas, together with the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Regarding the Perfection of Wisdom as explained by the Venerable One, who is able to receive its meaning?"
At that time, Ānanda addressed the assembly, saying:

"All those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive and possess right view, as well as those arhats whose outflows are exhausted—you should know that such persons are able to receive the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* as taught by Subhūti."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the assembly, saying:
"Regarding this Prajñāpāramitā that I have spoken of, there is no one capable of receiving it. Why is this?"
In this regard, there is no dharma that can be proclaimed, no dharma that can be indicated, nothing to be conceptually differentiated, and nothing to be cognized.
Because there is neither proclamation nor cognition, the Prajñāpāramitā is thus proclaimed and thus heard.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:
"Now that the Venerable Subhūti is proclaiming such a profound and true Dharma, I shall manifest exquisite flowers and scatter them over him."
Having formed this thought, he immediately manifested countless exquisite flowers and scattered them over the Venerable Subhūti. At that time, Subhūti had this thought:

"These countless exquisite flowers that have been manifested here are such as I have never before seen even in the Heaven of the Thirty-three; these flowers are so extraordinary and sublime that they were not produced by trees."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the Venerable Subhūti, addressed Subhūti, saying:
"These flowers are not phenomena that have arisen."
"Why is this? It does not arise from the mind, nor does it emerge from trees. Subhūti said:
“Kauśika! If these flowers do not arise from trees and are not produced by the mind, they are non-arising.
If they are non-arising, they cannot be called flowers.”
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, then thought to himself:

"This Venerable Subhūti possesses profound wisdom; he skillfully expounds upon names, phrases, and syllables. In accordance with what he teaches, he does not destroy conventional designations while explaining the meaning of reality as it is."
Having formed this thought, he addressed Subhūti, saying:
"As the Venerable One has explained, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this manner."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying: "Kauśika, it is so, it is so!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this way.

Training in this way, they do not train for the fruit of a srotāpanna, they do not train for the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, they do not train for the fruit of an anāgāmin, they do not train for the fruit of an arhat, and they do not train for the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.
If one does not train in such fruits, this is precisely training in omniscience and abiding in the Buddha-dharma.
One who thus abides trains in the immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.

One who trains in this manner, though training in form (*rūpa*), neither increases nor decreases it; though training in feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), likewise neither increases nor decreases them.

One who trains in form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness without increasing or decreasing them, does not train by grasping at form, nor does he train by grasping at feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.
One does not train by abandoning form, nor does one train by abandoning feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

If a dharma is without grasping and without abandoning, then that dharma is without arising and without cessation. One who understands all dharmas to be without grasping, without abandoning, without arising, and without cessation—training in this way is called training in omniscience and giving birth to omniscience.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at any phenomenon, and thus trains in non-arising and non-ceasing; and because he trains thus, he also does not grasp at that omniscience, and thus trains in non-arising and non-ceasing—such a one is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains."
"If one trains in this manner, should they not be training for the sake of all-knowledge? Subhūti replied, "So it is, so it is!"
All-knowledge, up to and including all Buddha-dharmas, is without grasping and without arising or ceasing; one who trains in this manner is a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in all-knowledge.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"Where should one seek the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva?"
Śāriputra said: “Kauśika!
The prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva should be sought within that which is being turned by Subhūti.”
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"Venerable Śāriputra! By what spiritual power is this Prajñāpāramitā being sustained by Subhūti as he speaks it?"
Śāriputra said: "Kauśika!
You should know that this is due to the empowerment of the Buddha's spiritual power."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
"You should know that all this which I have spoken regarding the Prajñāpāramitā is due to the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power."

Regarding the question of where one should seek the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, it should be known that the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is not to be sought within form (*rūpa*), nor is it to be sought apart from form.

In this way, one should not seek it within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor should one seek it apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Why is that?
Form is not the perfection of wisdom, and apart from form there is no perfection of wisdom;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not the perfection of wisdom, and apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness there is no perfection of wisdom.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"Venerable Subhūti! Is this Great Pāramitā the Prajñāpāramitā?"
Is the perfection of the immeasurable the perfection of wisdom?
Is the perfection of the boundless the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti said: “So it is, so it is, Kauśika!”
The great *pāramitā* is called the *prajñāpāramitā*; the immeasurable *pāramitā* is called the *prajñāpāramitā*; the boundless *pāramitā* is called the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Because form (*rūpa*) is vast, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is also vast;
because feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are vast, the perfection of wisdom is also vast.
Because form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is also immeasurable.
Because form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are boundless, the perfection of wisdom is also boundless.
"Furthermore, Kauśika! Because conditions are limitless, the Prajñāpāramitā is limitless.
Because the Prajñāpāramitā is limitless, sentient beings are also limitless."
In what sense is it called "conditioned by the boundless"?

It means that form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended at their prior limit, cannot be apprehended at their middle limit, and cannot be apprehended at their posterior limit;
this extends even to all phenomena, which likewise cannot be apprehended at their prior, middle, or posterior limits.
For this reason, it is called "boundless conditions," which is to say that the *prajñāpāramitā* is boundless.
Furthermore, for what reason is it said that sentient beings are boundless?
"Kauśika! You should know that throughout the past, future, and present limits, no sentient being can be found.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
“What do you think, Subhūti?
Is that realm of sentient beings not indeed limitless? Subhūti replied:
“Sentient beings are immeasurable and beyond calculation; for this reason, sentient beings are boundless.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
“Regarding what is called ‘sentient beings,’ by what meaning is the term ‘sentient beings’ defined?”
Subhūti said: "Kauśika, the meaning of all dharmas is the meaning of sentient beings."
"What do you think? For what purpose should it be said that there is a purpose for sentient beings?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:

"In my view, the meaning of 'sentient beings' does not consist in the principle of dharmas, nor does it consist in the principle of non-dharmas. One should know that sentient beings have no fundamental basis, no cause, no self, and no conditions; it is only through skillful means that their names are established."
Subhūti said: "Kauśika! Regarding what I previously stated—that sentient beings are limitless—what do you think?"
"Is there truly any sentient being who can be described or pointed out? Śakra,
Lord of the Devas, replied, "No, Subhūti!"
Then Subhūti said: "If all sentient beings have no reality and cannot be described or demonstrated, for this reason I say that sentient beings are infinite."

Kauśika! Suppose that a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and through skillful means and speech, were to speak of all sentient beings—those already born, those currently being born, or those yet to be born;
those already extinguished, those currently being extinguished, or those yet to be extinguished—would he be able to state their limit?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: "No, Subhūti! Why is that?"
"All sentient beings are fundamentally pure. Subhūti said: "So it is!"
“Because sentient beings are boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.
At that time, Śakra Devendra, Mahābrahmā, Maheśvara, along with the other devas, devīs, and hosts of ṛṣis in the assembly, all addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How wonderful! How excellent!”

When the Tathāgata appears in the world, the Venerable Subhūti is able to skillfully proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā; if a bodhisattva mahāsattva upholds this Dharma and does not depart from the Prajñāpāramitā of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, I shall revere them as I would the Buddhas themselves.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, Mahābrahmā, and all the other hosts of celestial sages, saying: "So it is, so it is!"

You should know this: in the past, when I was practicing the conduct for awakening under the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṅkara in the city of Uttamapradīpa, even then I was not separated from the Prajñāpāramitā.
That Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara then bestowed upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, speaking these words:

"In a future age, after incalculable kalpas have passed, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with the assembly of devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One! It is rare, Sugata!”
"This Prajñāpāramitā can encompass all-knowledge; Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train themselves in this manner.

Chapter Three: The Merits of the Jewel Stūpa (Part One) At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—as well as the hosts of devas in the desire realm, such as Śakra Devendra, and the hosts of devas in the form realm, such as Mahābrahmā, extending even to all the sons of gods in the Akaniṣṭha heaven:

"You should know this: if there are good sons or good daughters who are able to hear, receive, read, and recite this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and who practice according to its teaching, such persons will not be given an opportunity for harm by Māra, his followers, humans, or non-humans; they cannot be injured by malignant poisons, nor shall they meet an untimely death."

"Furthermore, if there are sons or daughters of good family who have not yet been able to hear, receive, read, or recite this Prajñāpāramitā, the assembly of devaputras who have already resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* shall go to those persons to provide them with protection and mindfulness."
One should encourage them to listen to, receive, read, recite, and practice this Prajñāpāramitā as it is taught.

Furthermore, if there are sons or daughters of good family who uphold, read, recite, and practice this Prajñāpāramitā as it is taught, whether they are in an empty room, among a multitude, beneath a tree, in a wilderness, on a path, or off the path, even unto the great ocean—in such places, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—they will be free from all fears and protected by the devas.
At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are good men or good women who hear, receive, read, recite, and practice according to the instructions this *prajñāpāramitā*, we shall go to them to protect and mind them, causing them to remain diligent and never give rise to weariness or retreat.”
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are good men or good women who hear, receive, read, recite, and practice this Prajñāpāramitā as it has been taught, I too shall go to protect such persons and ensure they suffer no decline or affliction.”
At that time, the Great Brahma King, together with the assembly of Brahmās, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are good sons or good daughters who hear, receive, read, recite, and practice according to the instructions this Prajñāpāramitā, we shall go to protect those persons and ensure they suffer no decline or affliction.”
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is marvelous, World-Honored One!
This profound Prajñāpāramitā brings such merit in the present life to those sons and daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, and recite it.”
"How is it, World-Honored One?
If a person upholds this *prajñāpāramitā*, are they able to encompass all the other *pāramitās*?
The Buddha said:
“Kauśika! It is so! If a person upholds this Prajñāpāramitā, they are thereby able to encompass all the pāramitās.”
Kauśika! If there are those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this Prajñāpāramitā, their merit will be vast and profound.
You should listen attentively and apply your mind well; I shall explain it for you.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
I pray that you will proclaim it for us.”
The Buddha said,
“Kauśika! This Dharma-gate of my Prajñāpāramitā cannot be harmed, afflicted, or destroyed by any unwholesome dharmas.”
When any unwholesome states arise and one desires to produce harm or affliction, those states shall gradually extinguish themselves; though they may momentarily arise, they will not cause injury.
Why is this? Kauśika!

You should know that because of the power of the merit from upholding, reciting, and reading the Prajñāpāramitā, these good men and good women will cause even arisen unwholesome dharmas to naturally vanish and be extinguished.
Kauśika! It is as if there were various venomous snakes in the world wandering about in search of food; upon seeing small insects, they would wish to devour them.
At that time, there is a medicine called Majikī that can neutralize all poisons, and those small insects immediately go to where the medicine is.
At that time, upon smelling the scent of this medicine, the venomous snake immediately retreated of its own accord, and those small insects were no longer eaten by it.
Why is this? Because this Mañjiṣṭhā medicine is able to neutralize all poisons.

Kauśika! It is the same for sons and daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, and recite this Prajñāpāramitā, whether they explain it themselves or for others, and practice according to what they have taught. Such persons cannot be harmed by any unwholesome dharmas; even if unwholesome dharmas arise, they are immediately extinguished of their own accord.
Why is this? One should know that it is entirely due to the power of the merit of the *prajñāpāramitā* that it remains unmoved and unshakable in every place.
The *prajñāpāramitā* is able to eliminate all afflictions, such as greed, and can lead one to realize unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

Kauśika! If there are those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this Prajñāpāramitā, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, Mahābrahmā, and even all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will constantly protect such persons, ensuring they are free from decline and affliction.
