Chapter Five, Part Two: On Righteous Merit. "Furthermore, Kauśika!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct every single sentient being throughout Jambudvīpa, causing each of them to cultivate the four dhyānas, Kausika!
"What do you think? Would that person, by reason of this cause and condition, acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying, "Very much, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

Although these sons and daughters of good family obtain much merit by this cause and condition, it is not equal to that of someone who, regarding this *prajñāpāramitā*, gives rise to a mind of faith and understanding, gives rise to the bodhicitta, and abides in the dharma of a bodhisattva; who copies this *prajñāpāramitā* into a scroll, receives, maintains, reads, and recites it; who generates a heart of joy and expounds it for others, or further explains its meaning for others; who generates a pure heart toward this true dharma, becomes free from all doubt, and further exhorts others to receive and maintain it, saying:”
"O son of good family!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the path of the bodhisattva; you should train yourself within it according to what has been proclaimed."

One who trains in this manner is said to have attained the Dharma; such a person is able to swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and, exhausting the entire realm of sentient beings, cause them all to dwell peacefully in the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of true thusness (tathatā).
“Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family will acquire exceedingly great merit. Furthermore, Kauśika!”
Setting aside all the sentient beings who fill Jambudvīpa;
even if one were to fill the four great continents with sentient beings and instruct each of them to cultivate the four dhyānas, set that number aside as well;
even if one were to fill a small thousand-world system with sentient beings and instruct each of them to cultivate the four dhyānas, set that number aside too.
If all sentient beings filling a medium chiliocosm were each taught and led to practice the four dhyānas, that number would still be set aside;
if all sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm were each taught and led to practice the four dhyānas, that number would also be set aside;
and so on, even if all sentient beings filling as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were each taught and led to practice the four dhyānas.
"Kauśika! What do you think? Would that person, by reason of this cause and condition, acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very much so, World-Honored One! The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

Although these sons and daughters of good family obtain much merit by reason of this, it is not equal to that of someone who, regarding this *prajñāpāramitā*, gives rise to a mind of faith and understanding, gives rise to the bodhicitta, and abides in the dharma of a bodhisattva; who copies this *prajñāpāramitā* into a volume, receives, maintains, reads, and recites it; who generates a heart of joy and expounds it for others, or further explains its meaning for others; who generates a pure mind toward this true dharma, becomes free from all doubt, and further exhorts others to receive and maintain it, saying:
"O son of good family!..."
This Prajñāpāramitā is the path of the bodhisattva; you should train yourself within it exactly as it has been proclaimed.

One who trains in this way is said to have attained the Dharma, and shall swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, enabling them to bring the entire realm of sentient beings to rest universally within the reality-limit of true suchness (tathatā-bhūtakoṭi).
"Kauśika! You should know that such a person gains exceedingly great merit. Furthermore, Kauśika!"

Suppose all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa were each taught to cultivate the four immeasurable practices, the four formless absorptions, and even to universally practice all supernatural powers, Brahma-conduct, various dhyāna concentrations, and all meritorious deeds.
"Kauśika, what do you think? Would that person, by reason of this cause and condition, acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very much so, World-Honored One! The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

Although these sons and daughters of good family obtain much merit by reason of this cause and condition, it is not equal to that of someone who, regarding this *prajñāpāramitā*, gives rise to a mind of faith and understanding, gives rise to the bodhicitta, and abides in the dharma of a bodhisattva; who copies this *prajñāpāramitā* into a scroll, receives, maintains, reads, and recites it; who generates a heart of joy and expounds it for others, or further explains its meaning for others; who generates a pure mind toward this true dharma, becomes free from all doubt, and exhorts others to receive and maintain it, saying:
"O son of good family!..."
This Prajñāpāramitā is the path of the bodhisattva; you should train yourselves within it exactly as it has been proclaimed.

One who trains in this way is said to have attained the Dharma, and is able to swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), and is able to bring the entire realm of sentient beings to rest universally in the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of suchness (tathatā).
“Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family will obtain exceedingly great merit. Furthermore, Kauśika!”

Setting aside all these sentient beings who fill Jambudvīpa, suppose each were individually taught to cultivate immeasurable and boundless supernatural powers, pure conduct, various dhyāna concentrations, and various meritorious deeds.

Kauśika! Suppose there were as many sentient beings as fill the four great continents, or fill a small thousand-world system, or fill a medium two-thousand-world system, or fill a great trichiliocosm; and suppose each one were taught to cultivate immeasurable and boundless supernormal powers, the holy life of Brahma, various dhyāna-concentrations, and various meritorious deeds.
Kauśika, assign this same number to each and every one.

Suppose there were as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges filling a trichiliocosm, and you were to teach each of them to cultivate immeasurable and boundless supernormal powers, Brahma-conduct, various dhyāna-samādhis, and all manner of meritorious deeds.
"Kauśika! What do you think? Would this person, by reason of these causes and conditions, acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Very much so, World-Honored One! The Buddha said, "Kauśika!

Although these sons and daughters of good family obtain much merit by reason of this, it is not equal to that of someone who, regarding this *prajñāpāramitā*, gives rise to a mind of faith and understanding, gives rise to the bodhicitta, and abides in the dharma of a bodhisattva; who copies this *prajñāpāramitā* into a scroll, receives, upholds, reads, and recites it; who gives rise to a heart of joy and expounds it for others, or further explains its meaning for others; who generates a pure mind toward this true Dharma, becomes free from all doubt, and exhorts others to receive and uphold it, saying:
"O son of good family!..."
This Prajñāpāramitā is the path of the bodhisattvas; you should train yourselves within it exactly as it has been proclaimed.

One who trains in this manner is said to have attained the Dharma, and shall swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), enabling all realms of sentient beings to universally abide in the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of True Suchness (tathatā).
"Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family will gain exceedingly great merit. Furthermore, Kauśika!"

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to write out this Prajñāpāramitā as a scroll, personally uphold, read, and recite it, and further exhort others to do the same, they would indeed acquire great merit.
It is not as good as someone using this Dharma-door of the *prajñāpāramitā* to extensively explain its meaning for others. Kauśika!
You should know that such sons and daughters of good family will obtain far more merit.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what kind of persons should this Prajñāpāramitā be explained?”
The Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
"If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who are unable to fully comprehend this Prajñāpāramitā, you should explain it to them."
Why is this? Kauśika! In future ages, there will be those who preach a counterfeit Prajñāpāramitā.

If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to proceed toward the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet hear this counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā* and study within it, they will become confused and will not have correct understanding.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In future ages, how shall that counterfeit Prajñāpāramitā be described?”
Furthermore, how can one fully discern and understand them?
The Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying: “Kauśika!
In future ages, there will be bhikṣus who speak thus: "Form is impermanent;
whether body or mind, as well as ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom, all are non-existent and devoid of all objects of observation."
"One who speaks thus should be known as one who speaks a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*.
Kauśika, what is called a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*?"

He says this: "By disintegrating form, one contemplates the impermanence of form; by disintegrating feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, one contemplates the impermanence of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. To seek in this manner is to practice the perfection of wisdom."
"Kauśika! You should know that all such explanations are termed 'semblance prajñāpāramitā. Kauśika!"

You should now know this: one contemplates the impermanence of form by not destroying form; one contemplates the impermanence of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness by not destroying feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
To speak in this way is to proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* according to reality.
Kauśika, for this reason,

if a son of good family or a daughter of good family can explain the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* to others according to reality, you should know that such a son or daughter of good family gains exceedingly great merit.

"Furthermore, Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to cause all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa to universally abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna)."
"Kauśika! What do you think?
By this cause and condition, would that son of good family or daughter of good family acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

This Prajñāpāramitā is the path of the bodhisattvas; you should train yourselves within it exactly as it has been proclaimed.

One who trains in this manner is said to have attained the Dharma, and shall swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), enabling all realms of sentient beings to universally abide in the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of suchness (tathatā).
“Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family will gain exceedingly great merit. Why is this?
All the fruits of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) are born from this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Kausika!
As previously stated, suppose a person were to cause all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa to universally abide in the fruit of stream-entry; let alone the merit produced by such an act.

Kauśika! Suppose there were as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges filling a trichiliocosm, and you were to cause them all to dwell securely in the fruit of a srotāpanna.
“Kauśika! What do you think? Would that person, by reason of this, obtain much merit?

It is as it has arisen, and it is attained in accordance with reality. "Furthermore, Kausika!

Suppose all sentient beings throughout Jambudvipa were to resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; and suppose there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, having transcribed this Prajñāpāramitā into a volume, were to bestow it universally upon them all so that they might receive and uphold it."

It is not as good as someone who, by means of this *prajñāpāramitā*, writes out the scriptural volume and gives it to a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in non-retrogression, so that they may practice in accordance with this *prajñāpāramitā*, becoming firm, increasing, vast, and perfect, thereby accomplishing the Buddha-dharma.
Kauśika! You should know that these sons and daughters of good family will obtain exceedingly great merit. Why is this?
This is because this *prajñāpāramitā* gives birth to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Kausika! As previously stated, even if all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa were to resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, let alone count them as such.

Suppose that all sentient beings—whether filling the four great continents, or filling a small thousand-world system, or filling a medium thousand-world system, or filling a great trichiliocosm, or even filling as many great trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—were all to resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to transcribe this Prajñāpāramitā into a volume and universally bestow it upon all beings so that they may receive and uphold it.

Kauśika! It would not be as meritorious for someone to write out this Prajñāpāramitā in a volume and give it to a single bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells in the stage of non-retrogression, so that he may practice in accordance with this Prajñāpāramitā, becoming firm in his cultivation, increasing, and fully accomplishing the vast and perfect Buddha-dharmas.
Kauśika! You should know that these sons and daughters of good family will acquire exceedingly great merit. Why is this?
This is because this *prajñāpāramitā* gives birth to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. "Furthermore, Kauśika,
suppose all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa were to abide entirely on the stage of non-retrogression."
If there are good sons or good daughters who, by means of this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā, universally explain its meaning for the sake of all beings.
“Kauśika! What do you think? Would this person, by reason of this cause and condition, acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The merit obtained by these good sons and good daughters is even more vast, immeasurable, and boundless than before, such that it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.”
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

Although this person gains much merit by such causes and conditions, it is not equal to that of someone who, for the sake of one person seeking to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, explains the meaning of this Dharma-door of the *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this latter person gains far more merit.”

Kauśika! As previously stated, suppose all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa were to dwell on the stage of non-retrogression; even if someone were to explain their meaning to them all, let alone set aside that number.

Suppose that all sentient beings filling the four great continents, or filling a small thousand-world system, or filling a medium thousand-world system, or filling a great trichiliocosm, or even filling as many great trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, were all established in the stage of non-retrogression.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to universally explain the meaning of this Dharma-gate of the Perfection of Wisdom for the sake of all beings, Kausika!
"What do you think? Would this person, by reason of this cause and condition, obtain much merit?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One! [He would obtain much merit]."
"The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is immeasurable and boundless; it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
The Buddha said, "Kauśika!"

Although this person gains much merit by these causes and conditions, it is not equal to that of someone who, for the sake of one person seeking to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, explains the meaning of this Dharma-door of the *prajñāpāramitā*; you should know that such a person gains far more merit.
Kauśika! Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice and study this perfection of wisdom, they swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas accord with and turn according to the *prajñāpāramitā*, they draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Because one draws near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one should receive the *prajñāpāramitā* according to the instruction.
Because one receives it as instructed, one draws near to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Therefore, one should provide various offerings of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Whatever meritorious deeds one performs accordingly, the merit one obtains will be immeasurable and boundless.
"Why is this? Because one draws near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and achieves all-knowledge.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti praised Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!
You have skillfully guided all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and you are further able to protect and sustain them.”

Kauśika! All the disciples of the Buddha protect and mindfully attend to all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas by means of the dharma of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, causing them to resolve upon the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and causing them to abide in the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Why is this? Because all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, by virtue of training in these six pāramitās, gave rise to the bodhicitta and abided in the fruit of bodhi; the present Buddha, the World-Honored One, likewise attained the fruit of bodhi by training in these six pāramitās; and all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the future shall do the same.
Therefore, Kauśika, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in these six pāramitās, they will be unable to attain the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma (Shi Hu), Dharma Master and Imperially Appointed Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, during the Western Heavens (India). Chapter Six: Dedication through Rejoicing, Part One. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:

"If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva rejoices in and dedicates the merit obtained from this profound *prajñāpāramitā* dharma-gate, that merit is the most supreme, the most ultimate, the most excellent, and the most wondrous compared to the merit of other sentient beings’ giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation of concentration; it is vast, immeasurable, peerless, and equal to the unequaled."
"Therefore, regarding this profound and true Dharma, one should rejoice and dedicate [the merit] in accordance with reality.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in all places throughout the ten directions, [encounters] the immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless..."
In inconceivable and incalculable trichiliocosms, within each and every world,
there have been past Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas— immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless— who have already entered parinirvāṇa;
from the time these Tathāgatas first resolved their minds toward awakening until they achieved *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*— all such Tathāgatas...
Having attained the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and entered the realm of great *nirvāṇa* without remainder—

until the eventual extinction of the Dharma— in the interval between these events, all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, possess the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*), the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*),

the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*), the aggregate of liberation (*vimukti-skandha*), the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha*), and their six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*).
Roots of goodness associated with the *pāramitās*, roots of goodness associated with the merits of all Buddhas,
roots of goodness associated with the vast supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the *pāramitās* of skillful means, vows, power, and wisdom,

roots of goodness born from being associated with the correct practice of the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), and even those associated with great loving-kindness and great compassion that are immeasurable and boundless— ...
It is the mass of the Buddha’s merits that brings about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.

All such Dharma-gates of the *pāramitās* give rise to all supreme supernormal powers, the various practices free from hindrances and attachments, the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge as it truly is—which is invincible, peerless, immeasurable, and beyond all observation—as well as the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, up to and including the complete fulfillment of the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and all gates of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

All Tathāgatas turn the great wheel of Dharma, hold aloft the great torch of Dharma, beat the great drum of Dharma, blow the great conch of Dharma, perform the great music of Dharma, rain down the great rain of Dharma, and realize the great wisdom of Dharma; they bestow the great wealth of Dharma upon all sentient beings, preaching the teachings of the Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Śrāvakas, universally causing all sentient beings to cultivate and study therein all supreme roots of goodness.

Furthermore, it includes the roots of goodness associated with the six pāramitās belonging to those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas for whom those Buddhas have conferred the prediction that they shall attain the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, for those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, he bestows the prediction of their enlightenment as pratyekabuddhas, and [includes] all their roots of goodness.
Moreover, there are those of the Śrāvaka vehicle who possess the merit of practicing generosity, maintaining ethical discipline, and cultivating meditative concentration.
Furthermore, there are the untainted roots of goodness of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and the untainted roots of goodness of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Moreover, there are all the roots of goodness planted by foolish ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*), as well as the merits of giving, maintaining ethical discipline, and cultivating meditative concentration performed by the fourfold assembly—monks (*bhikṣu*), nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), laymen (*upāsaka*), and laywomen (*upāsikā*).

Even gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as various species of animals, have planted roots of goodness by hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma.
Furthermore, from the time until after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, all sentient beings plant roots of goodness within the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
All such various roots of goodness and various merits—whether their nature be finite or infinite—are gathered together, combined, calculated, and measured.
Those who practice as Bodhisattvas, with a mind that is supreme, ultimate, most excellent, most wondrous, vast, immeasurable, unequalled, and equal to the unequaled, rejoice in all of them.
Dedicating these merits of sympathetic joy toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one should speak thus:
"By means of these roots of goodness, may I attain the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Furthermore, for this practitioner of the bodhisattva path, all conditions, all matters, and all marks arise from the mind; can they be apprehended as the mind grasps their marks?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying: "No, Subhūti!
All conditions, all phenomena, and all marks arise from the mind; just as the mind grasps at marks, none of them can be apprehended."
Subhūti again addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:

"If all conditions, all objects, and all marks are as they are grasped by the mind and yet cannot be found, would this person not possess an inversion of perception, an inversion of mind, and an inversion of view?"
Why is this? Because there is that which arises.

To regard the impermanent as permanent, suffering as pleasure, the impure as pure, and the non-self as self; and to regard a mind of doubt as right reflection—by these means, one’s perceptions, thoughts, and views all become inverted.
If one abides in the reality of each and every condition, object, and characteristic exactly as it is, then there is neither that which arises nor that which is grasped.
Because of this, the mental factors are likewise, all phenomena are likewise, and awakening is likewise.
If all conditions, all objects, and all marks, as well as awakening and the mind, are all without distinction, then upon what object would one take up what mark?
And with what mind should one rejoice in merit?
"Furthermore, by what roots of goodness are these dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Regarding the dedication you have described, this method of dedication should not be explained in such a manner to bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds."

Why is this? Because if they were to hear this teaching, all their faith, understanding, affection, reverence, and pure mind would be entirely obscured and extinguished; for this reason, one should not speak of it to them.

If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abiding in non-retrogression who follow spiritual friends, one should proclaim this teaching to them; having heard this Dharma, those bodhisattvas will not be startled, nor terrified, nor will they fall back or sink into despondency.
"In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to truly dedicate the merit of sympathetic joy toward that omniscience.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:
"If a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and a mind of dedication, such a mind is exhausted, extinguished, and detached; by what mind, then, can one practice sympathetic joy?"
Furthermore, with what mind does one perform the dedication toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
If it is by means of a mind that one can dedicate, these two minds do not coexist and neither exists;
if it is by the intrinsic nature of the various minds, they likewise cannot perform the dedication.
"By means of what mind, then, can one perform this dedication?
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"If there are bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, upon hearing such a teaching, will they not be struck with fear, alarm, or despondency?"
"Venerable One!
What now is 'rejoicing in accordance with reality' and 'dedicating in accordance with reality'?
How should one properly rejoice in the Dharma?"
"Furthermore, what is this mind of dedication?
At that time, by the power of the majestic empowerment of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:

"All Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have already fully practiced the path of all past Buddhas; they have extinguished conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), removed the thorns, laid down their heavy burdens, and attained great and wholesome benefits. All fetters of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*) have been completely exhausted; their right knowledge is unimpeded, their minds have attained mastery, and all mental states are perfectly tranquil."
These bodhisattvas, in every single one of the infinite and countless trichiliocosm worlds throughout the ten directions,
[venerate] all the past Tathāgatas who have already entered parinirvāṇa—
those Tathāgatas from their first generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*...
Having attained the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and entered the realm of great *nirvāṇa* without remainder—
until the eventual extinction of the Dharma— all the roots of goodness associated with the *pāramitās* belonging to all those Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, during that interval,
as well as their various roots of goodness consisting of meritorious conduct, and the precepts and meditative concentrations of those Buddhas...
...the aggregates of wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; all roots of goodness;
up to the immeasurable and boundless mass of Buddha-merits consisting of great loving-kindness and great compassion that benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings;
and the various Dharma-gates taught by the Buddha.
All sentient beings train therein, having faith, understanding, and dwelling securely in all their roots of virtue;

as well as the roots of virtue associated with the six *pāramitās* belonging to those bodhisattvas for whom the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has bestowed the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, he bestows the prediction of enlightenment upon those of the pratyekabuddha vehicle for their pratyekabuddha path, and [includes] all their roots of goodness.

Moreover, there are those of the śrāvaka vehicle who practice generosity, maintain ethical discipline, and cultivate meditative concentration; he includes all such merits, as well as the untainted roots of goodness of both those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Furthermore, there are all the roots of goodness planted by ignorant ordinary beings, as well as those planted by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, and even by various species of animals who have heard the Buddha preach the Dharma.
Even including all the roots of goodness planted by all sentient beings after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa—
such various roots of goodness and various merits as these, combined, gathered together, calculated, and measured.
Each of these bodhisattvas rejoices accordingly, and by means of this merit of rejoicing, they dedicate it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Maitreya!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva performs such a dedication, how can they avoid falling into the inversion of perception, the inversion of mind, and the inversion of view?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva brings forth a mind of sympathetic joy and performs dedication, he does not give rise to the thought of 'mind' within that mind; he knows the mind as it truly is, without any grasped characteristics."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can dedicate such merit of sympathetic joy toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will immediately attain non-falling away from errors of perception, mind, and view.

If, moreover, one does not know the mind as it truly is, and dedicates [merit] with the notion of attainment, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is unable to remain far removed from the perversions of perception, mind, and view.

Furthermore, if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dedicate with a mind that perceives existence, that mind is itself exhausted, extinguished, and detached; and that exhausted and extinguished mind cannot perform dedication.
If one performs dedication with a mind of non-apprehension, this is precisely dedication in accordance with the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Because phenomena are dedicated in this way, the *dharmatā* is likewise;
because the *dharmatā* is dedicated in this way, all phenomena are likewise.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can dedicate in this manner, this constitutes right dedication and is not called wrong dedication.
Regarding this method of dedication, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should train in this way.
"Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva rejoices in and dedicates their roots of goodness in the same manner as the past buddhas have done."
If one has fully cultivated the path of all future Buddhas, having extinguished conceptual proliferation, one attains great and sublime benefit.
These Tathāgatas, from their initial generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, have already entered the realm of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

From now until the disappearance of the Dharma, all the roots of goodness associated with the perfections of all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, during that interval; as well as the roots of goodness of those Buddhas' aggregates of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; even their great love and great compassion, which bring immeasurable and boundless benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; the mass of the Buddhas' merits; and the various Dharma gates taught by the Buddhas.
All the roots of goodness of all sentient beings who train therein, develop faith and understanding, and abide [in this teaching];

as well as all the roots of goodness associated with the six *pāramitās* belonging to those bodhisattvas for whom the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has bestowed the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, for those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, he bestows the prediction of their enlightenment as Pratyekabuddhas, and [includes] all their roots of goodness.

Moreover, there are those of the Śrāvaka vehicle who practice generosity, maintain ethical discipline, and cultivate meditative concentration—all such roots of goodness, as well as the untainted roots of goodness of those in training (śaikṣa) and the untainted roots of goodness of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Furthermore, there are all the roots of goodness planted by foolish ordinary beings;
even those planted by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and various species of animals who have heard the Buddha preach the Dharma.
Even including all the roots of goodness planted by all sentient beings after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa—
such various roots of goodness and various merits, all combined, gathered together, calculated, and weighed.
Each of these bodhisattvas rejoices accordingly, and by means of this merit of rejoicing, they dedicate it toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Venerable Subhūti!

When that bodhisattva employs the mind of sympathetic joy and performs dedication, if within that mind no mental conception arises, and they know the mind as it truly is—without any grasped characteristics—and can thus dedicate the merit of such sympathetic joy toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, then this bodhisattva attains non-falling away from the inversions of perception, mind, and view.

If, moreover, one does not know the mind as it truly is, but dedicates with the notion of attainment, that bodhisattva is unable to distance themselves from the inversions of perception, mind, and view.
Furthermore, if bodhisattvas dedicate with a mind that perceives existence, that mind is itself exhausted, extinguished, and detached; that exhausted and extinguished mind cannot perform dedication.
If one dedicates with a mind of non-apprehension, this is precisely dedicating in accordance with the reality of the dharma-nature;
because the dharma is thus dedicated, the dharma-nature is likewise so; and because the dharma-nature is thus dedicated, all dharmas are likewise so.
If one dedicates in this manner, it is called right dedication and is not termed wrong dedication.
"Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva rejoices in and dedicates roots of goodness in the same way as all future buddhas do."

Regarding all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, of the present—from their first generation of the mind of awakening until their achievement of the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, through their entry into the realm of great *nirvāṇa* without remainder, and until the extinction of the Dharma—all the roots of goodness of these World-Honored Buddhas during that interval, as well as all the roots of goodness planted by all sentient beings after the Tathāgatas have entered *nirvāṇa*: such various roots of goodness and various merits are combined, gathered together, calculated, and measured.
Each of these bodhisattvas rejoices; by means of this merit of rejoicing, they dedicate it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Venerable Subhūti!

When that bodhisattva employs the mind of sympathetic joy and performs the dedication, within that mind he does not give rise to the thought of "mind"; he knows the mind as it truly is, without any grasped characteristics.
If one can thus rejoice in such merit and dedicate it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, that bodhisattva will immediately attain non-falling away from errors of perception, mind, and view.
If, moreover, one performs dedication with a mind that perceives something as existing, that bodhisattva cannot remain far removed from the inversions of perception, mind, and view.

When that bodhisattva mahāsattva knows, in accordance with reality, the mind used for dedication, that very mind is exhausted, extinguished, and detached; and that exhausted and extinguished mind cannot perform dedication.
If one performs dedication with a mind of non-apprehension, this is precisely dedication in accordance with the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Because phenomena are dedicated in this way, the *dharmatā* is likewise;
because the *dharmatā* is dedicated in this way, all phenomena are likewise.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding such dharmas of the past, future, and present, is able to know them as they truly are and dedicate them as they truly are, this is called right dedication; it is not called wrong dedication.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to dedicate [roots of goodness] to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment as it truly is, they should contemplate all phenomena as being like space, free from all marks."

Why is this? If one understands all phenomena as they truly are, there is neither mind nor non-mind that acts as the knower, and there is neither phenomenon nor non-phenomenon that serves as the characteristic of the known.

If a bodhisattva is able to dedicate within such dharmas as these, this is called the supreme dedication; for this reason, they are named a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who correctly cultivates meritorious conduct.
Why is this? Because all various phenomena and various practices are quiescent, so too is the dedication of all merit from sympathetic joy toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If one knows, as it truly is, that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are quiescent and immovable, then this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fulfill the skillful means (*upāya*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Regarding all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) following the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, the World-Honored One—whether their substance, their characteristics, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or their dharma-nature (*dharmatā*)—he knows them all as they truly are, and is thus able to dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because all the dharmas of corresponding practice belonging to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not belong to the three periods of time.
If they belong to the past, those dharmas have already been departed from, already ceased, and already exhausted.
If it refers to the future world, that which is yet to come has not arrived;
if it refers to the present world, it does not abide even now, and furthermore, nothing can be apprehended therein, for it is not a characteristic of an objective realm.

If one grasps at signs, one dwells in a state of inequality associated with wrong mindfulness regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, giving rise to thoughts of doubt and uncertainty; unable to abide in right mindfulness and right intention, one engages in perverse thoughts and reflections. In this way, it cannot be called dedication toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all roots of goodness, maintains no grasping at signs and a mind of non-apprehension, and dedicates with such a mind, this is dedication toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Bodhisattvas should train in this method of dedication.
If they train in this way, they will be able to fulfill skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
If their roots of goodness are dedicated with such skillful means, they will draw near to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to practice and study these skillful means, they should listen to, receive, read, recite, memorize, contemplate, and ponder this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā; they should inquire about its meaning and, having understood it as it is, explain it extensively to others—this is the skillful means of the Prajñāpāramitā.
If one does not obtain the skillful means of the Prajñāpāramitā, one will be unable to dedicate all roots of goodness toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Because the mark of self has already been extinguished and all conditioned phenomena have already become tranquil; one is far removed from various notions of attainment.

If, moreover, there is a person who gives rise to grasping at marks regarding all dharmas and falls into views of doubt, being unable to dwell securely within the dharma as it truly is, they will give rise to a notion of attainment regarding the dharma as it truly is.
If one dedicates such roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, will neither grant their seal of approval nor rejoice therein.

Why is this? Such dedication is called "great greed"; it gives rise to a mind of doubt regarding all phenomena, fails to attain tranquility amidst various signs, and produces the notion of attainment.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha does not say that it brings great benefit; rather, this dedication is called "mixed with poison" and is characterized by suffering and affliction.
For example, there may be a meal of supreme flavor in the world, complete with every excellence of form, fragrance, and taste, yet that food is mixed with poison.
Those who possess wisdom, knowing it is adulterated with poison, do not take it; but those who are foolish and ignorant, being unable to discern this, simply take and eat it.

When they first eat, although the color, fragrance, and delicious flavor are pleasing and delightful, once the power of the food has been digested, the retribution of suffering manifests; for this reason, they proceed toward the end of their lives.

"Venerable Subhūti! You should know now that it is likewise for those who, while possessing roots of goodness through sympathetic joy and having generated the mind of dedication, are nonetheless unable to receive, uphold, read, or recite the Prajñāpāramitā."

Why is this? Because they lack the skillful means (*upāya*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they cannot comprehend the profound and correct meaning, and thus they are unable to abide securely on the path of reality as it is.
Not understanding those dharmas as they truly are, they in turn teach them to others, saying:
"O son of good family!

You should [take] all the roots of goodness consisting of the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present; as well as all the merits belonging to those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, present, and future—from their first generation of the mind until their attainment of the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and including everything up to their entry into the realm of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*."
Furthermore, there are the roots of goodness possessed by all those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas for whom he has bestowed the prediction that they shall attain the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Furthermore, he bestows the prediction of enlightenment upon those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; he also [dedicates] all the roots of goodness belonging to those Pratyekabuddhas, as well as the roots of goodness from the practice of giving, morality, and so forth by those Śrāvakas.

From the time after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa until the extinction of the Dharma, whatever roots of goodness have been planted during that interval— even including the roots of goodness possessed by foolish ordinary beings—

all such various roots of goodness and various merits, when combined, gathered together, calculated, and measured, whether they appear as finite or infinite, you all should rejoice in each and every one of them.
"By means of these roots of goodness from sympathetic joy, one dedicates them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Subhūti! If that person were to speak thus, encouraging others to perform such sympathetic joy and dedication, it would be like mixing various poisons into delicious food; this method of dedication is called 'poisoned by admixture' and is characterized by suffering and affliction."
Those who practice as bodhisattvas should not even give rise to this mind of dedication regarding their own conduct, much less encourage others in such a way to cultivate this dharma.
If one grasps these characteristics as being real, it is not called rejoicing in the merits of all Buddhas, nor is it called upholding them, nor is it called dedicating them.

If bodhisattvas desire to truly rejoice in all the supreme roots of goodness belonging to all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, and truly dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should follow the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; just as the Buddha’s eye observes with reality, and just as the Buddha’s wisdom understands with reality, they should understand with reality that regarding all roots of goodness—whether their substance, their characteristics, their intrinsic nature, or their dharma-nature—they are unarisen and unobtainable.
If one can thus rejoice in these roots of goodness, it is approved by the Buddha and the Buddha also rejoices in it.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas rejoice in this manner, it is a correct rejoicing; dedicating these roots of goodness toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is what the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha most highly praises.
Such dedication is called the Great Dedication; it is perfectly fulfilled within the *dharmadhātu*, and the inner mind is pure, liberated, and unimpeded.

Furthermore, sons of good family who practice the Bodhisattva vehicle and cultivate this method of dedication do so with respect to all the morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas—without attachment or clinging. They are not bound to the desire realm, not bound to the form realm, and not bound to the formless realm; nor are they bound to the three periods of time—past, future, and present; they are not bound to any phenomena, nor are they bound to the dharma of dedication. Having understood this, the practitioner of the Bodhisattva path does not destroy the dharma of dedication.
This is the great dedication, which skillfully attains the perfection of dedicating within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Such dedication does not grasp at any signs; being free from erroneous dharmas, it is called "right dedication."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha truly authenticates and likewise rejoices in this.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this manner.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Venerable Subhūti, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”
You have performed the Buddha-work well, for you are able to inquire about this meaning on behalf of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Subhūti!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can thus dedicate [their merit] to the dharma-realm and the dharma-nature, just as the knowledge and vision of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they will realize all roots of goodness as they truly are—whether in terms of their substance, their characteristics, their self-nature, or their dharma-nature—and they will understand that they are neither produced nor can they be apprehended.
Thus, I authorize this dedication, and I too rejoice in such a mass of merit, which is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable. Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings throughout the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system were each to cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action; the mass of merit they would obtain would be exceedingly vast.

Furthermore, when this bodhisattva mahāsattva generates the most supreme mind and dedicates it to the dharma-realm, the mass of merit therein is, compared to the previous mass of merit, the most exalted, the most ultimate, the most superior, and the most wondrous; it is vast, immeasurable, unequalled, and equal to the unequaled.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Let us set aside this number for a moment.

Suppose all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm were each to cultivate the four immeasurable practices, and each were to attain the four dhyāna concentrations, the four formless absorptions, and the five supernormal powers; the amount of such meritorious action would be exceedingly vast."

Furthermore, when this bodhisattva-mahāsattva generates the most supreme mind and dedicates all their accumulations of merit toward the dharma-realm, these compared to the previous accumulations of merit are the most superior, the most ultimate, the most excellent, and the most wondrous—vast, immeasurable, unequalled, and equal to the unequaled.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīlagupta (Shihu), Imperially Conferred Title of Dharma-Master, Purple Robe Awardee, and Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices during the Song Dynasty. By Imperial Decree. Chapter Six, Part Two: Rejoicing and Dedication. "Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
Setting aside the aforementioned four immeasurable practices up to the five supernormal powers,
and even if every single sentient being in the trichiliocosm were to attain the fruits of stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, and arhat— setting aside this mass of merit as well.

Suppose all sentient beings in the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system were each to attain the fruit of a pratyekabuddha; even such a mass of merit would be included within this calculation.

Subhūti! Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to each resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; these sentient beings would then be called bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds.

Furthermore, in each and every one of these kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, this bodhisattva universally bestows food, clothing, bedding, medicine, and other articles of pleasure upon all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
When these bodhisattvas practice such giving, they each give rise to the most supreme and exalted mind and conceive a sense of profound respect.
Subhūti, what do you think? Would these bodhisattvas acquire much merit?
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
“It is very much so, World-Honored One!
This mass of merit is immeasurable and incalculable, without limit; it cannot be reached by any calculation, numerical fraction, analogy, or even by the *upaniṣad* (proportional) fraction.”
The Buddha said, “No, Subhūti!

If there are sons of good family who abide in the bodhisattva vehicle and practice the skillful means of this *prajñāpāramitā*, being protected by the *prajñāpāramitā*, and are able to dedicate even a small root of virtue toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they are dedicating in accordance with reality to the *dharmadhātu*.

When this mass of merit resulting from such dedication is compared to the mass of merit from the previous bodhisattva’s giving, the latter does not equal even one hundredth part of it; it does not equal one thousandth, ten thousandth, billionth, nayuta-th part, nor even an *upaniṣad*-part. It does not come close to even a fraction of it.

Why is this? Because these roots of merit from the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā* surpass the practice of giving performed by previous bodhisattvas with a mind of grasping; therefore, this mass of merit cannot be compared to them.

At that time, there were twenty thousand sons of gods from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings present in the Buddha’s assembly. Hearing these words, they joined their palms in reverence and together addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the skillful means of this *prajñāpāramitā* and is protected by the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to dedicate their roots of goodness toward that omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) as it truly is. Such a dedication is a "great dedication," and the mass of merit obtained thereby surpasses the mass of merit from the giving of a bodhisattva who possesses a mind of grasping.

At that time, there were one hundred thousand devaputras from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven who immediately rained down various celestial flowers, celestial incense, unguents, and powdered incense, as well as various other kinds of banners, pennants, precious parasols, exquisite celestial music, and even all manner of jewel-adorned celestial garments and divine treasures. With such offerings, they paid reverent homage and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices skillful means in this Prajñāpāramitā and is protected by the Prajñāpāramitā, they can dedicate their roots of goodness to the dharmadhātu; such a dedication is a "great dedication," and the mass of merit obtained thereby surpasses the mass of merit from the giving of a bodhisattva who possesses a mind of grasping.
"Bhagavān! We, the assembly of devaputras, all give rise to the most supreme mind toward such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, honoring, making offerings to, respecting, and praising them."
When those sons of the gods uttered these words, their voices were heard throughout all worlds.

At that time, there were one hundred thousand sons of the gods in the Yāma Heaven, one hundred thousand sons of the gods in the Tuṣita Heaven, one hundred thousand sons of the gods in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and one hundred thousand sons of the gods in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; such was the assembly of sons of the gods from the various heavens of the desire realm.

Furthermore, among the various hosts of devaputras in the heavens of the Form Realm—namely, the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahmā, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha—heavenly beings each joined their palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the skillful means of this *prajñāpāramitā* and is protected by the *prajñāpāramitā*, they can dedicate their roots of goodness to the *dharmadhātu*; such a dedication surpasses the mass of merit from the giving of a bodhisattva who possesses a mind of grasping.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the devaputras of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens and others, saying:

"As previously stated, let us set aside for a moment the measure of merit from all the bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds throughout the trichiliocosm, each of whom extensively bestowed gifts upon sentient beings for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges."
"O Son of Heaven!

Suppose all sentient beings in as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were each to resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Each of these bodhisattvas who have thus resolved their minds were to give, throughout as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, food, drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and all other articles of pleasure, universally bestowing them upon all sentient beings in as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the skillful means of this *prajñāpāramitā* and is protected by the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to take all the roots of goodness of the past, future, and present Buddhas—namely, their aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—as well as the roots of goodness of the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas; having combined, gathered, calculated, and measured these various roots of goodness, they rejoice in them with a mind that is supreme, ultimate, most excellent, most wondrous, vast, immeasurable, unequaled, and equal to the unequaled. With these roots of goodness born of such rejoicing, they dedicate them truly toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Subhūti! This accumulation of merit from such sympathetic joy on the part of this bodhisattva, compared to the meritorious conduct of giving by the former bodhisattva, does not equal even one hundredth part of it; it does not equal one thousandth part, nor ten-thousandth, nor a hundred-millionth (*koṭi*), nor a *nayuta*, nor even an *upaniṣad* part of it. It does not equal even a fraction thereof.

"Why is this? Because those who possess the skillful means (*upāya*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) surpass the former bodhisattvas' practice of giving performed with a mind that grasps at something.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As the Buddha has said, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā* and is protected by the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able, with a mind that is supreme, most extreme, most excellent, most wondrous, vast, immeasurable, unequaled, and equal to the unequaled, to truly rejoice in all roots of goodness and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
World-Honored One!
How should one understand that which is the most supreme, the most ultimate, even unto the unequaled mind?
Furthermore, what is meant by rejoicing in accordance with reality?

The Buddha told Subhūti: “If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all phenomena of the past, future, and present, neither grasps nor rejects them; is without thought and without attainment; is free from all doubt and does not give rise to discrimination—[seeing that] there are no past phenomena already arisen and already ceased, no future phenomena yet to arise and yet to cease, and no present phenomena arising and ceasing at this very moment—then they should contemplate all phenomena as being like space: free from all marks, unmoving, unarisen and unceasing, neither coming nor going. The characteristics of those phenomena are the very nature of phenomena; they should rejoice in accordance with reality according to that dharma-nature, and their dedication of merit should likewise be in accordance with that rejoicing.”

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva is able to give rise to this mind regarding all phenomena, it is called the most supreme, the most ultimate, the most excellent, the most wondrous, the vast, the immeasurable, the unequaled, and the mind equal to the unequaled.
If one rejoices with this very mind, it can be called rejoicing in accordance with reality.
To dedicate these roots of goodness born of such rejoicing toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is therefore called dedication in accordance with reality.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! As previously stated, suppose all the bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds toward enlightenment in as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River were each to practice the perfection of giving for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—let alone setting aside that number."

Subhūti! If all sentient beings in as many trichiliocosm great thousandfold world systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River were to each give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Each of these bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds toward awakening shall, throughout as many *gaṅgā* sands of eons as there are, practice the pure precepts—the good deeds of body, the good deeds of speech, and the good deeds of mind—and those bodhisattvas shall maintain such discipline for as many *gaṅgā* sands of eons as there are, without giving rise to any transgression.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the skillful means of this *prajñāpāramitā* and is protected by the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to take all the roots of goodness of the past, future, and present Buddhas—namely, their aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—as well as the roots of goodness of the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas; having thus combined, gathered, reckoned, and measured these various roots of goodness, they rejoice in them all with a mind that is supreme, ultimate, most excellent, most wondrous, vast, immeasurable, unequaled, and equal to the unequaled.
By means of this root of goodness born of sympathetic joy, one dedicates it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Subhūti! This mass of merit from such sympathetic joy by a bodhisattva, compared to the previous bodhisattva’s meritorious conduct of maintaining the precepts, does not equal even one part in a hundred; it does not equal one part in a thousand, ten thousand, a billion (*koṭi*), or a hundred billion (*nayuta*); indeed, it does not equal even one part in an *upaniṣad* fraction.
Why is this? Because one who is fully endowed with the skillful means (*upāya*) of the *prajñāpāramitā* surpasses the previous bodhisattvas who observe the precepts with a mind of grasping.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

Suppose all the bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds toward enlightenment throughout as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River were each to maintain pure conduct for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; let alone such a number.

Subhūti! Suppose all sentient beings in as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River were to each resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Each of these bodhisattvas who have thus resolved would, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, practice the perfection of patience—neither being angry nor resentful, and not giving rise to any evil thoughts whatsoever. Throughout those eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, these bodhisattvas would maintain such patience and never give way to anger or resentment.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the skillful means of this *prajñāpāramitā* and is protected by this *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to take all the roots of goodness of the past, future, and present Buddhas—namely, the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—as well as the roots of goodness of the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas; having thus combined, gathered, reckoned, and measured these various roots of goodness, they rejoice in them all with a mind that is supreme, ultimate, most excellent, most wondrous, vast, immeasurable, peerless, and equal to the unequaled.
By means of these roots of goodness born of sympathetic joy, they dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Subhūti! Compared to the previous bodhisattva’s meritorious practice of patience, this mass of merit from such sympathetic joy does not even equal a hundredth part of it; it does not equal a thousandth part, nor a ten-thousandth, nor a billionth, nor a *koṭi*, nor a *nayuta* part; indeed, it does not even equal a *upaniṣad* part of it.

Why is this? Because one who is fully endowed with the skillful means (*upāya*) of the *prajñāpāramitā* surpasses the previous bodhisattvas’ practice of patience (*kṣānti*) performed with a mind that grasps at something. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

Suppose all the bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds toward enlightenment throughout as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River were each to practice the perfection of patience for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; let alone that number.
Subhūti! Suppose all sentient beings in as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River were each to resolve their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Each of these bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds upon awakening practices the perfection of vigor throughout as many *gaṅgā* sands of eons as there are—courageous, firm, non-retrogressive, and unfailing, remaining far removed from sloth, torpor, and all obstructive dharmas—and throughout those *gaṅgā* sands of eons, these bodhisattvas do not give rise to weariness or regression in such vigor.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the skillful means of this *prajñāpāramitā* and is protected by this *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to take all the roots of goodness of the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as the roots of goodness of the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—having thus combined, gathered, calculated, and measured these various roots of goodness—they rejoice in them with a mind that is supreme, ultimate, most excellent, most wondrous, vast, immeasurable, unequaled, and equal to the unequaled; and they dedicate these roots of goodness of rejoicing toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Subhūti! This mass of merit from the bodhisattva’s such rejoicing, compared to the meritorious conduct of diligence of the former bodhisattva, does not equal even one hundredth part of it; it does not equal one thousandth part, nor ten-thousandth, nor a hundred-millionth, nor a koṭi, nor a nayuta part; indeed, it does not equal even an *upaniṣad* part of it.

Why is this? Because one who is fully endowed with the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā* surpasses the previous bodhisattvas who practice with a mind that grasps at attainments. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

As previously stated, suppose all the bodhisattvas who have generated the resolve for awakening in as many trichiliocosm world systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were each to practice with vigor for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; let alone that number.

Subhūti! Suppose all sentient beings in as many trichiliocosm great thousandfold world systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River were each to resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Each of these bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds upon enlightenment shall, throughout as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, cultivate the four dhyānas and abide in tranquility; for that many eons as the sands of the Ganges, these bodhisattvas will thus practice meditative concentration, remaining far removed from all signs of agitation and distraction.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the skillful means of this *prajñāpāramitā* and is protected by this *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to take all the roots of goodness from the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as the roots of goodness belonging to pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—having thus combined, gathered, reckoned, and measured these various roots of goodness—with a mind that is supreme, ultimate, most excellent, most wondrous, vast, immeasurable, unequaled, and equal to the unequaled, they rejoice in them all; and with these roots of goodness born of rejoicing, they dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Subhūti! This mass of merit resulting from such sympathetic joy of the bodhisattva, compared to the meritorious action of meditative concentration cultivated by the former bodhisattva, does not equal even one hundredth part of it; it does not equal one thousandth part, nor ten-thousandth, nor a hundred-millionth (*koṭi*), nor a *nayuta*, nor even an *upaniṣad* part of it. It does not equal even a fraction thereof.

"Why is this? Because those who possess the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) are superior to the aforementioned bodhisattvas who practice meditative cultivation with a mind that grasps at attainments.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If any bodhisattva mahāsattvas desire to study the dharma-gates of the six pāramitās of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present as they truly are, and wish to rejoice in them according to reality, they should abide in the true meaning of all phenomena."
The meaning as it truly is refers to the nature of liberation.
Just as there is liberation, so too is giving;
just as there is liberation, so too are morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—all likewise so.
As is liberation, so too is the state of being liberated;
as is liberation, so too is the knowledge and vision of liberation;
as is liberation, so too is the mind of sympathetic joy and the meritorious action of sympathetic joy.
As is liberation, so too are the mind of dedication and the phenomena of dedication;
as is liberation, so too are all past phenomena that have already ceased, future phenomena that have not yet arisen, and present phenomena that do not abide;
as is liberation, so too are all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time—immeasurable and innumerable—as well as all the Buddha-dharmas.
Just as liberation is, so too are all bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and their respective dharmas.
In this way, even all dharmas are without bondage and without liberation, without abiding and without attachment; the nature of liberation is itself the nature of all dharmas.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who understands all phenomena in this way should train in and rejoice in the dharma-gates of the six pāramitās in this very manner.
"By means of these roots of goodness born of sympathetic joy, I dedicate them as they truly are toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Chapter Seven: The Chapter on the Conditions of the Hells (Part One). At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Does the perfection of wisdom give birth to the knowledge of all modes, and is the nature of the knowledge of all modes itself the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!...”
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said.
Śāriputra then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“Bhagavān! The Prajñāpāramitā is worthy of prostration; the Prajñāpāramitā is worthy of reverence.
The Prajñāpāramitā is the great illumination.”
The *prajñāpāramitā* is pure and unstained;
the *prajñāpāramitā* is vast and illuminating;
the *prajñāpāramitā* encompasses the characteristics of the three realms and is the very nature of the three realms.
The Prajñāpāramitā is the eye of purity, capable of illuminating all defiled phenomena of affliction;
the Prajñāpāramitā is that which is relied upon;
the Prajñāpāramitā is the unsurpassed Dharma.
The Prajñāpāramitā extensively encompasses all factors conducive to enlightenment;
the Prajñāpāramitā is the great torch of the Dharma, universally illuminating all darkness in the world;
the Prajñāpāramitā is fearlessness, capable of rescuing all sentient beings from dread.
The Prajñāpāramitā is the five eyes, capable of illuminating all mundane and supramundane paths;
the Prajñāpāramitā is the light of wisdom, which pierces through all dharmas of delusion and darkness;
the Prajñāpāramitā is the foremost guide, leading sentient beings to enter the noble path.
The Prajñāpāramitā is the treasury of all-knowledge, universally encompassing the hindrances such as the afflictions to bring about their total eradication;
the Prajñāpāramitā is the dharma of non-arising, the dharma of non-ceasing, the dharma of non-origination, and the dharma of non-action;
the Prajñāpāramitā is empty by its own characteristic from the very beginning.
The perfection of wisdom is the mother of all bodhisattvas;
the perfection of wisdom is the eye of all dharmas, illuminating all the ten powers and four fearlessnesses of the Buddhas;
the perfection of wisdom is that which is relied upon, capable of rescuing all sentient beings who are without refuge.
The Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma of peace and bliss, capable of severing the suffering and affliction of birth and death for sentient beings;
the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the true intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
the Prajñāpāramitā accords with the characteristics of dharmas, perfecting the wheel of the three turnings and twelve aspects.
"Bhagavān! Since the Prajñāpāramitā possesses such various merits as these, how should the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gaze upon, pay homage to, and revere this Dharma-gate?"
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:

“Regarding this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should regard it as their teacher and as all the Buddhas; they should honor, revere, gaze upon it with devotion, and praise it.”
"In this way, by revering and honoring the Perfection of Wisdom, one is thereby revering and honoring all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had this thought:
"For what reason has the Venerable Śāriputra now posed this question?"
Having had this thought, he approached the Venerable Śāriputra and said to him:
"Venerable One!
For what cause and reason do you thus question the Buddha?"
Śāriputra said: “Kauśika!

As the Buddha has taught, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom and are protected by the perfection of wisdom, they are then able to truly rejoice in all those roots of goodness and truly dedicate them toward that omniscience.”

Moreover, this Prajñāpāramitā possesses great merit, surpassing the meritorious practices of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration performed by bodhisattvas who harbor a mind of grasping.
For this reason, I have asked this question. Kausika,
you should now know that this Prajñāpāramitā serves as the leader for the five other pāramitās, guiding and showing them how to enter the path to omniscience.

For example, suppose there were blind people in the world; even if a multitude of hundreds of thousands or millions gathered with the desire to go somewhere, they would all be unable to know the path to be traveled.
Without a guide, they would ultimately be unable to advance toward a city, a village, or any destination.
If those with sight act as guides for the blind, then those blind people will be able to reach all their destinations. Kausika!

All acts of giving, morality, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration are like the blind; although they cultivate immeasurable meritorious deeds, if one does not take this Prajñāpāramitā as the guide, one can ultimately never truly advance upon the path to omniscience, much less attain the fruit of omniscience.

If these dharmas, such as giving and the rest, take the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) as their guide, they will obtain the eye of wisdom and be able to illuminate and penetrate the path to all-knowledge, thereby attaining the fruit of the realization of all-knowledge.

Furthermore, when generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration are assisted by the power of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), these five are therefore designated as "perfections" (pāramitās).
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for the sake of what dharma does the Prajñāpāramitā arise?”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

In the perfection of wisdom, form is not perceived, nor does it arise for the sake of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not perceived, nor do they arise for the sake of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.”
If these five aggregates possessed the characteristic of arising, then the perfection of wisdom would arise for their sake;
however, since these five aggregates do not arise, the perfection of wisdom does not arise for the sake of any phenomena.
Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the perfection of wisdom arises in this manner, what dharma should it accomplish?”
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! Although the perfection of wisdom arises in this way, there is not the slightest dharma that can be established.”
"Because it is established by way of non-existence, it is named Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, having heard these words, Śakra Devendra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Does the perfection of wisdom not, indeed, constitute all-knowledge? The Buddha said, “Kauśika!”

As you have said, the Prajñāpāramitā also accomplishes all-knowledge; however, it does not accomplish it by way of anything attained, nor does it accomplish it by way of the arising of names and signs.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"World-Honored One,
how shall it be accomplished?"
The Buddha said,
“Kauśika! All dharmas are accomplished in such a way that they are not accomplished.”
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is marvelous, World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is without arising and without cessation."
"All those dharmas are likewise without arising and without cessation, without abiding and without attachment; this is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If one gives rise to such a mind that engages in conceptual discrimination, one is far removed from the *prajñāpāramitā*, one loses the *prajñāpāramitā*, and one does not achieve the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha said, “Subhūti, it is so, it is so!”
Because of these causes and conditions, one remains far removed from the *prajñāpāramitā*, loses the *prajñāpāramitā*, and fails to accomplish the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? This Prajñāpāramitā does not represent anything regarding form; it likewise does not represent feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Because the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, and the Buddha, the World-Honored One, are all entirely without any indication.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is this Great Pāramitā the Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti, what do you think? For what reason is this great pāramitā called the prajñāpāramitā?”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Form has neither greatness nor smallness, neither accumulation nor dispersion; it is free from all conditioned activity. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise have neither greatness nor smallness, neither accumulation nor dispersion; they are free from all conditioned activity.”
