All dharmas such as the ten powers of the Tathāgatas neither possess power nor lack power, and they are without accumulation or dispersal.
Even up to omniscience, there is likewise no large or small, no accumulation or dispersal, and no arising or activity.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are without smallness or greatness, without gathering or dispersing, free from arising and activity, and abide in equality.
If a bodhisattva makes distinctions regarding any phenomenon and forms such a thought:
"I have attained the fruit of omniscience in its full perfection; for the sake of sentient beings, I shall expound various Dharma gates, able to deliver countless beings and lead them to nirvana."
If that bodhisattva forms such a thought, they are not said to be practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Why is this? The perfection of wisdom has no such characteristics; it does not perceive any sentient beings who are to be delivered, nor any who are to be attained.
Because sentient beings lack intrinsic nature, the *prajñāpāramitā* also lacks intrinsic nature;
because sentient beings are free from marks, the *prajñāpāramitā* is also free from marks;
because sentient beings are unarisen, the *prajñāpāramitā* is also unarisen.
Because sentient beings are not extinguished, the Prajñāpāramitā is also not extinguished;
because sentient beings are inconceivable, the Prajñāpāramitā is also inconceivable;
because sentient beings lack cognitive realization, the Prajñāpāramitā also lacks cognitive realization.
Because sentient beings know the ultimate truth as it truly is, the perfection of wisdom also knows the ultimate truth as it truly is;
because the powers of sentient beings are gathered, the powers of the Tathāgata are also gathered.
“World-Honored One!
By such causes and conditions as these, I say that the great pāramitā is the prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having heard this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, receive it with earnest attention, do not doubt or find it difficult, and give rise to pure faith and understanding;”
“From where did these bodhisattvas pass away to come and be born here?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“You should know that these bodhisattvas have already heard and received this Dharma in the various buddha-fields of other directions; they have questioned its meaning and understood it in accordance with it. Having passed away from those places, they have come to be born here.”
Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a person briefly hears this profound Dharma-gate of the Perfection of Wisdom and immediately gives rise to faith and understanding, leaping for joy with great delight, and honors, respects, and regards it as the Buddha himself, you should know that this person has already heard and received this Dharma from countless Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and has long cultivated the most supreme and wondrous practices of a bodhisattva.
“Such persons as these are praised by the Buddha.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma (Shi Hu), Imperially Appointed Grand Officer for Court Service, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, recipient of the purple robe, under imperial decree. The Seventh Chapter, Part Two: On the Causes and Conditions of the Hells. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“Can the Prajñāpāramitā be heard or attained?
Is there anything that can be spoken of in terms of sound or characteristics?
The Buddha said:

"No, Subhūti! The perfection of wisdom is without speech and without demonstration; it is without hearing and without attainment; it is not a characteristic that can be perceived within the aggregates, the sense bases, or the elements."
Why is this? Because all those phenomena are free from manifold natures, and the aggregates, bases, and elements are themselves the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Why is this?

Because the aggregates, bases, and elements are empty, detached, and quiescent, the perfection of wisdom is also empty, detached, and quiescent; moreover, the perfection of wisdom and the aggregates, bases, and elements are non-dual and indivisible, without characteristics and without differentiation.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If there should be someone within this assembly of the Buddha who, upon hearing this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, does not give rise to faith and understanding, lacks love and joy in their heart, and rises from the assembly unable to listen and receive it—for what causes and conditions does that person manifest such characteristics?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"I shall now explain this to you according to reality.

If there are those who, upon hearing this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, do not give rise to faith and understanding, nor delight in listening to or receiving it, you should know that although such persons have practiced various pure conducts (*brahmacarya*) in the presence of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, they do not love or delight in listening to or receiving this Dharma. Subhūti, if, when this *prajñāpāramitā* Dharma-gate is being preached in the presence of the Buddhas, they rise from the assembly..."

That person, having already planted such causes and conditions for obstructive dharmas under previous Buddhas, likewise fails to give rise to love, joy, faith, or understanding upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* dharma-gate within my Dharma; lacking any sense of reverence, they depart and abandon it.

It should be known that such a person, whether in body or mind, is unable to achieve harmony; therefore, regarding this Dharma-door of the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not give rise to even a single thought of pure faith and understanding, nor do they produce the perception of correct knowledge and vision according to reality. Instead, they harbor doubt and confusion toward the profound Dharma and create karma born of ignorance.
Because they have accumulated such karma of ignorance, upon hearing this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā, they give rise to a mind of opposition and commit acts of slander.
Because they oppose and slander the *prajñāpāramitā*, they thereby oppose and slander the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Subhūti! I say that such a person has little wisdom and little insight, and lacks the karma of right merit.
They are unable to accomplish the roots of goodness of pure faith.
At all times and in all places, they destroy their own bodies and further destroy the bodies of others, severing the causes of great benefit and happiness for all sentient beings. Subhūti!

Because of these causes and conditions of slandering the Dharma, that person will certainly fall into the great hells in the future, where they shall undergo various sufferings for many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, many hundreds of thousands of years, many hundreds of koṭis of years, many thousands of koṭis of years, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of years, and for many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of years.

From one great hell to another great hell, passing successively from one to another; when this great earth is consumed by the fires of the kalpa, those who have slandered the Dharma will undergo various sufferings within the great hells of other world-systems, likewise passing from one great hell to another great hell.

When the hells in other world-systems are consumed by the fires at the end of the kalpa, they likewise pass on in succession to the great hells in yet other world-systems, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction in this same way, moving from one to another.

Furthermore, when that realm is consumed by the fires at the end of the kalpa and this realm is reconstituted, they return once more to this great hell, undergoing various sufferings as they pass from one state to another.
In this manner, they pass successively from this world-system to other world-systems, undergoing various sufferings for as many years as the aforementioned number within each individual hell.
This continues until, finally, the kalpa-ending fire arises once more in this world’s hells; only when they are consumed by that conflagration do their sufferings come to an end.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Because those people, through the unwholesome karma of their speech, have slandered this profound Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā, they obtain such a fruit.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Are all sentient beings who commit the five extremely grave offenses of the *ānantarya* comparable to those who commit the offense of slandering the Dharma?”
The Buddha said,
“Śāriputra! Do not say that those five deeds of immediate retribution are similar to this grave offense of slandering the Dharma.”
Śāriputra! The transgression of one who opposes and slanders the profound True Dharma is exceedingly grave, surpassing all karmic offenses of the five immediate retributions. Why is this?
When those who slander the Dharma hear this teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā dharma-gate, they immediately say:
"This was not spoken by the Buddha; I cannot study within it."
That person destroys their own pure faith and further destroys the pure faith of others;
they drink various poisons themselves and cause others to drink those poisons as well;
having brought ruin upon themselves, they likewise cause others to bring about that same ruin.
They themselves do not believe in, accept, know, or understand the Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā, and thus do not practice it;
furthermore, they cause others not to give rise to faith and acceptance, not to attain correct knowledge and understanding, and likewise not to practice it.

Śāriputra! I say that such a person is a destroyer of the Dharma; their nature is turbid and black, and not pure. Among the white dharmas, they act as a *kaṃsaka* (a defiler), destroying pure faith, and they are further named a defiler of the Dharma.
"Śāriputra! For this reason, the offense of slandering the Dharma is most extremely grave; even the five deeds of immediate retribution cannot be compared to it.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, those who slander the Dharma fall into the great hells.
We do not know what the dimensions of the bodies they must suffer will be.”
The Buddha said: "Stop, Śāriputra!"
There is no need to inquire about the dimensions of the body through which they suffer. Why is this?
If those people were to hear the size and proportions of the body they must endure, hot blood would immediately gush from their mouths, and they would be on the verge of death.
Thus reborn, they experience grief, sorrow, and affliction; their bodies, both internally and externally, become parched and emaciated, giving rise to great terror.
For this reason, I shall not now describe the physical dimensions of those suffering beings.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha once more, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We pray that you will proclaim the dimensions of the bodies of suffering experienced by those who slander the Dharma, so as to serve as a clear illumination and instruction for all sentient beings in the final age, causing them not to give rise to slander against the True Dharma.”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra, stop!
"There is no need to speak.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra thus earnestly entreated him for a second and third time.
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! Stop! Stop!”
Regarding this matter, you should now know: as I have said, those who slander the Dharma will fall into the great hells and undergo extreme suffering for that many years.
"By means of this very condition, it serves as a sufficient illumination for all sentient beings; therefore, one should not speak of the dimensions of its body.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
All sons and daughters of good family should, at all times, always skillfully guard the actions of body, speech, and mind, so as not to perform any unwholesome deeds.
Why is this? As the Buddha has taught, those who fall into hell do so because their unwholesome verbal karma can produce such an extremely vast accumulation of non-merit.
“World-Honored One!
Is it truly through vocal karma that those who slander the true Dharma incur this retribution for their offenses?
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Subhūti!
Because they have given rise to unwholesome verbal karma, they have slandered the True Dharma; by this cause and condition, they undergo this retribution for their offenses."
Subhūti! I say that such a person should not go forth into homelessness within my Dharma. Why is this?
Because that person opposes and slanders the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are thereby slandering *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because they slander *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they are thereby slandering the entire Jewel of the Buddha.
Because one slanders the Buddha Jewel, one slanders the omniscience of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Because one slanders omniscience, one thereby slanders the entire Jewel of the Dharma.
Because they slander the Jewel of the Dharma, they likewise slander the entire Sangha Jewel of the Śrāvakas.

Thus, in every way, at all times, and in all places, they revile the Three Jewels, accumulating immeasurable and innumerable unwholesome karmic actions, and shall consequently fall into hell to undergo great suffering and affliction.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions do those people give rise to a mind of contempt and slander toward this Dharma-gate of the Perfection of Wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“You should know that such persons have four causes. What are the four?
First, being instigated by Māra;
second, destroying all pure faith and understanding through the causes of unwise karma accumulated by oneself;
and third, following after all unwholesome associates and conceiving a notion of harmony regarding what is not the Dharma.
Fourth, by clinging to the mark of a self, they fail to give rise to right view and, following that deviant mind, commit various transgressions. Subhūti,
it is due to these four causes and conditions that they give rise to slander toward this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti! For this reason, all sons and daughters of good family should give rise to pure faith and understanding toward the True Dharma spoken by the Buddhas, and must not harbor contempt or slander.

One who slanders the True Dharma is one who destroys the Dharma; if one destroys the Dharma, they sever their life-span and give rise to karma of ignorance, whereby they shall fall into hell and undergo great suffering and affliction.
Chapter Eight: On Purity (1) At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, if there are those who follow evil associates, who have abandoned roots of goodness, and who lack diligence, will it be extremely difficult for them to believe and understand this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said.”

Such persons as these have seen little and heard little, are far removed from roots of goodness, cultivate inferior wisdom, and are unable to exert diligence; furthermore, they follow after evil associates. For these reasons, it is extremely difficult for them to believe in and understand this profound Dharma-gate.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
for what reason is this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* difficult to believe and difficult to understand?"
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.”
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of form is form, it is neither bound nor liberated;
because the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is consciousness, they are neither bound nor liberated.
Form at the prior limit is neither bound nor liberated. Why?
Because the self-nature of form at the prior limit is itself form.
Form is neither bound nor liberated at its posterior limit, because the self-nature of form at its posterior limit is itself form.
Form is neither bound nor liberated at its middle limit, because the self-nature of form at its middle limit is itself form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated in the past, future, or present limits.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of consciousness in the past, future, and present limits is simply consciousness itself.
"For this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā is profound and difficult to understand.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
This Dharma gate of the Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to believe and difficult to understand; as the Buddha has taught, it is most extremely profound and even more difficult to comprehend.
World-Honored One!

If there are those who are indolent, deficient in vigor, lacking mindfulness, or devoid of wisdom, you should know that for such as these, this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Because form is pure, the fruit is pure; because the fruit is pure, form is pure.
Whether it be the purity of form or the purity of the fruit, they are non-dual and undifferentiated, for they are neither severed nor destroyed."
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, the fruit is pure; because the fruit is pure, consciousness is pure.
Whether it be the purity of consciousness or the purity of the fruit, they are non-dual and without distinction, being neither severed nor destroyed.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Because form is pure, omniscience is pure; because omniscience is pure, form is pure."
Whether it be the purity of form or the purity of omniscience, they are non-dual and undifferentiated, because they are neither severed nor destroyed.
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, omniscience is pure; because omniscience is pure, consciousness is pure.
“Whether it be the purity of consciousness or the purity of all-knowledge, they are non-dual and without distinction, because they are neither severed nor destroyed.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"The Prajñāpāramitā is most supreme and profound.
The Buddha said,
"Because its nature is pure."
Śāriputra said, “The perfection of wisdom is a great illumination.
The Buddha said:
“Because its nature is pure. Śāriputra said,
“The Prajñāpāramitā is vast and brilliantly illuminating.”
The Buddha said,
"Because its nature is pure. Śāriputra said:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is without conjunction.
The Buddha said:
“Because its nature is pure.”
Śāriputra said: “The perfection of wisdom is non-apprehensible.
The Buddha said:
"Because its nature is pure. Śāriputra said:
"The Prajñāpāramitā has nothing to be realized."
The Buddha said,
"Because its nature is pure. Śāriputra said:
“Prajñāpāramitā is ultimately non-arising in the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
The Buddha said,
“Because its nature is pure.”
Śāriputra said, “The perfection of wisdom is ultimately non-extinguished.
The Buddha said:
"Because its nature is pure. Śāriputra said:
"The Prajñāpāramitā has nothing to be cognized."
The Buddha said:
"Because its nature is pure. Śāriputra said:
“How is it that the Prajñāpāramitā has nothing to be cognized?
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!...”
The perfection of wisdom does not know form; it does not know feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. Why is this?
Because the nature of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness is pure.
Śāriputra said: "The Prajñāpāramitā neither arises nor acts with respect to all-knowledge.
The Buddha said:
"Because its nature is pure. Śāriputra said:
"In the Prajñāpāramitā, there is no dharma that can be grasped and no dharma that can be abandoned."
The Buddha said,
“Because its nature is pure.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Because I am pure, form is pure.
The Buddha said:
“Because of ultimate purity.
“Because I am pure, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are pure.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is ultimately pure. Subhūti said:
“Because I am pure, the fruit is pure.”
The Buddha said:
"Because it is ultimately pure. Subhūti said:
“Because I am pure, all-knowledge is pure.
The Buddha said,
“Because it is ultimately pure.”
Subhūti said: “Because I am pure, there is nothing to be attained and nothing to be realized.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is ultimately pure. Subhūti said:
“Because I am boundless, form is also boundless.”
The Buddha said,
“Because it is ultimately pure. Subhūti said:
"Because the self is infinite, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also infinite.
The Buddha said:
"Because they are ultimately pure."
Subhūti said: “A bodhisattva mahāsattva has no realization whatsoever regarding the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is ultimately pure. Subhūti said:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is not this shore, not the other shore, and not the middle current; its intrinsic nature has no place of abiding.”
The Buddha said,
“Because it is ultimately pure.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva makes any conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena, they immediately lose the perfection of wisdom and immediately distance themselves from the perfection of wisdom.”
The Buddha praised Subhūti, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”
So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said. Why is this?
"If one gives rise to conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena, this is because one is attached to names and signs.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If one makes conceptual distinctions regarding the names of the Prajñāpāramitā as they have been taught, this is called 'attachment.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"What is meant by the characteristic of attachment?"

Subhūti said: "If a bodhisattva discriminates the emptiness of form, and discriminates the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, this constitutes attachment to signs."

Furthermore, if one discriminates between these as past dharmas, future dharmas, or present dharmas—such as how much an aggregate of merit is obtained by one who has first resolved for bodhicitta, or how much merit is accomplished by one who has long practiced the bodhisattva path.
"One who makes such distinctions is said to be attached to signs.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"For what reason is it that when a bodhisattva acquires a mass of merit, it is called being attached to signs?"
Subhūti said: “Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening discriminates with the mind, ‘This is the bodhicitta,’ and then dedicates the roots of goodness from that resolution toward anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi.”
If one can perform dedication, it is not called "dedication"; such conceptualization is itself an attachment to signs. Kausika!

If there are bodhisattvas who wish to cause good sons and good daughters to dwell securely in the Bodhisattva Vehicle, they should, regarding Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, represent it through the true Dharma according to principle, instruct them according to reality, benefit them as is appropriate, and generate joy in accordance with the truth.
If a bodhisattva can thus instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden others with such dharmas, they will remain unharmed themselves; they are approved by all Buddhas and taught by all Buddhas.
Those good sons and good daughters likewise remain free from attachment.
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”
You have skillfully expounded the Dharma-gate of detachment, causing all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to give rise to no attachment toward any phenomena.
Subhūti! I shall further expound for you the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate of detachment; you should listen well and attend to it with proper mindfulness.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain it for us.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If there is anyone who conceives the notion of attainment regarding the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and thereby gives rise to grasping and attachment, this is called a great attachment to dharmas."
Why is this? Because they do not depart from all marks, Subhūti!

If there is a bodhisattva who gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward all the untainted dharmas of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, and dedicates these roots of goodness born of sympathetic joy toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this too is attachment.
Why is this? Subhūti!
All dharmas cannot be apprehended as past, future, or present; that mind of sympathetic joy is likewise not of the three times.
With what mind should one rejoice in what dharma?
Therefore, you should know that all dharmas are signless, without seeing, without hearing, without cognition, and without knowledge.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The nature of all dharmas is exceedingly profound.”
The Buddha said:
“It is free from various natures. Subhūti said:
“The nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* is profoundly deep.
The Buddha said,
“The *prajñāpāramitā* is pure by its own nature (*svabhāva-viśuddha*) and is free from manifold natures.”
Subhūti said: “I now pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā, which is of the nature of detachment.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.
Because all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, the perfection of wisdom is likewise devoid of intrinsic nature.”
"Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has realized, according to reality, that all dharmas are without intrinsic nature.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Has the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha realized that dharmas lack intrinsic nature?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Neither non-existence nor the absence of existence—
whether those all dharmas have an intrinsic nature or lack one— they are unified in a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness. Subhūti!
Therefore, the Buddhas realize all those phenomena in this manner.
Why is this? Because the Dharma-eye of the Buddhas is non-conceptual, and the nature of all phenomena is singular and non-dual.
All those phenomena, whether as intrinsic nature or non-intrinsic nature, are what is called "naturelessness.
This nature of naturelessness is termed "the single nature," yet even this single nature cannot be apprehended.
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva understands in this way, they will attain freedom from all attachments.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is most supreme and profoundly deep.
The Buddha said:
"As the profundity of space is the profundity of the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said,
"The perfection of wisdom is difficult to know."
The Buddha said:
"Because there is no knower. Subhūti said:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is inconceivable.
The Buddha said:
“It is not known by the mind, for it transcends the mental factors.”
Subhūti said: "The Prajñāpāramitā is free from all conditioned activity.
The Buddha said:
"Because an agent cannot be apprehended.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?

The Buddha replied, "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice with respect to form, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom."

Not practicing the notion that form is impermanent is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the notion that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are impermanent is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the notion that form is empty is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the notion that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are empty is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Not practicing the notions of the fulfillment or non-fulfillment of form is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? If one practices with the characteristics of the fulfillment or non-fulfillment of form, that is not form.
To not practice with the characteristics of the fulfillment or non-fulfillment of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is to practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Why is this? If one practices with the marks of fulfillment or non-fulfillment regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, that is not consciousness.
If one does not practice with respect to these dharmas in such a manner, this is called practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is marvelous, World-Honored One!
You have skillfully taught the dharma of non-attachment for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas within the midst of attached dharmas.”
The Buddha said:

“If one does not practice with regard to form as having attachment or non-attachment, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); if one does not practice with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as having attachment or non-attachment, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom;

if one does not practice with regard to the feelings produced conditioned by eye-contact, up to and including those produced conditioned by mind-contact, as having attachment or non-attachment, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing with regard to the element of earth, up to and including not practicing with regard to the element of consciousness, as being either with attachment or without attachment, is the practice of the perfection of wisdom;

not practicing with regard to the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as being either with attachment or without attachment, is the practice of the perfection of wisdom;

not practicing with regard to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as being either with attachment or without attachment, is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Not practicing with attachment or non-attachment toward the stages of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, or tathāgata is the practice of the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing with attachment or non-attachment toward omniscience (sarvajñatā) is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus not give rise to attachment toward form, nor toward feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
and does not give rise to attachment toward the various feelings produced with eye-contact through to mind-contact as conditions;
They do not give rise to attachment toward the element of earth, up to and including the element of consciousness;
they do not give rise to attachment toward the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

nor do they give rise to attachment toward the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—all such accumulations of merit.
One does not give rise to attachment even toward the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, tathāgata, or even omniscience.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are neither bound nor liberated, having transcended all attachments; therefore, it is named "unimpeded omniscience free from attachment. Subhūti!
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the perfection of wisdom in this manner.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is marvelous, World-Honored One!"
The Prajñāpāramitā is a profound dharma. If it is spoken of, it does not increase;
if it is not spoken of, it does not decrease. Even when spoken of, it does not decrease; even when not spoken of, it does not increase.
The Buddha praised Subhūti, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”

It is so, it is so! Even if a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were to praise empty space for the duration of his entire lifespan, that empty space would not increase by such praise, nor would it decrease by its lack of praise; it would not diminish through praise, nor would it grow through its lack of praise.

For example, it is like praising a person created by illusion: they do not rejoice when praised, nor do they feel resentment when not praised; they do not increase because of praise, nor do they diminish because of its absence.
“Subhūti, the nature of all dharmas is thus: it is beyond speech and non-speech, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The *prajñāpāramitā* is vast and profound; the conduct of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is exceedingly difficult.
Just as space is without movement or transformation, without marks or activity, so too is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
World-Honored One!
For the sake of sentient beings, bodhisattvas don great armor and perform adornment. Why is this so?
Because Bodhisattvas desire to accomplish the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and deliver all sentient beings, they practice and study the Prajñāpāramitā.

"Bhagavān! It is as if a person were to don armor and engage in battle with empty space; yet that empty space is fundamentally equal, the dharma-realm is equal, and sentient beings are equal. Thus, although bodhisattvas may be courageous and achieve the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), they can ultimately never win a victory over space."
"Therefore, the practice of the perfection of wisdom by the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is difficult to perform.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"If it is thus, then the practice of the perfection of wisdom is without anything produced; how, then, can it be practiced?"
Subhūti said: "Kauśika! Just as the practice of space arises, so too does the practice of the perfection of wisdom arise."
Kauśika! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to practice the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā* should practice like space.
To learn in this manner is to be in accord with it.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly who, having heard this Dharma, rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"In the Prajñāpāramitā, there is not the slightest dharma that can arise, nor the slightest dharma that can cease; therefore, I now pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā."

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma, Dharma Master and Imperially Appointed Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (on trial as Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices), under the Imperial Edict. Chapter Eight, Part Two: On Purity. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"If there be anyone who upholds this Dharma-gate of the Perfection of Wisdom, I shall protect that person as well as this Dharma-gate.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying: "Kauśika!..."
"Do you see any dharma that can be protected?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied, "No, Subhūti."
Then Subhūti said: "Lord of Devas!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in accordance with the Prajñāpāramitā as it has been taught, acting in accord with and conforming to it, this is precisely what is called 'true protection.'"
If at any time they are separated from the perfection of wisdom, then in all places humans and non-humans will find an opportunity to exploit them.
Furthermore, Kauśika!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to guard and protect the perfection of wisdom, they should do so as one would guard empty space; this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Kauśika! What do you think? Can that sound of the call provide protection?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"Venerable Subhūti! That sound of the call cannot be protected."
Subhūti said: "So it is, so it is, Kauśika!"
One should know that all phenomena are like the sound of an echo.
If one knows them thus, then regarding all phenomena there is nothing to be observed, nothing to be pointed out, nothing to be produced, and nothing to be attained.
"This is the practice of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

At that time, within each of the worlds of the trichiliocosm, from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Great Brahmā, all the respective lords of the Sahā world—the Great Brahmā Kings, Śakra Devendra, and the other sons of gods—through the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual sustenance, immediately came one by one to where the Buddha was. They prostrated with their heads at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, all those Brahma kings, Śakras, and the hosts of Brahmās, as well as the other sons of the gods of the Four Great Kings, each beheld a thousand Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, proclaiming the Dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā* in their respective locations, each according to what was appropriate. The names, phrases, and syllables were all identical in their mode of expression; every category, chapter, and sentence of the *Prajñāpāramitā* Dharma-gate was entirely without difference. Those who received the teaching were all named Subhūti, and those who posed questions were likewise like Śakra, Lord of Devas.
At that time, the Buddha addressed those Brahma kings, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the others, saying:

"In this very place, you now behold all the Buddhas thus proclaiming the Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā; likewise, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya attains the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he too shall proclaim the Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā in this very place."
Chapter Nine: Praising the Excellence At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One! The *prajñāpāramitā* is profoundly deep and subtle; within its name, it is ultimately unobtainable. It cannot be proclaimed by means of language. Just as the name ‘*prajñāpāramitā*’ is unobtainable, so too the dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā* is unobtainable.”
Furthermore, World-Honored One, this Prajñāpāramitā—both its name and its dharma—are without distinction; they are all unarisen and both are unattainable.
World-Honored One!

As the Buddha has said, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya attains the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he too shall proclaim this *prajñāpāramitā* in this very place. Since this Dharma is so profound, how will he explain it?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:

“When that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya has attained the fruit of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and teaches the Prajñāpāramitā in this place, he will not speak of form as being either permanent or impermanent, nor as being liberated or bound; he will not speak of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being either permanent or impermanent, nor as being liberated or bound.”
He teaches that form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are ultimately pure.
Subhūti, it is by means of such names, phrases, and syllables that those bodhisattvas proclaim the perfection of wisdom as it truly is.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is pure.”
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti! Because form is pure, the prajñāpāramitā is pure."
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
Because form is neither produced nor extinguished, is not attached to afflictions, and does not emerge from the world, it is pure; the perfection of wisdom is likewise pure.

Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither arising nor ceasing, are unattached to afflictions, and do not emerge from the world, they are pure; the perfection of wisdom is likewise pure.
Because form is unstained, the perfection of wisdom is pure; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unstained, the perfection of wisdom is pure;
because all phenomena are unstained, the perfection of wisdom is pure;
and because space is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
“Because all phenomena are like space and like echoes, they are pure; the perfection of wisdom is likewise pure.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If there are good sons or good daughters who, regarding this Dharma-door of the Prajñāpāramitā, give rise to a pure mind, listen to, receive, read, recite, and explain it for others, you should know that such persons shall obtain great and wholesome benefit: their faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body will be purified; they will be free from all suffering of illness; no evil poisons will be able to harm them; and their lifespan will increase, free from the calamity of premature death.
They shall always have a multitude of a thousand devaputras who, sometimes leading from the front and sometimes following behind, will secretly provide protection in all places.
World-Honored One!

Those sons and daughters of good family who uphold the Dharma should, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the bright fortnight, purify their physical, verbal, and mental actions, and in various locations recite this *Prajñāpāramitā* dharma-gate, or explain its meaning for others.
"You should know that these sons and daughters of good family will obtain exceedingly great merit.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "So it is, so it is!"

As you have said, if there are sons or daughters of good family who, in all places, read, recite, explain, and expound this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there will always be a multitude of a thousand devaputras who go to those who uphold the Dharma to secretly protect them, desiring to hear and receive the great benefit of the True Dharma.
Why is this? Because this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā is the most supreme treasure among gods and humans.
For this reason, sons and daughters of good family who are able to receive and uphold it shall obtain exceedingly great merit.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain this profound Dharma-gate of the Perfection of Wisdom, they shall obtain great and wholesome benefit in this present life; they will acquire the most supreme treasure and be honored by both gods and humans alike."
Why is this? Because this Dharma-door of the Perfection of Wisdom can bring about vast benefit and happiness for sentient beings. Subhūti!

All those dharmas are neither produced nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither grasped nor abandoned; they are non-existent and unattainable. Prajñāpāramitā, likewise, is neither produced nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither grasped nor abandoned; it is non-existent and unattainable.

Why is this? Because form is unstained, the perfection of wisdom is also unstained; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unstained, the perfection of wisdom is also unstained.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding any phenomena, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is neither internal nor external; it neither goes out nor comes in; there is no phenomenon that can be shown, and no phenomenon that can be observed.
At that time, all the Brahma kings, Śakras, and sons of gods who had gathered from throughout the trichiliocosm leaped for joy and spoke thus:
"Today, within Jambudvīpa, we have heard the World-Honored One turn for a second time this most profound wheel of Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā."
"In that future age, when the Bodhisattva Maitreya has attained perfect enlightenment and turns this wheel of Dharma, may I also hear this teaching.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The Dharma is not turned for the first time, nor is it turned for a second time; one should know that all dharmas are ultimately non-existent and cannot be turned."
"Subhūti! It is just the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This great pāramitā is the prajñāpāramitā. Why is this so?
Because all those dharmas are free from all attachments.”
Furthermore, although all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate all dharmas, even until they realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, there is no dharma that can be realized.
Although one turns the wheel of Dharma, there is no dharma that can be shown and no dharma that can be apprehended.
Because there is nothing realized, nothing shown, and nothing attained, all dharmas are empty and ultimately free from attachment.
Because of being free from attachment, all phenomena neither return nor revolve. Why is this so,
World-Honored One?
"All dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature; therefore, there is no returning and no turning.
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying: "So it is, so it is!"
As you have said, Subhūti!
That door of liberation of emptiness has no returning and no turning; the doors of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness likewise have no returning and no turning.

Subhūti! Although one thus proclaims all dharmas, the nature of all dharmas is ultimately quiescent; there is no speaking, no showing, no hearing, and no attainment, for there is no dharma that can be realized.
"Because there is nothing to be realized, there is also no realizer.
Therefore, all dharmas are neither extinguished nor non-extinguished.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The boundless *pāramitā* is the *prajñāpāramitā*, because space is boundless.
The unequaled *pāramitā* is the *prajñāpāramitā*, because all phenomena (*dharma*) are unapprehendable.”
The perfection of detachment is the perfection of wisdom, because it is ultimately empty.
The perfection of indestructibility is the perfection of wisdom, because the nature of all phenomena cannot be apprehended.
The perfection of non-phrase is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena are without name and without mark.
The perfection of non-nature is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena have no coming.
The perfection of non-discourse is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena are without differentiation.
The perfection of non-coming is the perfection of wisdom, because the aggregates cannot be apprehended.
The perfection of non-departure is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena have no coming.
The perfection of non-accumulation is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena have no grasping.
The perfection of inexhaustibility is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena have the characteristic of inexhaustibility.
The perfection of non-arising is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena are without attachment.
The perfection of non-action is the perfection of wisdom, because an agent cannot be apprehended.
The perfection of non-knower is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena lack a sovereign master.
The perfection of non-arrival is the perfection of wisdom, because there is no falling back.
The perfection of non-extinction is the perfection of wisdom, because the prior, middle, and subsequent limits are unapprehendable.
The perfection of dream, illusion, mirage, and so forth is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena are unarisen.
The perfection of the absence of afflictions is the perfection of wisdom, because the nature of greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth is pure.
The perfection that is without transcendence is the perfection of wisdom, because a basis for it cannot be apprehended.
The perfection that is without defilement is the perfection of wisdom, because space is pure.
The perfection of non-proliferation is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena are equal.
The perfection of non-recollection is the perfection of wisdom, because no recollections arise.
The perfection of immovability is the perfection of wisdom, because the nature of all phenomena is eternally abiding.
The perfection of detachment from desire is the perfection of wisdom, because the nature of all phenomena is reality.
The perfection of non-arising is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena are free from doubt.
The perfection of tranquility is the perfection of wisdom, because the characteristics of all phenomena cannot be apprehended.
The perfection that is free from fault is the perfection of wisdom, because it is fully endowed with all virtues.
The perfection that is without sentient beings is the perfection of wisdom, because the limit of sentient beings cannot be apprehended.
The perfection of non-interruption is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena do not arise.
The perfection of non-duality is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena are free from attachment.
The perfection of non-differentiation is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena lack any combination.
The perfection of non-attachment is the perfection of wisdom, because it does not discriminate between the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The perfection of non-discrimination is the perfection of wisdom, because discrimination is equal.
The perfection of the immeasurable is the perfection of wisdom, because the measure of phenomena is equal.
The perfection of space is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena are without obstruction.
The perfection of impermanence is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena are conditioned.
The perfection of suffering is the perfection of wisdom, because of the equality of space.
The perfection of emptiness is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena are unapprehendable.
The perfection of selflessness is the perfection of wisdom, because a self cannot be apprehended.
The perfection of signlessness is the perfection of wisdom, because all phenomena cannot be turned back.
The perfection of emptiness is the perfection of wisdom, because it is ultimately boundless.

The perfections of the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path are the perfection of wisdom, because the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are unapprehendable.
The perfection of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness is the perfection of wisdom, because the three gates of liberation are unapprehendable.
The perfections of one possessing internal form observing external forms, and so forth, are the perfection of wisdom, because the eight liberations are unapprehendable.
The perfection of the first dhyāna and so forth is the perfection of wisdom, because the nine preliminary dharmas are non-apprehendable.
The perfections of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path are the perfection of wisdom, because the dharmas of the four noble truths are non-apprehendable.
The perfection of giving and the other perfections are the perfection of wisdom, because the ten perfections are non-apprehendable.
The perfection of the ten powers is the perfection of wisdom, because it is indestructible.
The perfection of the four fearlessnesses is the perfection of wisdom, because it is without timidity, without dread, without retreat, and without sinking.
The perfection of liberation from fetters is the perfection of wisdom, because the knowledge of all modes is unattached and unimpeded.
The perfection of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable merits is this perfection of wisdom, because it transcends all calculable phenomena.
The perfection of the Tathāgata’s suchness is this perfection of wisdom, because the suchness of all phenomena is equal.
The perfection of natural wisdom is the perfection of prajñā, because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is equal.
The perfection of the wisdom of all-knowledge is the perfection of prajñā, because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are unobtainable and unknowable.
Chapter Ten: Praise for Upholding (Prajñāpāramitāstutiparivarta). Part One of Ten. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had this thought:

"If any sons or daughters of good family should even briefly hear this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, such persons have already planted roots of goodness in the presence of the Buddhas; how much more so for those who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, remember, contemplate, and explain this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* to others, training as it is taught, practicing as it is taught, and acting in accordance with the truth."
This person has already, in the presence of immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-Bhagavāns, paid respectful homage and made offerings, thereby planting various roots of goodness.

Furthermore, if there is anyone who, upon hearing this Dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, is not startled, not terrified, does not retreat, and does not sink into despondency, it is because in the past, in the presence of Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, they have already heard and received this profound Dharma and inquired about its meaning; they have practiced this Dharma according to principle. Therefore, hearing it now, they do not give rise to alarm or fear, but study as it is taught, practice as it is taught, and correspond to it through correct application.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, having understood the thoughts in the mind of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If there is anyone who hears this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, gives rise to a mind of faith and understanding, respects and honors it, receives, upholds, reads, and recites it, explains it for others, trains as taught, practices as taught, and accords with the principle of reality—such a person should be no different from a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is non-retrogressive in their merits."
Why is this? Because this Dharma-gate of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be heard by those who possess only meager roots of virtue.
Furthermore, those who have not previously cultivated it under former Buddhas will, for that reason, be unable to give rise to pure faith and understanding at this time.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If there are those who, upon hearing this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, give rise to opposition and slander, one should know that these persons have previously heard this Dharma in the presence of past Buddhas, and at that time already gave rise to opposition and slander.

Why is this? Although such a person has previously heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* dharma-gate by means of even a small root of virtue, they are shrouded by indolence and fail to arouse diligence. Lacking faith and patience, they do not give rise to love or joy for the profound Dharma; because they lack such joy, they cannot comprehend it. Failing to comprehend it, they further fail to inquire about it from the Buddhas or the disciples of the Buddha.
"For this reason, you should know that those who now hear this Dharma and give rise to opposition or slander have already produced such opposition and slander in the past.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If anyone pays homage to the Prajñāpāramitā, they are paying homage to the all-knowledge of all Buddhas.
The Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "So it is, so it is!"
Kauśika! If a person pays homage to the Prajñāpāramitā, they are paying homage to the omniscient wisdom of all Buddhas. Why is this?
From the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) arises the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and from the perfection of wisdom, in turn, arises the knowledge of all modes.
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner and train in the perfection of wisdom in this manner.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), how is it that they are said to 'abide thus' and 'practice thus'?"
The Buddha praised Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!"
You have now well questioned the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding this profound meaning.
Yet that you are able to ask is entirely due to the Tathāgata’s spiritual power and protective mindfulness.
Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not dwell in form, nor do they dwell in the marks of form.
If a bodhisattva does not dwell in form and does not dwell in the marks of form, this is called training in form.
He does not abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; he does not abide in the characteristics of consciousness.
If a bodhisattva does not abide in consciousness and does not abide in the characteristics of consciousness, this is called practicing with respect to consciousness.
Kauśika! If a bodhisattva does not practice with regard to form nor practices with regard to the characteristics of form, this is called not abiding in form.

If they do not practice with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor practice with regard to the characteristics of consciousness, this is called not abiding in consciousness.
Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they are said to "dwell" in this way and to "cultivate" it in this way.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The *prajñāpāramitā* is most profoundly deep; one cannot reach its limits or its source, for the *prajñāpāramitā* is vast and immeasurable.”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra! So it is, so it is!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not dwell on the profundity of form, nor do they dwell on the profundity of the characteristics of form.
If a bodhisattva does not dwell on the profundity of form, nor dwell on the profundity of the characteristics of form, this is what constitutes practicing the profundity of form.
One does not dwell in the profundity of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; one does not dwell in the profundity of the characteristics of consciousness.

If a bodhisattva does not dwell in the profundity of consciousness and does not dwell in the profundity of the characteristics of consciousness, this is called practicing the profundity of consciousness.
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva does not practice the profundity of form, nor practice the profundity of the characteristics of form, this is called not abiding in the profundity of form.

If they do not practice the profundity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, nor practice the profundity of the characteristics of consciousness, this is called not abiding in the profundity of consciousness.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This profound Dharma gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* should be correctly expounded for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the stage of non-retrogression and have already received their prediction.”
"Why is this? Because when those bodhisattvas hear what is taught, they will have no doubt, no regret, and will be free from all obstacles.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, then addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"As the Venerable One has said, the matter is indeed so.
Even if one were to explain it to those bodhisattvas who have not yet received their prediction, what fault would there be?"
The Venerable Śāriputra said:
"Kauśika! If one were to speak thus for the sake of a bodhisattva who has not yet received a prediction, there would be no fault."

Why is this? Although that bodhisattva has not yet received a prediction [of enlightenment], if they hear this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and with sympathetic joy, faith, and acceptance, gaze upon it, pay homage, and revere it—without being startled, terrified, retreating, or sinking—they should know that this bodhisattva has long been securely established within the Mahāyāna Dharma and has matured their roots of goodness; before long, they shall receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from one, two, or three Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

Kauśika! Although that bodhisattva has not yet received a prediction from the present Buddha, the World-Honored One, he will certainly behold all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in future ages; he shall gaze upon them, pay homage, and make offerings, receive the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, cultivate all wholesome dharmas, and even realize the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva merely hears this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, gazes upon it with reverence, and accepts it with faith, it is already said that this bodhisattva has long since been established within the Mahāyāna and has matured their roots of goodness; how much more so for one who is able to read, recite, contemplate, explain it to others, and practice it according to the principle? What can be said of such a matter?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said."

If a bodhisattva, upon briefly hearing this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, gazes upon it, pays homage, and accepts it with faith, I declare that such a bodhisattva has long since been established within the Mahāyāna and has matured their roots of goodness; how much more so for one who is able to read, recite, contemplate, explain it to others, and practice it according to the principle within this Dharma—such a person will certainly and swiftly achieve the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I would now like to employ a parable to clarify this meaning.”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra, speak as you wish.”
Śāriputra said: “World-Honored One!
It is as if there were one dwelling in the Bodhisattva vehicle who diligently seeks awakening, and at some time in a dream, finds himself already seated upon the seat of awakening.”
“World-Honored One!
When those bodhisattvas have had such a dream, it should be known that they are gradually approaching the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
It is the same for all who seek enlightenment.”

If one hears this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā and rejoices in it with faith and acceptance, you should know that such a person has long since dwelt securely within the Mahāyāna, having matured their roots of goodness, and will certainly receive the prediction of enlightenment.

How much more so for those who are able to read, recite, contemplate, explain it to others, and practice it according to the principle—know that such persons will certainly and swiftly realize the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? World-Honored One!

There are sentient beings who, due to karmic obstructions, turn their backs on wisdom as it truly is; therefore, they distance themselves from this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* and are unable to give rise to pure faith and understanding. Because of this, they cannot bring their roots of goodness to maturity.
There are sentient beings who, for a long time, have heard, accepted, and understood this Dharma; they abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and bring their roots of goodness to maturity.
World-Honored One!
You should know that such persons, abiding as in the limit of reality, shall no longer regress and will gradually draw near to the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“World-Honored One!

It is as if there were someone who wished to traverse a wilderness path of one hundred yojanas, or even up to five hundred yojanas, and who, while on that road, felt fear and doubt whether to advance or retreat.”
As this person gradually proceeds, wishing to emerge from the perilous path, he suddenly sees cowherds and shepherds; he immediately knows that the city is not far away.
At once, his mind attains peace and security, and he no longer gives rise to fears such as those of robbers and thieves.
Why is this? Because when such a person sees someone tending cattle or sheep, they know that they are gradually approaching a city or a village.
World-Honored One!

It is the same for those who seek awakening: if they hear this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, one should know that they are gradually approaching the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; before long they will receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of great awakening, and shall no longer fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
Why is this? Because hearing, beholding, paying homage to, and faithfully accepting this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā serves as a precursor.
Therefore, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should respect and revere this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā and practice it according to the principle.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma, Imperially Conferred Title of Dharma-Master, Purple Robe Awardee, and Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, under the Imperial Edict. Chapter Ten, Part Two: Praise for Upholding. At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Śāriputra! So it is, so it is!
It is just as you have said; you have skillfully drawn this analogy.
"Now, by the Buddha's spiritual power, you shall further explain this meaning through a simile.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

Furthermore, it is like a person who wishes to see the great ocean and travels toward it by stages; if they see a tree or the sign of a tree, or if they see a mountain or the sign of a mountain, one should know that this person is still far from the sea.

Furthermore, as he proceeds forward, if he no longer sees trees or the appearance of trees, nor mountains or the appearance of mountains, one should know that this person is drawing closer to the ocean. Why is this?
The great ocean is profound, vast, and boundless; near its shores, there are no signs whatsoever of mountains, trees, or the like.
Although this person has not yet reached the sea, because they no longer see those signs of mountains and trees, they know that they are gradually approaching the great ocean.
“World-Honored One!

It is likewise for a bodhisattva mahāsattva: if they hear this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā and gaze upon, prostrate to, and make offerings to it, although that person has not yet received a prediction of enlightenment in the presence of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, one should know that they are gradually approaching Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and are soon to receive their prediction.”
Why is this? Because hearing this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā serves as a preceding sign.
World-Honored One!

Furthermore, it is like the various trees in the world that, during the springtime, have branches and leaves so lush, verdant, and lovely that when the people of Jambudvīpa see these signs, they all give rise to joy and think:
"These trees will soon bloom and bear fruit."
"For what reason?
Because the signs of its blossoming have already appeared beforehand.
"World-Honored One! [he said.]

It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: if they hear this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, gaze upon it, pay homage to it, and make offerings to it, one should know that these bodhisattvas have long since matured their most excellent roots of goodness. Because of the wholesome causes and conditions from their past lives, they now personally hear and receive this true Dharma assembly of the *prajñāpāramitā* within this gathering. They are able to see all Buddhas and the multitude of worthy sages, and furthermore, the Buddhas and worthy sages, with hearts full of joy, form this thought:
"The past bodhisattvas who were about to receive their prediction of enlightenment were also like this; hearing this true Dharma served as the preliminary sign."
It should be known that this bodhisattva is now gradually approaching anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and will receive the prediction [of enlightenment] before long.
Why is this? Because the preceding signs have appeared.

Furthermore, it is like a woman in the world who is pregnant; as the months of her gestation draw to a close, her physical strength becomes exhausted and her mental consciousness becomes disturbed. Her appetite for food and drink diminishes, she grows indolent in sitting and reclining, and she no longer diligently pursues her usual desires. All manner of suffering arises, and she comes to loathe what she formerly practiced.
Having seen these signs, one should know that this person will give birth before long.
Why is this? Because the preceding signs have appeared.
“World-Honored One!

It is likewise for a bodhisattva mahāsattva: if they hear this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* and behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to it, one should know that this bodhisattva has long since matured their roots of goodness, is gradually approaching *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and will soon receive the prediction [of enlightenment].”
"Why is this? Because hearing the true Dharma serves as its precursor.
At that time, the World-Honored One further praised the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!
All that you have joyfully expounded is protected by the spiritual power of the Tathāgata."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is marvelous, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha well protects and keeps in mind the assembly of bodhisattvas, and is able to skillfully proclaim the dharmas of the bodhisattvas.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have, throughout the long night, brought great benefit to all sentient beings, providing them with profit and happiness through skillful means, out of compassion for the world and for the sake of its deliverance."

Furthermore, because these bodhisattvas diligently seek the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and having realized that fruit, desire to proclaim the essential teachings of the Dharma to all sentient beings according to what is appropriate for them, they are thus protected and remembered by all the Buddhas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), how should they contemplate so as to attain the fulfillment of the perfection of wisdom?"
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), does not perceive any characteristic of increase in form (rūpa), and does not perceive any characteristic of increase in feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), or consciousness (vijñāna), this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”
Not perceiving any sign of diminution in form, nor perceiving any sign of diminution in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Even to the point of not perceiving these as either dharmas or non-dharmas— this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and contemplates in this manner, they shall attain the fulfillment of the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, the Prajñāpāramitā is inconceivable.”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inconceivable. If a bodhisattva does not discriminate that form is inconceivable, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”
"Not discriminating that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inconceivable—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"The Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā is most supreme and profoundly deep; who will be able to believe and understand it as it truly is?

The Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying, "Those who have long practiced the bodhisattva path, upon hearing this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā, will immediately be able to believe and understand it."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
who are those bodhisattvas who have long practiced the bodhisattva path?”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not differentiate the Tathāgata’s ten powers and four fearlessnesses, does not differentiate the various meritorious qualities of the Tathāgata, and even does not differentiate all-knowledge— if they do not differentiate dharmas in this manner, such a person is one who has long practiced the bodhisattva path.”

Why is this? Because all the ten powers and four fearlessnesses of the Tathāgatas are inconceivable; all dharmas of merit, up to and including omniscience, are inconceivable. Therefore, the bodhisattva makes no conceptual distinctions regarding any phenomena.
"Because of this, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices by not practicing anything regarding phenomena, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is marvelous, World-Honored One!"
This profound Dharma gate of the Prajñāpāramitā is a great treasury of jewels, the supreme and untainted Prajñāpāramitā, which is intrinsically pure like space.

"Bhagavān! There are good sons and good daughters who, regarding this Dharma-door of the Prajñāpāramitā, receive, uphold, read, recite, remember, contemplate, and even explain it to others—how is it that many difficulties arise to create obstacles for them?"
The Buddha said to the Venerable Subhūti:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said."

When sons or daughters of good family receive, uphold, read, recite, remember, contemplate, and even explain the meaning of this Dharma-door of the Perfection of Wisdom for others, many difficult events will arise to create obstacles.
Subhūti! You should now know that when difficult circumstances arise, it is the evil Māra who creates these demonic obstacles.
Therefore, sons and daughters of good family who uphold, read, recite, and even expound this for others should act with speed and according to what is appropriate.

"Furthermore, if there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to write this Dharma-door of the Prajñāpāramitā themselves, or cause others to write it, they should complete the writing swiftly within one month, or even up to one year."
"Why is this? Within this great Dharma-treasure of the Prajñāpāramitā, there are many enemies and thieves who constantly seek to cause harm.
Furthermore, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When any sons or daughters of good family receive, uphold, recite, or even transcribe this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, if hosts of Māras seek an opportunity to cause destruction and disruption, at that time, how should they practice distancing themselves [from such influences]?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"You should now know that if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, or even transcribe this Dharma-gate, they should simply maintain a mind focused on what is to be done in accordance with reason."

Although those evil Māras may, for a long time, harbor a mind intent on destroying the Dharma and seek to annihilate this Dharma-gate, or wish to cause the subversion of those who uphold it, even if many kalpas were to pass, they would ultimately never be able to find an opportunity to do so.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When good sons and good daughters receive, uphold, read, and recite this True Dharma, if they are able to remain far removed from the activities of Māras, these persons will then be able to read and recite it with mastery, and even to transcribe it without any obstacles.”
World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, that those evil Māras seek an opportunity to harm them but cannot find it—by what power is such a thing possible?
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:

"You should know now that it is entirely through the power of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha’s majestic spiritual authority, his sustaining grace, and his protective mindfulness, that all Māras are subdued and find no opportunity. Therefore, those who uphold the Dharma are enabled to read and recite it with mastery, and even to train as taught, practice as taught, and accord with the principle of reality, all without obstruction."

Why is this? Because this profound and true Dharma encompasses the characteristics of all phenomena, which are themselves the nature of all phenomena; all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas currently dwelling and preaching the Dharma in the infinite, incalculable worlds of the ten directions, proclaim this very Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā.

Therefore, all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, by means of their supernormal powers and majestic authority, collectively protect and sustain those who uphold the Dharma, causing them to receive, maintain, read, recite, and master it, even to the point of copying it and making offerings to it; they enable them to learn as taught, to practice as taught, and to accord with reality, attaining freedom from all obstacles.

Śāriputra! As for those sons and daughters of good family who uphold the Dharma and are protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas, I do not see any hosts of evil Māras who would be able to cause them harm.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas uphold, recite, copy, and make offerings to this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā, and even study it as it is taught, practice it as it is taught, and accord with its principles, thereby being able to remain far removed from all demonic obstacles—is this also because they are protected and mindful of by the supernatural power and majesty of the Tathāgata?”
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: “It is so, it is so!
