All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have already attained the empowerment, protection, and mindfulness of the supernatural powers of all Tathāgatas; therefore, they are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and master this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and even as they train according to what is taught, practice according to what is taught, and accord with reality, they are entirely able to remain far removed from all demonic obstacles.”

Śāriputra! You should know that this bodhisattva has obtained the empowerment of the supernatural powers of all Tathāgatas; he is known and remembered by all Tathāgatas, and is collectively observed by all Tathāgatas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to receive, uphold, read, recite, remember, contemplate, and reflect upon this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and extensively explains its meaning to others, and even studies as it is taught, practices as it is taught, and accords with reality, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already drawn near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and will before long attain the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a person merely receives, maintains, reads, and recites this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā, although that person gains much merit, it is not equal to a person who, regarding this Dharma-gate, trains as taught, practices as taught, and accords with the principle."

Śāriputra! You should know that such a person is sustained by the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas; they are known and remembered by all Tathāgatas, and are the object of the collective observation of all Tathāgatas.
Such a person will possess great majesty and renown in the present life, and shall certainly attain a great fruit of retribution in the future. Why is this?

This Prajñāpāramitā is the supreme and wondrous Dharma-gate of the ultimate truth; it accords with all phenomena as they truly are and universally gathers sentient beings to abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, this Dharma gate associated with the perfection of wisdom is sustained and protected by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."

In the future age, it will first spread widely in the south; from the south, it will spread to the west, and from the west, it will spread to the north, thus circulating successively throughout all directions.

Śāriputra! After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma is about to perish, in order that good sons and good daughters may receive, uphold, read, recite, remember, contemplate, and explain its meaning to others regarding this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā, and even gain great benefit through copying and making offerings to it, the Tathāgata therefore empowers and protects it so that it may be widely disseminated.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If there are good men or good women who are able to receive and uphold this True Dharma, you should know that such persons are sustained by the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas; they are known and remembered by all Tathāgatas, and they are collectively observed by all Tathāgatas."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma-gate of the Perfection of Wisdom is most supreme and profound; how will it also be disseminated in the north during the final age at the end of time?”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

In the future final age, this Dharma shall likewise circulate in the northern direction. There, in that region, there will be sons and daughters of good family who practice the bodhisattva path; having heard this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they will be able to receive, uphold, read, recite, memorize, contemplate, transcribe, and make offerings to it.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How many people will there be in that northern direction who will be able to receive, uphold, and maintain this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*?"
"How many people are there who can read, recite, and master [this teaching], and who practice as taught, act as taught,
and accord with the principle? The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!"

Moreover, although there are many sons and daughters of good family in the northern direction who practice as bodhisattvas and are able to receive and uphold this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, few among them are able to read, recite, and master it, or to study, practice, and accord with reality as it has been taught.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If there be sons or daughters of good family in that region who, upon hearing this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, are not startled, not terrified, do not regress, and do not sink into despondency, you should know that these persons have long dwelt in the Mahāyāna and cultivated the bodhisattva practices. They have already in the past questioned the meaning of this before the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas; they have long since fully cultivated the dharmas of the bodhisattva path, and for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they have extensively practiced various deeds, diligently seeking the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Why is this? Because I have now, for the sake of these sons and daughters of good family, proclaimed the Dharma-gate of the Perfection of Wisdom associated with omniscience.

When such a person changes bodies, they will likewise delight in hearing this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, receiving it with joy and faith, and diligently cultivate the path of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. They will dwell well in the supreme practices associated with *samāhita* concentration; even all Māras cannot destroy their resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, let alone any humans or non-humans.
Why is this? Because such a person is firm and courageous, never regressing from the mind set upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, upon hearing this *prajñāpāramitā* dharma-gate, their heart is filled with great joy and attains purity; they cause all sentient beings universally to plant various roots of goodness and practice according to the principle, thereby accomplishing the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family are able to speak thus before the Buddha:

"I shall, by means of this Dharma-gate, for the sake of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *koṭi-nayuta* sentient beings, represent it according to principle, instruct them according to reality, benefit them as is appropriate, generate joy according to principle, and cause them to realize it according to reality; without ever regressing, I shall cause them all to dwell securely in the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
“Śāriputra! These sons and daughters of good family abide in the vast benefit of the Bodhisattva vehicle.
Observing their minds, I give rise to sympathetic joy.”

I, too, by means of this most profound and correct Dharma, instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of sentient beings, causing them to abide in the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

In this way, sons and daughters of good family who possess vast faith, understanding, and devotion to the Mahāyāna, and who aspire to be born within the buddha-fields of the present Buddhas to hear the sublime Dharma, shall continuously hear the exposition of this profound *prajñāpāramitā* dharma-gate.

In that buddha-field, he likewise uses this profound and correct Dharma to instruct, benefit, and gladden immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of trillions of sentient beings, causing them to abide in the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is marvelous, World-Honored One!

Regarding all phenomena of the past, future, and present, there is not the slightest thing that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha does not see, does not hear, does not know, or does not understand. He fully comprehends the various modes of conduct of all sentient beings and has attained thorough mastery over all the dharmas of the bodhisattvas.”

Furthermore, the Tathāgata fully knows all those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, in future ages, for the sake of awakening, will exert great diligence to earnestly seek this Prajñāpāramitā, obtain this Dharma-gate, receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and train as taught, practice as taught, and accord with reality.
The Tathāgata also knows those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, regarding this Dharma-door of the Perfection of Wisdom, obtain it without seeking.
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
“So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said.”

Śāriputra! Regarding all phenomena of the past, future, and present, there is not the slightest phenomenon that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha does not see, does not hear, does not know, or does not understand.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata fully knows all those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in future ages who, regarding this dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā, shall obtain it through seeking or obtain it without seeking.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha fully knows all the past roots of goodness and aspirations of bodhisattvas, as well as the dharmas of the path practiced by bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Will other profound sūtras that correspond to this Prajñāpāramitā also be obtained spontaneously without diligent seeking?”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is! Śāriputra!"
"Furthermore, all other profound sūtras that correspond to this Prajñāpāramitā will also be obtained spontaneously without seeking.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
Will all other profound sūtras associated with the six pāramitās also be spontaneously attained by good sons and good daughters in future ages, even without diligent seeking?
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra! As for all other profound sūtras associated with the six pāramitās, there will also be those in future ages that are obtained spontaneously without being sought."
Why is this? Such is the fundamental nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Sons and daughters of good family who practice the bodhisattva path should always instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *koṭi-nayuta* sentient beings through the Dharma, causing them to abide in the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, while they themselves likewise practice and study within it according to the principle.

When this person transitions to another life, they will encounter other profound sūtras that correspond to the non-apprehension of the six pāramitās and correspond to the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; such a person will likewise not seek them, yet they will obtain them spontaneously.
The Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom, the Mother of Buddhas,
Giving Birth to the Three Dharma Treasuries, Scroll Eleven.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma, Imperially Conferred Title of *Chao Feng Da Fu*, Acting *Guang Lu Qing*, and *Dharma-Transmitting Master* with the Rank of *Cizhen*, under Imperial Decree. Chapter Eleven: The Obstruction of the Dharma by the Wicked, Part One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
The Buddha has already previously explained all the merits possessed by those sons and daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, and recite the *Prajñāpāramitā* Dharma.
However, when those sons and daughters of good family receive, uphold, read, and recite this Dharma-gate, will there not be evil Māras who create obstacles?
The Buddha said to the Venerable Subhūti: "So it is, so it is!
It is very much so."
“Subhūti! There are many evil Māras who create obstacles, seeking at all times for an opportunity to strike.
Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are the characteristics of those difficult circumstances as described by the Buddha? The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If there is one who abides in the bodhisattva vehicle and practices this Dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and when they wish to explain this Dharma to others, they do not speak immediately or their speaking does not cease, they should recognize that this is the work of Māra.”
Furthermore, if a teacher of the Dharma gives rise to a mind of pride and arrogance while preaching the Dharma, they should recognize this as the work of Māra.
If anyone, while copying, upholding, reading, or reciting this dharma-gate, gives rise to a mind of contempt and mocks it with derision, they should recognize that this is the work of Māra.
If those who uphold the Dharma experience mental distraction, they should recognize this as the work of Māra.
If those who uphold the Dharma speak in mutual contradiction, they should recognize this as the work of Māra.
If there are those who uphold the Dharma whose mindfulness is unclear and who forget much, they should recognize this as the work of Māra.

If there are those who uphold the Dharma who obstruct one another and cannot harmonize, failing to give rise to reverence and faith toward this Dharma-gate, they should recognize this as the work of Māra.
If, when a person writes, maintains, reads, or recites this Dharma-gate, they are unable to discipline their own sense faculties, they should recognize this as the work of Māra.
Furthermore, if any listeners of the Dharma should suddenly think:
"I find no flavor in this Prajñāpāramitā Dharma; I have no understanding or realization of it."
"Having abandoned this teaching, they rise from their seats; one should recognize this as the work of Māra.
Furthermore, if a listener of the Dharma thinks:
'In this Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā, no prediction of my own future enlightenment is spoken; I cannot give rise to pure faith and understanding.'"
Having thought thus, they abandon [the teaching] and rise from their seats; one should recognize this as the work of Māra.
Furthermore, if a listener of the Dharma thinks:

"In this *prajñāpāramitā* dharma, my name is not mentioned, nor the city, village, or region where I dwell, nor the clan, father, mother, or personal name of those from whom I was born; for these reasons, I am unable to listen to and receive this *prajñāpāramitā* dharma-gate, and I shall therefore abandon it."
"In accordance with the thoughts that arise, one will immediately undergo retrogression for a certain number of kalpas.
Later, however, by virtue of superior causes and conditions, one shall once again be able to practice this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā."
Why is this? Because if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not hear and receive this Dharma-gate of the Perfection of Wisdom, they will be unable to accomplish mundane and supramundane dharmas.
Therefore, Subhūti, if a mind of regression arises, one should recognize that this is the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti:

If there are those who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle and are unable to seek the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) within this Dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā*, but instead cultivate and pursue the knowledge of all modes within the teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they should recognize this as the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If there are those who wish to study and accomplish mundane and supramundane dharmas, yet do not study the dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, but instead seek their path within the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
Subhūti! Those who do not study the dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā* will be unable to accomplish mundane or supramundane dharmas.

Such persons give rise to inverted wisdom; regarding this *prajñāpāramitā* dharma, they are unable to cultivate it or understand it as it truly is, but rather abandon the root and grasp at the branches and leaves.

Subhūti! It is as if there were a person in the world who, while traveling in search of food during a famine, abandons his master and goes instead to the place where laborers work to seek out food and drink.

Subhūti! All those sons and daughters of good family in future ages who fall away from the bodhisattva-dharma will likewise act in this way: they will abandon the *prajñāpāramitā*, the root dharma-gate of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and instead take up the branches and leaves within the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Subhūti! These causal conditions should be recognized as the work of Māra. Why is this?

Such a person possesses little wisdom and little insight; they claim that this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* cannot lead to that omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*). For this reason, they abandon it and instead claim that the Dharma-gates of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas can indeed accomplish omniscient wisdom; thus, they grasp only its branches and leaves.

Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize such signs as these; having recognized them, he should remain far removed from them and should not take delight in practicing or training within them. To train in such a manner is not what is appropriate.
If there are those who take delight in the teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they train in this very way. How do they train in this way? Subhūti!

That which is called the Dharma of the Śrāvakas involves merely practicing the subduing of the mark of self and realizing the quiescent nirvāṇa of self-emptiness; they claim to have attained the ultimate fruit of the Dharma, yet they are unable to apply themselves with diligence to that supreme Dharma, nor can they extensively bring great benefit to sentient beings. Therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should not train in such a manner.
What is called the training of a bodhisattva? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

having established himself in the dharma of suchness through all that he practices and learns, extensively cultivates all corresponding roots of goodness, universally gathers all immeasurable and boundless sentient beings of the world, and causes them all to dwell securely in the reality-limit (*tathatā-bhūtakoṭi*), so that each and every one realizes the supreme nirvāṇa— this is what is called the bodhisattva’s method of training.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! It is as if there were a person who wished to observe an elephant; although they have seen it, they cannot truly observe its physical characteristics. This person then turns back to seek the elephant's tracks, intending to observe and grasp the elephant's features through them."
Subhūti, what do you think? Is this person wise?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"In future ages, all those who fall away from the bodhisattva-dharma will be just like this.

These people have previously established themselves within the bodhisattva-vehicle; although they have practiced this profound *prajñāpāramitā* dharma-gate, they are unable to inquire about its meaning therein, nor can they understand its superior practices as they truly are, and thus they give rise to a mind of abandonment toward this dharma-gate."

Because they have abandoned the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are unable to realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; consequently, they instead realize *nirvāṇa* within the teachings of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, claiming for themselves that they have attained the ultimate fruit of the Dharma.
Subhūti! These causal conditions should be recognized as the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is like those people in the world who, seeking jewels, go to the great ocean desiring precious gems; yet having arrived, they are unable to extract the gems from the great ocean, and instead seek those precious gems within the water of a cow’s footprint, claiming it to be equal to the waters of the ocean.
Subhūti, what do you think? Is this person wise?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"In future ages, all those who fall away from the bodhisattva-dharma will be just like this.

These people have previously established themselves within the Bodhisattva Vehicle; although they practice this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are unable to inquire about its meaning therein, nor can they truly understand its superior practices. They give rise to a mind of renunciation toward this Dharma-gate and instead take pleasure in seeking the dharmas of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, desiring to subdue the notion of a self and realize the quiescent Nirvāṇa of self-emptiness—namely, the fruits of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhat, and Pratyekabuddha."

Within those various fruits, they perceive such phenomena and realize such principles; having attained the exhaustion of all outflows and the sublime liberation of mind, they achieve dissociation from the fetters within each respective fruit.
Subhūti! These causal conditions should be recognized as the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to such a thought. Why is this?

Because these bodhisattvas have already attained stable abiding within the Mahāyāna Dharma; they have donned the armor of diligence and performed great adornments, having long practiced the dharma-gates associated with the pāramitās, out of compassion for the world, extensively performing great benefit for all sentient beings.

Therefore, Subhūti! You should know that all those whose minds are not pliant and who give rise to inverted wisdom, who are unable to practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā* dharma-gate, who fail to perceive or understand it and thus give rise to a mind of abandonment, who cannot dwell securely within the bodhisattva-dharmas, and who do not correspond with the supreme practices of the various *pāramitās*, but instead delight only in the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—all such as these are those whose roots of goodness have not yet matured.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! It is as if there were a skilled craftsman in the world who, intending to construct a magnificent palace like that of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, instead measures the dimensions and proportions of the palaces of the sun and the moon."
Subhūti, what do you think? Can those palaces of the sun and moon surpass the exquisite palace of Śakra?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"In the future age, all those who shall fall away from the bodhisattva-dharma will be just like this.

These people have previously established themselves within the Bodhisattva Vehicle; yet, although they have heard, received, and practiced this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are unable to inquire about its meaning therein, nor can they truly understand its superior practices as they really are."

Due to this lack of understanding, they develop a mind of rejection toward this Dharma-gate and, conversely, within the teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they delight in and seek out the subduing of the mark of self; they grasp at the realization of the quiescent Nirvāṇa of self-emptiness, claiming for themselves that they have already attained the ultimate fruit of the Dharma.
Subhūti! These causal conditions should be recognized as the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!

Furthermore, it is like a person who desires to see a universal monarch (cakravartin); although they do manage to see him, they are unable to truly perceive his physical marks, majestic power, or merit, and instead observe the physical marks of various minor kings, claiming that he is no different from them.
Subhūti, what do you think? Is the physical appearance and majestic virtue of that wheel-turning sage king equal to those of the various minor kings?
Subhūti said, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Subhūti:
"In future ages, all those who shall fall away from the bodhisattva-dharma will be just like this.

Such persons have previously established themselves within the Bodhisattva Vehicle; yet, although they may hear, receive, and practice this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are unable to inquire about its meaning therein, nor can they truly understand its supreme practices as they really are."
Due to this lack of understanding, they develop a mind of rejection toward this Dharma gate, instead seeking with longing and interest within the teachings of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Subhūti! These causal conditions should be recognized as the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!

For the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the Tathāgata has expounded the profound Dharma-gate of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) through various skillful means, so that by practicing and training therein, these bodhisattvas may achieve the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Subhūti! Therefore, by means of this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā, the Tathāgata provides correct representation, authentic instruction, beneficial guidance, and appropriate inspiration for the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, so that they may enter and abide in the Dharma-gate of the ultimate truth, and cause those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas not to regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who thus dwells in non-retrogression and is already securely established in this Mahāyāna Dharma should, having abandoned it, instead give rise to a mind of seeking and pursuit toward the inferior vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
"What do you think? Is this person wise? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Regarding these causes and conditions, one should recognize them as the work of Māra."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! It is as if there were a person, oppressed by hunger and thirst, who wandered about seeking food. Upon seeing a hundred-flavored, exquisite meal, he conceived a mind of rejection and could not take it; instead, he took some sixty-day-old rice, and having eaten it, he found it delightful."
Subhūti, what do you think? Would this person be considered wise?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"In future ages, all those who fall away from the bodhisattva-dharma will be just like this.

These people have previously established themselves within the Bodhisattva Vehicle; yet, although they have heard and practiced this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are unable to inquire about its meaning therein, nor can they truly understand its supreme practices."
Due to this lack of understanding, they develop a mind of rejection toward this Dharma-gate, and instead take pleasure in seeking and pursuing the teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Subhūti! These causal conditions should be recognized as the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!
Furthermore, it is like a person who, upon seeing a priceless mani-jewel, is unable to take it and instead takes a crystal gem, claiming that it is no different from that mani-jewel.
Subhūti, what do you think? Would such a person be considered wise?
Subhūti said, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Subhūti:
"In the future age, all those who fall away from the bodhisattva-dharma will be just like this.

These people have previously established themselves within the Bodhisattva Vehicle; yet, although they have heard and practiced this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are unable to inquire about its meaning therein, nor are they able to understand the superior practices as they truly are."

Due to this lack of understanding, they develop a mind of rejection toward this Dharma-gate, instead seeking all-knowledge within the teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, claiming that these are no different from the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattvas.
Subhūti! These causal conditions should be recognized as the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!

If, when someone writes down, receives, upholds, recites, or explains this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā, their mind becomes distracted whether they are advancing or retreating, one should know that each such instance is the work of Māra.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
can the Prajñāpāramitā be written down?”
The Buddha said, “No, Subhūti!
The perfection of wisdom cannot be apprehended through letters; all letters serve only to reveal this dharma-gate.”
Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is free from the characteristics of letters; ultimately, it cannot be found by seeking it within letters.
If someone were to say: "I am writing letters, and that is precisely what constitutes writing the Prajñāpāramitā," [they would be mistaken].
"Subhūti! By these causes and conditions, one should recognize this as the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If there is anyone who, while writing, upholding, reading, or reciting this Dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, does not maintain a single-pointed mind but gives rise to various thoughts—namely, thoughts of cities, towns, villages, gardens, groves, ponds, and pools;

of parents, teachers, elders, and various relatives and friends; of one's own body or the bodies of others, whether internal or external; of all things such as food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine; of song, dance, play, and laughter; of suffering and pleasure, sorrow and joy, or objects that are agreeable and disagreeable; and even thoughts of greed, hatred, and delusion.

One should know that each and every such thought that arises is a hindrance created by Māra, intended to cause the practitioner’s mind to become distracted so that they cannot write down, uphold, read, or recite this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti! Regarding these causes and conditions, one should recognize them as the work of Māra.
Therefore, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having recognized them, should remain far removed from them, so that Māras do not find an opportunity to exploit them.

Furthermore, if, while a person is writing, upholding, reading, or reciting this Dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, they think of matters of state and thereby create obstacles and hindrances such that they are unable to write, uphold, read, or recite this Dharma-gate, one should recognize this as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, if when a person writes, upholds, reads, or recites this Dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, they calculate and deliberate over wealth, treasures, and the necessities of life, using these as causes and conditions to create obstacles and hindrances, such that they are unable to write, uphold, read, or recite this Dharma-gate, one should recognize this as the work of Māra.

"Furthermore, if, when a person writes, upholds, reads, or recites this Dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, they dwell upon worldly speech and phrases, thereby creating obstacles and hindrances such that they are unable to write, uphold, read, or recite this Dharma-gate, one should recognize this as the work of Māra."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If there should be someone who writes down, maintains, reads, or recites this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, various evil Māras may manifest in the guise of bhikṣus and come before them, saying:
'I have a Dharma-gate that you should study; by writing it down, receiving, maintaining, reading, reciting, and practicing it in this way, you will be able to reach the fruit of omniscience.'"
"Subhūti! By these causes and conditions, one should recognize this as the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If there are those who abide in the Bodhisattva Vehicle and desire to master the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, yet are unable to understand the Bodhisattva teachings as they truly are, and instead give rise to a mind of seeking within the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—thinking that because those teachings also speak of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they are equal to and no different from the Bodhisattva vehicle—[they are mistaken].

Subhūti! If one wishes to thoroughly understand the supreme wisdom of the skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, one should seek it as it truly is within this profound *prajñāpāramitā* dharma. Furthermore, if one should practice other dharmas of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, one should recognize that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If those who hear this Dharma-gate of the Perfection of Wisdom desire to listen, while the speaker becomes weary, one should recognize this as the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, if at any time the speaker desires to speak while the listener is weary and indolent, one should recognize this as the work of Māra.

Moreover, if at any time those listeners desire to hear and receive this Dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and having heard it, wish to copy, read, and recite it, yet the speaker does not immediately teach it for them, but instead speaks of other sūtras and dharmas with a mind of frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*)."

Due to these causes and conditions, they will be unable to reach an agreement, causing those who would listen to the Dharma to be unable to write down, uphold, read, or recite the Prajñāpāramitā; one should recognize this as the work of Māra.

"Furthermore, there may be a time when that teacher of the Dharma is not weary or discouraged and desires to proclaim the Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, yet the listener of the Dharma resides in a different location."
For these reasons, they will be unable to reach a harmonious accord; one should recognize this as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, at times when that Dharma-preacher has few desires, is joyful, avoids meaningless speech, and delights in preaching the Dharma, yet the listener’s physical strength is exhausted and weary, and their consciousness is dull and heavy.
Due to these causes and conditions, they will be unable to harmonize; they will not obtain the Prajñāpāramitā to copy, uphold, read, or recite. One should recognize this as the work of Māra.
Furthermore, at times when those who hear the Dharma possess faith and joy and desire to hear this teaching, yet the teacher of the Dharma creates various obstacles and is unwilling to speak it.

Due to these causes and conditions, they will be unable to reach an agreement, thereby preventing those who wish to hear the Dharma from copying, upholding, reading, or reciting the *Prajñāpāramitā*. One should recognize this as the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, if at that time the listener desires to hear this Dharma, yet the speaker has not mastered the recitation and study, the listener will take no pleasure in hearing it."
Due to these causes and conditions, they will be unable to harmonize; they will not be able to write down, uphold, read, or recite the Prajñāpāramitā. One should recognize this as the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, if at a time when that teacher of the Dharma desires to preach it, the listener, due to other circumstances, does not desire to listen and receive it;
because of this cause and condition, they are unable to come together and thus fail to copy, maintain, read, or recite the Prajñāpāramitā—this should be recognized as the work of Māra."

Furthermore, at times when that teacher of the Dharma desires to preach the Dharma, the listeners may be overcome by sleep, being so heavy with lethargy and fatigue that they are unable to listen and receive it.
Due to these causes and conditions, they will be unable to harmonize; they will not be able to write down, uphold, read, or recite the Prajñāpāramitā. One should recognize this as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, at times when those who listen to the Dharma desire to hear it, yet the teacher of the Dharma is overcome by sleep, weighed down by lethargy and fatigue, and takes no pleasure in teaching the Dharma.
Due to these causes and conditions, they will be unable to harmonize; they will not be able to write down, uphold, read, or recite the Prajñāpāramitā. One should recognize this as the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If someone were to write down, uphold, read, or recite this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and someone else were to come and say to them:

'You should know that in the various realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras there are manifold sufferings; you ought to distance yourselves from such painful sensations and instead practice so as to transcend all such destinies, bring an end to suffering, and realize nirvāṇa.'"
"Subhūti! One who speaks in this manner should recognize that this is the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If, while someone is writing, upholding, reading, or reciting this Dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, someone should come and say:

"In the various heavenly realms there is supreme and wondrous bliss; that is to say, in the desire realm there are the pleasures of the five desires, in the form realm there is the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and in the formless realm there is the bliss of the concentration of cessation."

All such pleasures are conditioned and impermanent; their characteristics of decay and ruin are ultimately devoid of reality. The three realms are entirely empty and all phenomena are without self. You who possess wisdom should understand this clearly, rather than seeking to realize the fruits of a srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat.
"Having attained this fruit, one will no longer undergo future rebirths. Subhūti!
To speak in such a way is to create an obstacle to the sublime practice of a bodhisattva; one should recognize this as the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a Dharma-preacher stays alone in a single place but thinks of a retinue, he will say:
'If there is anyone who can follow me, I shall give them the Prajñāpāramitā. "
‘To those who do not follow me, I shall not grant this Prajñāpāramitā.
Then, certain sons of good family, out of a desire to seek the Dharma and out of reverence for the True Dharma, each went forth to follow that Dharma teacher.

Then, at another time, that Dharma teacher suddenly finds his mind no longer inclined to preach the Prajñāpāramitā to his assembly of followers; he shall instead go to places of perilous difficulty—regions of famine and drought, teeming with tigers, wolves, insects, and beasts, and filled with the terrors of bandits.
Then that Dharma Master addressed his assembly, saying:
"O sons of good family!
This place is plagued by famine and perilous hardships, and is utterly terrifying; how can you endure such suffering?"
"You should deliberate for yourself; it would not be right to regret this later.
By means of such subtle causes, conditions, and skillful means, the speaker of the Dharma distances himself from the assembly of listeners.
At that time, when those people learned of this matter, they said to one another:
"This mark of seclusion is not the mark of the *prajñāpāramitā*."
"Therefore, those people each withdrew and no longer followed him. Subhūti!
For this reason, they were unable to come together; they could not copy, uphold, read, or recite the Prajñāpāramitā. You should recognize this as the work of Māra."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a Dharma-preacher should at times wish to go into a place filled with extremely terrifying and wicked insects, beasts, and non-human beings, or into places such as famine-stricken regions, parched lands, or perilous difficulties, he should say to the listeners of the Dharma:
'O sons of good family!'"
"You should know, sirs, that the place where I am going is extremely perilous and evil; you should not follow after me.

Subhūti, when a teacher of the Dharma uses such subtle causes and conditions as a skillful means to distance themselves, and the listeners are unable to remain in harmony, such that they do not obtain, write down, uphold, read, or recite the *prajñāpāramitā*, one should recognize this as the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a Dharma-preacher frequently visits the homes of his relatives and later says to those who listen to the Dharma:
'I have relatives; you should go to them to beg for whatever you require, such as food, drink, clothing, and articles for use.'"

For this reason, they will be hindered and obstructed from hearing and receiving the Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*; consequently, they will be unable to write it down, uphold it, read it, or recite it. One should recognize that this is the work of Māra.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Regarding such signs as these, you should know that each one is a skillful means employed by Māra to create obstacles and difficulties. His intent is to prevent those who practice the Bodhisattva path from obtaining this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and to hinder them from hearing, receiving, practicing, writing, maintaining, reading, and reciting it."

Therefore, those who practice the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas should always maintain awareness at all times; having become aware, they should remain detached, so that those Māras may find no opportunity.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma (Shi Hu), Imperially Appointed Grand Officer for Court Service, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, Holder of the Purple Robe, under Imperial Edict. Chapter Eleven, Part Two: The Obstruction of the Dharma by the Wicked. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

For what reason does Māra, over a long period of time, diligently employ skillful means to create various obstacles and difficulties, thereby preventing those who practice the Bodhisattva Dharma from hearing, receiving, practicing, copying, upholding, and reciting the true Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:

"You should now know that this Prajñāpāramitā gives birth to the omniscience of all Buddhas; from that omniscience, the True Dharma of all Buddhas is further produced; and from the Dharma of all Buddhas, immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings are born."
By means of their power of skillful wisdom, the Buddhas cause all sentient beings to sever all afflictions.

Because the afflictions are severed, those evil Māras find no opportunity to observe them; since they cannot find such an opportunity to create obstacles and difficulties, their minds give rise to suffering and distress.

With a mind of suffering and distress, they therefore exert themselves for a long time through diligent means to perform difficult tasks, thereby preventing those who practice the Bodhisattva Dharma from hearing, receiving, practicing, copying, maintaining, and reciting the sublime Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Those evil Māras may employ skillful means to appear before a son of good family who has newly entered the Great Vehicle and say to him:
'What you have heard and received is not the true Prajñāpāramitā. I possess a sūtra and dharma that is the true Prajñāpāramitā; you should follow me and practice and study in this way.'"

"Subhūti! By such means, those evil Māras seek to destroy wholesome dharmas; yet, sons of good family who have newly entered the Mahāyāna, possessing little wisdom and little faith, and who have not yet received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, will find their minds timid and weak, and thus be seized by Māra."

Because they are possessed by Māra, they will not obtain this true Dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor will they listen to it, receive it, practice it, write it down, uphold it, or recite it. Subhūti!
Regarding these causes and conditions, one should recognize them as the work of Māra.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, those evil Māras may at times manifest themselves in the form of bhikṣus; with a mind intent on destroying the Dharma, they falsely cultivate the profound and supreme practices of a bodhisattva, yet within that context, they claim to have realized the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) by means of the fruit of a śrāvaka."
Subhūti! These causal conditions should be recognized as the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!

Those evil Māras, by means of such various expedients, create all manner of obstacles and difficulties against this true Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā, so that no one may write it down, uphold it, read it, or recite it.

Therefore, those who cultivate the Dharma of a bodhisattva should always maintain clear awareness; having become aware, they should distance themselves from [unwholesome states], immediately giving rise to a courageous and superior mind of diligence, and remaining firm and stable in right mindfulness and right situational awareness.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Sugata!”
It is like a great heap of precious jewels, for which many enemies and bandits constantly lie in wait, seeking to steal them.
Why is this? Because such treasures are difficult to obtain and their value is immeasurable.
For these reasons, there are many enemies and bandits.
Now, this great Dharma-treasure of the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise beset by many obstacles and difficulties; evil Māras constantly watch for and seek opportunities to harm it.

Therefore, you should know that any sons of good family who have newly entered the Great Vehicle, possessing little wisdom and little faith, with hearts that are timid and weak, and who are unable to hear, receive, practice, copy, maintain, read, or recite this most profound and vast Dharma, are all under the influence of the power of Māra.
World-Honored One!

If there should be a person who, amidst such various difficult matters, exerts courageous diligence with a mind that does not slacken or retreat, and firmly practices, transcribes, upholds, reads, and recites this Dharma-gate—would this not be sustained by the supernatural power and majesty of all Buddhas?
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, it is so, it is so!”
It is as you have said.

If there are those who, amidst such difficult circumstances as these, are able to hear, receive, practice, copy, maintain, read, and recite this Dharma-gate, you should know that they are all protected and mindful of by the supernatural power and majesty of all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Why is this? Although those hosts of evil Māras have for a long time diligently applied skillful means to create obstacles to this Dharma-gate,
the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has likewise for a long time diligently applied skillful means to empower and protect this Prajñāpāramitā Dharma-gate through his majestic spiritual power.
Chapter Twelve: Revealing the World, Part One. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
“It is like a worldly mother who gives birth to children—whether one, ten, a hundred, or a thousand.”
Suddenly, at one time, his mother fell ill; each of her sons diligently sought various means and applied many treatments.
They all thought to themselves:

"How can we cause our mother to quickly be freed from the manifold sufferings of diseases such as wind, bile, phlegm, and swelling, and how can we bring peace, ease, and harmony to her faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind?"
How can one cause the mother’s food and drink to increase, her physical strength and complexion to become firm, and her various painful sensations to cease so that she attains great happiness?
How can one cause the mother’s lifespan to be long and enduring, so that she remains in this world for a long time?

Why is this? Because this body of mine currently exists in the world, having been born from a mother and brought forth with great difficulty; for these reasons, the debt of gratitude toward one's mother is paramount.

"Subhūti! All the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently residing in the ten directions likewise do so; each, through the majestic power of their supernormal knowledges, empowers and protects this profound Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā, out of compassion for all sentient beings in the world, so that they may everywhere hear, write, uphold, read, and recite it."
Those Tathāgatas all had this thought:
"How may this sublime Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā long abide in the world?
How may this sublime Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā remain free from the signs of destruction?"

How may this sublime Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā be obtained so that it may be universally written down, upheld, recited, and propagated throughout the world, ensuring that no evil Māras may find an opportunity to prevail?
"Subhūti! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, at all times diligently employs skillful means to praise and protectively mind the Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā."
Why is this? This Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas.

All the omniscience of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas is truly born from this Prajñāpāramitā; furthermore, this Prajñāpāramitā is able to reveal the Buddhas and manifest the characteristics of all worlds.

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past and future—whether they have already attained or shall attain it—it is solely because of this Prajñāpāramitā that they achieve the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Furthermore, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently residing in the infinite asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions, who dwell in the world preaching the Dharma and extensively bringing benefit to sentient beings, have likewise attained the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of this Prajñāpāramitā.

Subhūti! You should know that all Buddhas of the three periods of time come forth from the Prajñāpāramitā; the Prajñāpāramitā is able to give birth to them well. Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the Buddhas and can manifest the characteristics of all worlds.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

As the Buddha has taught, if the *prajñāpāramitā* is able to manifest the characteristics of the world, how should the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha explain what constitutes the characteristics of the world?"
“I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will extensively reveal this for us.
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:

“The Buddha has taught that the five aggregates are the characteristics of the world—namely, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—and it is through the Prajñāpāramitā that such characteristics are revealed.”
Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does the prajñāpāramitā demonstrate the five aggregates as being the world?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“You should know that the Prajñāpāramitā reveals the mark of the destruction and non-destruction of the five aggregates; the intrinsic nature of the five aggregates is without action, without arising, and in their destruction there is nothing to be destroyed.”

Why is this? Because that emptiness is by its very nature without action, without arising, without destruction, and nothing to be destroyed; signlessness and wishlessness are by their very nature without action, without arising, without destruction, and nothing to be destroyed; the nature of the dharma-realm is likewise without action, without arising, without destruction, and nothing to be destroyed—and these five aggregates are also thus.
Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has taught the Prajñāpāramitā to reveal the characteristics of the world. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Tathāgata comes from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and is able to know, exactly as they truly are, the natures of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.
How does the Tathāgata know them as they truly are?

That which is called the intrinsic nature of sentient beings is the nature of reality as it is (*yathābhūtatā*); it is born from the *prajñāpāramitā*, and the Tathāgata is likewise born from the *prajñāpāramitā*. Therefore, the Tathāgata is able to know the natures of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings exactly as they are.
Because he truly understands the nature of sentient beings, he likewise knows, in accordance with reality, all the mental activities of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings.
Because he understands the mental activities of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, the Buddha says that the *prajñāpāramitā* reveals the characteristics of the world.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, it is by means of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the concentrated minds and the distracted minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings."
How does the Tathāgata know the concentrated minds of sentient beings?
It is said that whether gathered or dispersed, he knows them as they truly are as they abide within the *dharmatā*.
To know them as they truly are is precisely to know the concentrated minds of sentient beings.
Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Tathāgata is able to know that immeasurable and incalculable number of sentient beings thus collect their minds.
How does the Tathāgata know the distracted minds of sentient beings?
That which is called abiding within the dharma-nature means knowing that the mind is signless; because the mind is signless, it is neither exhausted nor inexhaustible.
To know, as it truly is, the characteristics of exhaustion and non-exhaustion is precisely to know the distracted minds of sentient beings.

Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Tathāgata is able to know that the minds of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings are thus distracted. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
By means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the inexhaustible minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.
How does the Tathāgata know the inexhaustible minds of sentient beings?

Subhūti! What is called knowing that the mind is indestructible: because the mind is indestructible, the mind has neither arising nor ceasing; because there is no arising or ceasing, it has neither abiding nor dependence. It is without any characteristic of exhaustion, as vast and inexhaustible as space, and the nature of the mind is likewise so.
Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Tathāgata is able to know that the minds of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings are thus inexhaustible.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
By means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the defiled minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.
How does the Tathāgata know the defiled minds of sentient beings?
Subhūti! That which is called knowing the defiled mind as it truly is, is itself not a defiled mind.
Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the Tathāgata is able to know such defiled minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, it is by means of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings that are free from defilement."
How does the Tathāgata know that sentient beings have minds free from defilement?
Subhūti, it is by thoroughly understanding the intrinsic nature of the defiled mind; for within a mind free from defilement, there is no characteristic of a "mind free from defilement."
Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Tathāgata is able to know that immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings have thus become free from defiled minds.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
By means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the various cognizing minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.
How does the Tathāgata know the cognizing minds of sentient beings?
Subhūti! That which is called "knowing" refers to the realization that the various cognizing minds, such as the ālayavijñāna and others, lack the characteristic of being a cognizing mind.
Therefore, by means of the prajñāpāramitā, the Tathāgata is able to know the cognizing minds of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings in this way.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, by means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the grasping minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings."
How does the Tathāgata know the grasping mind of sentient beings?
Subhūti, it is by understanding that there is no characteristic of anything to be grasped; because the characteristic of grasping is absent, it is ungraspable.
Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Tathāgata is able to know that such grasping minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings exist.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
By means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the defiled minds (*sāsrava-citta*) of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings.
How does the Tathāgata know the defiled minds of sentient beings?
Subhūti! What is called the thorough understanding that the mind has no intrinsic nature—because it lacks intrinsic nature, there is no conceptual differentiation.
Therefore, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgata is able to know that the defiled minds (*sāsrava-citta*) of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings are thus.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, it is by means of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the untainted minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings."
How does the Tathāgata know the untainted mind of sentient beings?
Subhūti, it is by realizing that the mind has no intrinsic nature, which is to say it is not a portion of the mind.
Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the Tathāgata is able to know such untainted minds of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
By means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the greedy minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.
How does the Tathāgata know the greedy minds of sentient beings?

Subhūti! That which is called "thoroughly knowing" is this: if one dwells in desire, the mind is not in accordance with reality; if the mind is in accordance with reality, one does not dwell in desire. Within the dharma of equality, no mind of desire can be found.
Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the Tathāgata is able to know such greedy minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings. "Furthermore, Subhūti!
It is by means of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, that immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings have abandoned the mind of greed.
How does the Tathāgata know that sentient beings have abandoned the mind of greed?

Subhūti! What is called knowing the mind as it truly is: whether it be greed or freedom from greed, neither can be apprehended; because they cannot be apprehended, there is no characteristic of a mind free from greed.
Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata is able to know that immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings have thus become free from a mind of greed.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
It is by means of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the minds of ill-will of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.
How does the Tathāgata know the minds of ill-will of sentient beings?

Subhūti! That which is called the thorough understanding that the mind abides in emptiness and stillness, being free from the marks of objects of perception and devoid of all conceptual discrimination—
therefore, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgata is able to know such minds of anger in immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, it is by means of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, that immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings are free from a mind of malice."
How does the Tathāgata know that sentient beings are free from a mind of ill-will? Subhūti,
it is because he understands that the dharmas of the mind are non-dual and arise from reality.
Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata is able to know that immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings are thus free from a mind of malice. "Furthermore, Subhūti!
By means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the deluded minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.
How does the Tathāgata know the deluded minds of sentient beings?
Subhūti! That which is called "knowing" means that if the mind abides in delusion, the mind is not as it truly is; if the mind is as it truly is, it does not abide in delusion.
Therefore, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgata is able to know such deluded minds of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, it is by means of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings that are free from delusion."
How does the Tathāgata know that sentient beings have minds free from delusion?

Subhūti, it is because he understands that if the mind has any attachment, the mind follows the characteristics of delusion; if the mind abides in suchness, it does not follow the characteristics of delusion. For this reason, no characteristic of a mind "free from delusion" can be apprehended.
Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata is able to know that immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings have thus become free from deluded minds. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
It is because of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the faulty minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.
How does the Tathāgata know the faulty minds of sentient beings?

Subhūti! What is called "thoroughly knowing" is this: if a mind gives rise to faults, that mind is not as it truly is; if a mind is as it truly is, faults do not arise. Within the dharma of equality, no faulty mind can be found.
Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the Tathāgata is able to know such faulty minds of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings. "Furthermore, Subhūti!
By means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, that immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings are free from a mind of transgression.
How does the Tathāgata know that sentient beings are free from a mind of transgression?
Subhūti! That which is called "thoroughly knowing" means that if the mind has any attachment, faults will arise accordingly.
If the mind abides in suchness, faults do not arise; because of this, no mental characteristic apart from faultlessness can be apprehended.
Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Tathāgata is able to know that immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings possess minds thus free from faults.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
By means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the vast minds of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings.
How does the Tathāgata know the vast minds of sentient beings?
Subhūti! That which is called "knowing this mind" means knowing it as neither increasing nor decreasing, without abiding and without attachment.
Therefore, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgata is able to know such vast minds of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, by means of the perfection of wisdom,
the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, that immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings do not possess expansive minds."
How does the Tathāgata know that sentient beings do not have expansive minds?
Subhūti, it is because he thoroughly understands that the mind has no location; since it has no location, it neither arises nor expands.
Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata is able to know that immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings have such non-expansive minds. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
It is because of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the great minds of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings.
How does the Tathāgata know the great minds of sentient beings?
Subhūti! What is called "knowing this mind" is to understand that its self-nature is equal and without differentiation.
Therefore, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgata is able to know such great minds of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, it is by means of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, that immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings do not possess the great mind."
How does the Tathāgata know that sentient beings do not possess a great mind?
Subhūti, it is because he thoroughly understands that the mind has neither coming nor going.
Therefore, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgata is able to know that immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings do not possess such a great mind.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
It is because of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the immeasurable and innumerable minds of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings.
How does the Tathāgata know the immeasurable minds of sentient beings?
Subhūti! That which is called "understanding that the mind has no basis" means that because it has no basis, it is immeasurable.
Therefore, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgata is able to know such immeasurable minds of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, it is by means of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the present minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings."
"How does the Tathāgata know the present minds of sentient beings?
Subhūti, it is by knowing that the intrinsic nature of all minds is without manifestation."

Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Tathāgata is able to know the present minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings in this way. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
By means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings whose minds are not manifest.
How does the Tathāgata know the non-manifest minds of sentient beings?
Subhūti! It is because the mind is understood to be without form or characteristics and its self-nature is detached; because its nature is detached, it neither manifests nor does not manifest.
Therefore, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgata is able to know that the minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings do not manifest in this way.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! By means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the superior minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings."
"How does the Tathāgata know the superior minds of sentient beings?
Subhūti, it is by thoroughly knowing that if the mind abides in accordance with reality, it is neither produced nor existent; this is what is called 'superior.'"
Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*),
the Tathāgata is able to know such supreme minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
It is by means of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the unsurpassed minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.
How does the Tathāgata know the unsurpassed minds of sentient beings?
Subhūti! That which is called the thorough understanding that the mind is ungraspable and free from all conceptual proliferation—
by means of this, the Tathāgata, through the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), is able to know such unsurpassed minds of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, it is by means of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the concentrated minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings."
How does the Tathāgata know the concentrated mind of sentient beings?
Subhūti, it is because he thoroughly understands that this mind is equal; within the state of equality, there are no signs of concentration or distraction, just as space is tranquil and unmoving.

Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Tathāgata is able to know that such minds of concentration belong to immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
By means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, that immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings have minds that are not fixed.
How does the Tathāgata know that the minds of sentient beings are not fixed?

Subhūti! That which is called "understanding that the mind is neither equal nor unequal" is precisely the equality of the mind; because the mind is equal, it cannot be apprehended as having the characteristics of a fixed mind.
Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata is able to know that the minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings are not fixed in this way.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
It is because of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the liberated minds of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings.
How does the Tathāgata know the liberated minds of sentient beings?
Subhūti! That which is called the thorough knowledge of the self-nature liberation of sentient beings is that the nature of those sentient beings is itself the nature of liberation.
Therefore, it is by means of the Prajñāpāramitā that the Tathāgata [attains this].
He is able to know that the minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings are thus liberated. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
it is by means of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings that are not liberated."
How does the Tathāgata know that the minds of sentient beings are not liberated?

Subhūti, it is because he understands that the nature of the mind neither comes nor goes and has no abiding; it cannot be apprehended within the three periods of time—past, future, or present—and since the nature of liberation is detached, that which is characterized as "not liberated" is likewise unapprehendable.
Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Tathāgata is able to know that the minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings are not liberated in this way.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
It is because of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the invisible minds of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings.
How does the Tathāgata know the invisible minds of sentient beings?

Subhūti! What is called knowing the minds of those sentient beings is that they are neither produced nor accomplished, without discrimination and nothing to be grasped; they are free from all marks and invisible. Even the wisdom-eye and the divine eye cannot perceive them, let alone the fleshly eye.
"Therefore, by means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Tathāgata is able to know the minds of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings as they are—invisible.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Regarding all such minds, the Tathāgata, by means of the perfection of wisdom, knows each one exactly as it is."
For this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā is able to manifest the characteristics of all worlds.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma (Shi Hu), Imperially Conferred Title of Zifu, Dharma-Master and Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, under the decree of the Great Tang. Chapter Twelve, Part Two: Manifesting the World. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:

“Furthermore, by means of the Prajñāpāramitā, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, as well as the arising and ceasing of the various activities of individuals (*pudgala*) who hold diverse views.”
How does the Tathāgata know the arising and ceasing of the various activities (*saṃskāra*) of all sentient beings and of individuals (*pudgala*) with diverse views?

Subhūti, it is by thoroughly knowing the arising and ceasing of the various activities that sentient beings initiate— those which arise in dependence upon form (*rūpa*), and those which arise in dependence upon feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
How do they arise in dependence upon form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?

It refers to those individuals with various views who give rise to such views as: "The self and the world are eternal," or "Form is eternal," or "The self and the world are impermanent," or "Both eternal and impermanent," or "Neither eternal nor impermanent."

In this way, the self and the world are eternal; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are eternal; the self and the world are impermanent; they are both eternal and impermanent; they are neither eternal nor impermanent.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent; they are both permanent and impermanent; they are neither permanent nor impermanent.
Furthermore, the self and the world are finite; form is finite.
I and the world are infinite; they are both finite and infinite; they are neither finite nor infinite.
Form is infinite; it is both finite and infinite; it is neither finite nor infinite.
In this way, the self and the world are finite; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are finite.
The self and the world are infinite; they are both finite and infinite; they are neither finite nor infinite.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are infinite, both finite and infinite, neither finite nor infinite.
Furthermore, after death, form is identical to the transmigrating self, not identical to it, both identical and not identical, or neither identical nor not identical.

In the same way, after death, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness neither go on, nor do they not go on, nor do they both go on and not go on, nor is it that they neither go on nor do not go on.
Furthermore, [one might hold that] the body is identical to the self, or that the body and the self are distinct.

Likewise, one might hold that form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are identical to the body and the self, or that form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are distinct from the body and the self.
All these views arise based upon the five aggregates; these are all the various deluded views regarding the person (pudgala), which the Tathāgata understands individually and exactly as they are.

Subhūti! For this reason, by means of the prajñāpāramitā, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is able to know the emergence and disappearance of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, as well as those individuals (pudgala) with various views.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! By means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the characteristics of the form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings."
"How does the Tathāgata know the physical forms of sentient beings?
Subhūti, it is by means of thoroughly knowing the suchness (tathatā) of form."
How does the Tathāgata know the characteristics of the feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousness of sentient beings? Subhūti,
it is by means of thoroughly knowing the suchness (tathatā) of feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness.

Subhūti! For this reason, the suchness of the arising and passing away of sentient beings as spoken of by the Tathāgata is the very suchness of the five aggregates; the suchness of the five aggregates is the very suchness of the world.
Why is this? Because the suchness of the five aggregates and the suchness of the world are not different.
Therefore, the suchness of the five aggregates is the suchness of the world, and the suchness of the world is the suchness of all phenomena.

The suchness of all dharmas is the suchness of the fruit of stream-entry; the suchness of the fruit of stream-entry is the suchness of the fruit of once-returning; the suchness of the fruit of once-returning is the suchness of the fruit of non-returning; the suchness of the fruit of non-returning is the suchness of the fruit of arhatship; the suchness of the fruit of arhatship is the suchness of the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood; and the suchness of the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood is the suchness of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, the Tathāgata, the fruits of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the world of the five aggregates, and indeed all phenomena, are of one and the same suchness (*tathatā*).

Thus, these various suchnesses are neither of a single nature nor of multiple natures; they transcend both manifold natures and the absence of manifold natures. They are non-dual and without discrimination, unconditioned and inexhaustible.
Subhūti! It is because of the *prajñāpāramitā* that the Tathāgata attains this suchness (*tathatā*); because he has realized this suchness, he is called the Tathāgata.
For this reason, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, declares that the *prajñāpāramitā* can reveal the world.

The Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas, giving birth to all Buddhas; because they are born from this, they realize all phenomena exactly as they are, without distinction, and by realizing this suchness (tathatā), they appear in the world and achieve the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, the dharma of suchness (*tathatā*) is most supreme and profoundly deep; it is because of this suchness that the Buddha attains the fruit of bodhi.”
"Bhagavān! This Dharma is extremely profound; who is able to believe and understand it?
Is it not only those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas established in non-retrogression, arhats whose vows are fulfilled, and individuals possessing right view who are able to believe and understand it?"
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, it is so, it is so!
It is as you have said.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, that which is the suchness of dharmas is an inexhaustible characteristic, most supreme and profound."
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has proclaimed that mark of inexhaustibility exactly as it is.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, along with the other sons of the gods in the desire realm, and twenty thousand sons of the gods from the Brahma assembly of the form realm, came to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, they prostrated with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the sons of the gods each addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“The Dharma taught by the Buddha is most supreme and profoundly deep; how could there be the formation of signs within it?
The Buddha said, “O sons of the gods!...”
All phenomena have emptiness as their characteristic, and signlessness and wishlessness as their characteristics.

These characteristics are without arising or cessation, without defilement or purity; the dharma-realm is quiescent like empty space, having no basis of reliance, such that its characteristic is itself characteristicless.
