The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught that form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also have this same characteristic: namely, that their characteristics are without characteristics (*lakṣaṇālakṣaṇa*). Yet these various characteristics cannot be destroyed; they cannot be destroyed by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Why is this? Because those gods, humans, asuras, and others possess marks of existence.
O sons of the gods!
"If someone were to ask, 'Who created space?
would that person be asking correctly?
The devaputras addressed the Buddha, saying:
"No, World-Honored One!
Space performs no action. Why is this? Because..."
"Space is unconditioned; who could be its creator?
The Buddha addressed the sons of the gods, saying: "So it is, so it is!"
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha arises from the non-dual Dharma, and he teaches that the characteristics of all phenomena are likewise without dual characteristics. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata has attained these characteristics, he abides nowhere; therefore, the Buddha says that all phenomena have the characteristic of non-action.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This mark is profoundly deep; it is because the Tathāgata has attained this mark that he has realized equal and perfect enlightenment. He teaches the Prajñāpāramitā with unimpeded wisdom, and this Prajñāpāramitā is indeed the sphere of practice of all Buddhas.”
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"So it is, so it is! It is by means of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha reveals the characteristics of that world as they truly are."
Subhūti! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha relies upon the Dharma; he makes offerings to, reveres, honors, and praises the Dharma.
That which is called "Dharma" is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā; whether a Buddha appears or not, this Dharma abides eternally. Therefore, the Tathāgata relies upon the Prajñāpāramitā.
By relying upon this, the Tathāgata cultivates the perfection of wisdom; through such cultivation, he attains all-knowledge. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
"You should now know that the Buddha is one who knows gratitude and is able to repay it. Suppose someone were to ask:
'Who is it that knows gratitude and is able to repay it?'"
One should answer: "The Buddha is one who knows gratitude and is able to repay it. Why is this so?
Because the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the path he traveled and the dharmas he studied, he now further protects and mindfully remembers this path and these dharmas.
Subhūti! That which the Tathāgata practices and that which he studies is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā; for this reason, the Tathāgata is called one who truly repays kindness.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, because the Tathāgata knows that all dharmas are without activity and have the characteristic of being without activity, he has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; now, to again truly teach that all dharmas are without activity and have the characteristic of being without activity is also one who truly repays the kindness of the Tathāgata."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows that all dharmas arise from within the Prajñāpāramitā; now, to again teach the Prajñāpāramitā as it truly is and reveal it to the world is likewise the true way for one to repay the Tathāgata’s kindness."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since all those dharmas have no knower and no seer, how does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, teach the Prajñāpāramitā to reveal the world?”
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! You are able to ask the Buddha about this most profound meaning."
Subhūti! It is so, it is so! All dharmas have no knower; all dharmas have no seer.
Why is it that all phenomena have neither a knower nor a seer?
It is because all phenomena are empty and all phenomena are without dependence; therefore, all phenomena have neither a knower nor a seer.
Because the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has realized this Dharma, he teaches that the Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the world.
How does it reveal the world?
“Subhūti! If one does not perceive form, and does not perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, this is what is called ‘revealing the world.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘not seeing form, and not seeing feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness’?
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! If consciousness does not arise conditioned by form, this is called ‘not seeing form.
If consciousness does not arise conditioned by feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is called ‘not seeing feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.’”

Subhūti! If one does not perceive form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, then one does not perceive the world. To thus not perceive the world is called truly perceiving the world.
How does one truly see the world?
It is by seeing that the world is empty, that the world is devoid of marks, that the world is quiescent, and that the world is undefiled.
"The Prajñāpāramitā reveals it in this way; the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha also speaks thus.
Chapter Thirteen: The Inconceivable. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

This Prajñāpāramitā is most supreme and profound; it has emerged for the sake of a great matter, for the sake of an inconceivable matter, an incomparable matter, an immeasurable matter, an incalculable matter, and a matter equal to the unequaled.
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, it is so, it is so!”

The Perfection of Wisdom is most supreme and profound; it has appeared for the sake of a great matter—for the sake of an inconceivable matter, an incomparable matter, an immeasurable matter, an incalculable matter, and a matter equal to the unequaled.
“Subhūti! For what inconceivable purpose has it emerged?

It is for the sake of the Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Dharma of the Buddha, the Dharma of self-arisen wisdom, and the Dharma of omniscience. Such dharmas as these are inconceivable; they cannot be turned by the mind or mental factors, and within them there is no discrimination. Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā has emerged for the sake of an inconceivable purpose.”
“Subhūti! For what reason of the incalculable does it arise?

It is for the sake of what are called the Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Dharma of the Buddha, the Dharma of self-existent wisdom, and the Dharma of omniscience. Such dharmas as these cannot be measured by the mind; therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā arises for the sake of that which is incalculable.”
“Subhūti! For what immeasurable purpose does it arise?

That is to say, for the sake of the Tathāgata-dharma, the Buddha-dharma, the self-arisen wisdom-dharma, and the all-knowing wisdom-dharma. Since these dharmas transcend all measure and are without limit, the Prajñāpāramitā arises for the sake of this immeasurable purpose.”
“Subhūti! For what reason is it said that [the Prajñāpāramitā] emerges for the sake of that which is incalculable?

It is because of the Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Dharma of the Buddha, the Dharma of self-arisen wisdom, and the Dharma of omniscience. Such dharmas as these transcend all calculation and cannot be reached by any number; therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā emerges for the sake of that which is incalculable.”
“Subhūti! For what reason is it said that [the perfection of wisdom] emerges for the sake of the peerless (asama-sama) task?

It is because of the Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Dharma of the Buddha, the Dharma of self-arisen knowledge (svayaṃbhū-jñāna), and the Dharma of omniscience (sarvajñatā). Such dharmas have no equal, let alone anything superior; therefore, the prajñāpāramitā emerges for the sake of the peerless task.”
Furthermore, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If the Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Dharma of the Buddha, the Dharma of self-existent wisdom (svayaṃbhujñāna), and the Dharma of all-knowledge—these various dharmas are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.”

Is that form also inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled? Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled?
The Buddha said to the Venerable Subhūti: “So it is, so it is! Subhūti!”

Because form is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; and so on, up to all dharmas, which are likewise inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.

Why is this? Because within the dharma-nature, form has neither mind nor mental factors; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness likewise have neither mind nor mental factors within the dharma-nature; and so on, until all dharmas also have neither mind nor mental factors within the dharma-nature.

“Subhūti! Because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within the dharma-nature are without mind and without mental factors, they are inconceivable and incomparable; even all dharmas are likewise inconceivable and incomparable.”
Subhūti! Because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are immeasurable, even all dharmas are likewise immeasurable. Why is this?
The measure of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended; even the measure of all phenomena cannot be apprehended.
Because they cannot be apprehended, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and indeed all phenomena are without activity.
Because there is nothing that is produced, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—even all phenomena—have no arising.
Because there is no arising, therefore form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—even all phenomena—are immeasurable.
Subhūti! Because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are incalculable, even all phenomena are likewise incalculable. Why is this?
Because they transcend all numerical categories, Subhūti!
Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are equal to the unequaled; even all dharmas are equal to the unequaled.
Why is this? Because as space is equal, so too are all dharmas. "Furthermore, Subhūti!
"What do you think? Does space possess mind or mental factors? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said: "Subhūti!

All phenomena are likewise thus. Because space is inconceivable, all phenomena are also inconceivable; because space is incomparable, all phenomena are also incomparable; because space is immeasurable, all phenomena are also immeasurable; because space is incalculable, all phenomena are also incalculable; and because space is unequaled, all phenomena are also unequaled.
Therefore, all phenomena are free from conceptual discrimination; whatever is conceptually discriminated is the activity of consciousness.

"Subhūti! The cessation of all deliberations is called 'inconceivable' (acintya); because it cannot be weighed, it is called 'immeasurable' (atulya); because it has no measure, it is called 'unquantifiable' (aprameya); because it transcends all numbers, it is called 'uncountable' (asaṃkhyeya); and because it is like space, it is called 'unequaled' (asamasama)."

For this reason, you should know that the Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Buddha-Dharma, the Dharma of self-arisen wisdom, the Dharma of omniscience, and indeed all dharmas, are like empty space—inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.

When this inconceivable Dharma-gate, up to and including the "unequaled," was being taught, five hundred bhikṣus and twenty bhikṣuṇīs in the assembly, no longer grasping at any phenomena, attained the exhaustion of all outflows, and their minds were well-liberated.
Sixty upāsakas and thirty upāsikās were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye;
they all received their predictions of enlightenment before the Buddha.

Twenty bodhisattvas all realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and these bodhisattvas shall, within this Bhadrakalpa, attain the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is most supreme and profoundly deep.”
“The Buddha previously stated that he has appeared for a great matter;
what are its characteristics? The Buddha said, “Subhūti!”

Regarding the statement that the *prajñāpāramitā* has emerged for a great purpose, you should now know this: namely, that the teachings of the Buddhas, the teachings of the Pratyekabuddhas, and the teachings of the Śrāvakas all abide within the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti! It is, for example, like a prince of the kṣatriya caste who, having received the consecration, occupies the royal throne.

All matters of state, matters concerning the kingdom and cities, and matters concerning the people are entrusted to the great ministers; once the ministers have received these commands, they govern and carry them out.

The Prajñāpāramitā is likewise: all the dharmas of the Buddhas, the dharmas of the Pratyekabuddhas, and the dharmas of the Śrāvakas abide within the Prajñāpāramitā, and the Prajñāpāramitā encompasses and governs all dharmas.
Such dharmas as these are called "great matters"; therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā has emerged for the sake of great matters. Furthermore, Subhūti!

The Prajñāpāramitā emerges because it does not accept or cling to form; it emerges because it does not accept or cling to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it emerges because it does not accept or cling to the fruit of a srotāpanna, the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an anāgāmin, or the fruit of an arhat; it emerges because it does not accept or cling to the fruit of a pratyekabuddha; and it emerges because it does not accept or cling to all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does the perfection of wisdom emerge by not grasping and not clinging to all-knowledge?”
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, what do you think?"
"In the dharma of Arhatship that you have realized, is there anything seen?
Is there anything that can be grasped or clung to? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
Regarding the Dharma that I have realized, within it there is no view, nor can it be grasped, nor can one be attached to it.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! The perfection of wisdom is likewise.

Among all the dharmas of the Tathāgata, up to and including the dharmas of omniscience, nothing at all is seen, accepted, or clung to. Therefore, the perfection of wisdom emerges because it neither accepts nor clings to omniscience.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, the *prajñāpāramitā* is neither received nor clung to; it is most supreme, profoundly deep, rare, and difficult to encounter."
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first set out in the Great Vehicle, upon hearing this teaching, is not startled, not terrified, and does not fall back, but instead gives rise to faith and understanding, it should be known that this bodhisattva is fully endowed with the correct cause; he has already planted roots of goodness in the presence of previous Buddhas. Therefore, now that he hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he likewise does not give rise to alarm or fear, but his mind is pure, faithful, and resolved.”
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, it is so, it is so!”
"It is as you have said.
At that time, the devaputras of the desire and form realms addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
This true Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā is most supreme, profound, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter.

If a person hears this profound true Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā and gives rise to faith and understanding, one should know that this person has already planted roots of goodness in the presence of previous Buddhas.

"Bhagavān! Even if all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were each already established on the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryābhūmi*), and these beings were to practice according to the principle for a full kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa, it would not equal the merit of someone who, within a single day, could properly contemplate this true Dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā* and abide in the dharma of patience (*kṣānti*). The merit of such a person would be many times superior to that of the former."
The Buddha addressed the sons of the gods, saying:

“It is so, it is so! The true Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā is most supreme and profound. Even if all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm were each to abide in the stage of practice through faith and practice this Dharma for a full kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa, practicing according to the principle, it would not equal the merit of someone who, regarding this true Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā, reflects according to the principle and abides in the dharma of patience; the latter’s merit is many times superior to the former.”
"Therefore, you all should respect and revere this True Dharma and practice it according to the principle.
At that time, the sons of the gods from the realms of desire and form each addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
This Great Pāramitā is the Prajñāpāramitā; it is supreme, most profound, rare, and difficult to encounter. We each rejoice in it and receive it upon our heads with reverence.

After those devaputras had offered such praise, they each bowed their heads at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and departed from the Buddha’s assembly. Not far from there, they vanished from sight and returned each to their respective celestial realms.

The Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom, the Mother of Buddhas, from which the Three Dharma Treasuries Are Born, Scroll Thirteen. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīlagupta, Imperial Honorary Court Attendant, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, and Recipient of the Purple Robe, by Imperial Decree. Chapter Fourteen: The Chapter on Similes (Upamā-parivarta). At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* true Dharma, is not startled, not terrified, does not regress or fall away, does not doubt or hesitate, does not regret or sink in despondency, but gives rise to faith and understanding—where did such a bodhisattva pass away before coming to be born here?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* true Dharma, is not startled, not terrified, does not retreat or lose heart, and neither doubts, nor finds it difficult, nor regrets, nor sinks into despondency, but gives rise to faith and understanding—such a bodhisattva has passed away from among those supreme humans and come to be born here. Furthermore, having heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* true Dharma, they delight in listening to and receiving it, never for a moment parting from that teacher of the Dharma.”
Subhūti, it is just as a newborn calf does not leave its mother;
so too is it with a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Regarding this sublime Dharma of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they maintain pure faith, understanding, and joyful devotion, listening to and receiving it while never for a moment parting from the teacher who expounds it.
"Because they do not depart from the teacher of the Dharma, they do not abandon the Prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are fully endowed with such merit, have they not passed away from other buddha-fields to be born here?
The Buddha said, "Subhūti!"

"So it is, so it is! If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with such merit, you should know that he has already, at the abodes of various Buddhas in other Buddha-fields, reverently heard and received this profound Dharma, and furthermore questioned them regarding its meaning; having passed away from those places, he has come to be born here."
By these causes and conditions, when one now hears this profound Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā, one likewise becomes fully endowed with such merit.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there will be bodhisattvas who,

in the presence of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya in the Tuṣita Heaven, hear this profound Dharma of the Perfection of Wisdom, and without doubt or hesitation, further inquire about its meaning."
By these causes and conditions, having passed away from that place, they have come to be born here.
Now, at this time when they hear this profound Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā, they likewise become fully endowed with such merit and virtue.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, although having previously heard this profound Dharma in a former life, was unable to inquire about its meaning as it truly is and gave rise to doubt and regret, you should know that when this bodhisattva is reborn here, even upon hearing this profound and correct Dharma, doubt and regret will again arise within his mind."
Why is this? Because it was brought about by their failure to inquire in previous lives. Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when hearing this profound Dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā* in a previous life, was able to generate pure faith for one, two, three, four, or five days and inquire about its meaning, that bodhisattva, having been reborn here, upon hearing this true Dharma, immediately gains faith and understanding, becomes free from all doubt and regret, and likewise inquires about its meaning therein.
Why is this? Because such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If there are bodhisattvas who, in previous lives, although they heard this profound Dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā*, were unable to decisively inquire about its meaning, nor were they able to practice according to what was taught.

Therefore, at this time, regarding this profound Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā, they may at times delight in hearing it and at other times not; their minds are light and fickle, unable to reach certainty, just like a fine, delicate cotton garment that turns with the wind.

Subhūti! You should know that when this bodhisattva first abides within the Mahāyāna Dharma, because their mind is not pure, they are unable to generate resolute faith and understanding; they do not grasp the prajñāpāramitā, nor do they practice in accordance with the prajñāpāramitā. For this reason, they fall into one or the other of the two stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is as if a person were to board a boat and enter the ocean, and the boat should suddenly be wrecked. If this person does not grasp hold of a life-preserver, or wood, or a plank, you should know that this person will sink and die midway, and for this reason will not reach the other shore.
Subhūti! It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they possess faith and patience; they possess love and desire; they possess understanding and practice; they possess joy and delight; they possess equanimity and diligence; they possess reverence, a profound mind, and a pure mind; and they are free from negligence and distraction.

Although they possess such virtues, if they do not receive the protection and mindfulness of the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, these bodhisattvas will be unable to achieve the fruit of omniscience and will suffer regression along the way.
Subhūti! What is meant by "the middle path"?
Furthermore, from what dharma do they regress and fall away?
Subhūti! That which is called the "middle path" refers to the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
that which is "retrogressed from and lost" refers to the fruit of omniscience (sarvajñatā).

“Subhūti! It is as if, for example, there were a person who boarded a boat to enter the ocean, and while on the way, the boat suddenly broke apart; that person would immediately seize a life-preserver, or a piece of wood, or a plank, and so forth.”

"You should know that such a person will escape from calamities; they shall not be drowned by the waters of the sea and die, but will attain great peace and security, reaching the other shore. Subhūti!"
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this.

Regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they possess faith and forbearance; they possess love and desire; they possess understanding and practice; they possess joy and delight; they possess equanimity and diligence; they possess reverence, a profound mind, and a pure mind; and they are free from negligence and distraction.

Having been fully endowed with such merits, and further being protected and sustained by the skillful means of the Prajñāpāramitā, this bodhisattva shall not suffer any retrogression along the way; they will not fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, but will immediately be able to accomplish the fruit of omniscience.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! It is as if someone were to take an unbaked earthen jar and go to a river, a pond, a well, or a spring wishing to fetch water; yet before long, the jar would break along the way, and for this reason, the water could not be obtained."
Why is this? Because the jar has not yet matured, it therefore breaks and returns to earth. Subhūti!

The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they possess faith, patience, affection, and aspiration; they possess understanding, practice, joy, and delight; they possess equanimity and diligence; they possess reverence and a profound mind, as well as a pure mind; and they are free from negligence and distraction. Although they are endowed with such virtues, if they do not receive the protection and mindfulness of the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, that bodhisattva will suffer a setback along the way, falling to the level of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, and will be unable to achieve the fruit of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

“Subhūti! It is as if there were a person who, taking a well-fired jar, went to a river, pond, well, or spring wishing to fetch water. Wherever that person went, they would immediately obtain water; having obtained it, they would carry it back home, for that jar was sturdy and would not break.”
Why is this? Because the jar has already been fired, Subhūti!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this.

Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, if they possess faith, patience, aspiration, and love; understanding, practice, joy, and delight; equanimity, diligence, and reverence; a pure mind and a profound mind; and are free from negligence and distraction—having been endowed with such merits as these, and further being protected and sustained by the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the Prajñāpāramitā—it should be known that this Bodhisattva will not suffer any retrogression along the way, will not fall into the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, and will immediately be able to accomplish the fruit of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

"Furthermore, Subhūti! It is as if there were certain merchants in the world who, possessing little wisdom and little insight, take a boat at random from the shore of the great ocean, load it with various goods, and set out upon the sea; yet before long, this boat leaks and breaks apart."

Why is this? Because that which was originally constructed was not sturdy, and the various provisions for the ship were likewise incomplete; due to the lack of wisdom on the part of those merchants, they failed to perceive this and took on cargo. Consequently, midway through their journey, the ship was wrecked and the wealth was lost and submerged; at that time, the merchants merely suffered in vain from grief and distress.
Subhūti! It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, even if they possess patience and faith, up to and including freedom from negligence and lack of distraction, and though they are endowed with such merits, if they do not receive the protection and mindfulness of the skillful means of the prajñāpāramitā, you should know that this bodhisattva will suffer a setback along the way.

Subhūti! Those who retreat midway are those who fall into the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; those who lose are those who lose that jewel of omniscience and fail to achieve success in both practices for their own benefit and for the benefit of others.

“Subhūti! Furthermore, it is as if there were certain merchants who possess wisdom and discernment; they seek out an excellent ship by the great ocean, knowing that it was originally constructed to be sturdy and complete, with all its necessary equipment fully prepared. Taking it to load their goods and enter the great ocean, this ship encounters no difficulties and reaches every destination it is intended for, and their wealth and goods are neither scattered nor lost.”
Why is this? Because those merchants possess wisdom, they do not give rise to anxiety or distress along the way. Subhūti!
It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, when they possess faith and forbearance, up to and including freedom from negligence and non-distraction, and having fulfilled such merits, they further obtain the protection and mindfulness of the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*. It should be known that such a bodhisattva will not suffer any retrogression along the way; they will not fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, but will immediately be able to accomplish the fruit of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

"Furthermore, Subhūti! It is as if an old man of one hundred and twenty years were suddenly afflicted at one time by various ailments such as wind, bile, phlegm, and swelling; for this reason, he would endure suffering upon his bed."
Subhūti, what do you think?
If this person were at a time when no one was there to support or attend him, would he be able to rise from his bed by himself?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! Even if such a person were somehow able to rise from their bed, they would still be unable to walk even one or two *li*, let alone a *yojana*. Why is this?
Because they have already been afflicted and distressed by old age and sickness, Subhūti,
it is the same for the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, even if one possesses faith, patience, and so forth up to freedom from negligence and non-distraction—though endowed with such merits—if one does not receive the protection and mindfulness of the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*, it should be known that this bodhisattva will suffer a retrogression midway, falling into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, and will be unable to accomplish the fruit of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Suppose there is an old man of one hundred and twenty years who, though afflicted by illness and enduring pain upon his bed, is addressed by two strong men who say to him:
'We two shall each support you from our left and right; you should quickly rise and go wherever you wish.'"
"I shall cause you to reach your destination; do not worry about falling back or losing your way along the road.
Because the old and sick man accepted these words, he was able to rise from his bed and follow until he reached his destination.
Subhūti! It is the same for the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, if they possess faith and forbearance, up to being free from negligence and distraction, and having fulfilled such virtues, they further receive the protective mindfulness of the skillful means of the prajñā-pāramitā; you should know that such a bodhisattva will not suffer any retrogression along the way, will not fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, and will immediately be able to accomplish the fruit of all-knowledge.
Why is this? Because such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Subhūti!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess faith and patience regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and even reach the point of being free from negligence and distraction, having thus fulfilled such merits; and if they further receive the protective mindfulness of the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, it should be known that these bodhisattvas will certainly not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but will immediately be able to achieve the fruit of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), dedicating all these merits toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Chapter Fifteen: On the Noble Ones (Ārya-varga), Part One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"How should a beginner bodhisattva train in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:

"Any beginner bodhisattva who wishes to train in this profound *prajñāpāramitā* should draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and with reverence and respect, practice and study the *prajñāpāramitā*."
Such a spiritual friend should provide proper instruction and explain the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* according to reality to that beginner bodhisattva, speaking as follows:
"O son of good family!

All the merits derived from the perfection of generosity that you have cultivated, as well as those of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, you should all dedicate toward unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, son of good family!

When you dedicate the merit of your giving toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you should not grasp at or become attached to the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Do not grasp at form, thinking it is *bodhi*; do not grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, thinking they are *bodhi*.
Why is this? Because that omniscience is free from grasping and attachment.
O son of good family!

Regarding what you have cultivated—guarding the precepts, accepting patience, being untiring in diligence, tranquility in meditative concentration, and superior understanding through wisdom—when you dedicate these merits toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you should not grasp at or cling to the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Do not grasp at form, thinking it is *bodhi*; do not grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, thinking they are *bodhi*.
Why is this? Because that omniscience is free from grasping and attachment. Noble son!
For this reason, you also should not cling to the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Subhūti!
Those spiritual friends should instruct the beginner bodhisattva in this manner, causing them to gradually enter into the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi because he desires to cause all sentient beings everywhere to sever all suffering and affliction and abide securely in nirvāṇa.”

Yet the deeds performed by bodhisattvas are exceedingly difficult; that is to say, the characteristics of the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), and the characteristics of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are all profound and their performance is extremely difficult. Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to accomplish unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) should arouse diligence within saṃsāra and not give rise to fear or trepidation.
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, it is so, it is so!”
The deeds performed by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are exceedingly difficult, Subhūti!
For it is out of a desire to benefit, bring peace and happiness to, and have compassion for all the world that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek after anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
He formed this thought:

"When I have attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I shall act as a great protector for the world; I shall act as a place of refuge for the world; I shall act as a dwelling-place for the world; I shall act as the ultimate path for the world; I shall act as a vast island for the world; I shall act as a great light for the world; I shall act as a skillful guide for the world; and I shall act as the true destination for the world."
For this reason, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva exerts great diligence toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, become a great refuge for the world?

It is said that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva desires to cause all sentient beings in the world to sever the suffering of saṃsāra, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva acting as a great refuge for the world.
“Subhūti! How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi, they are able to serve as a refuge for the world?”

That which is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva desiring to cause all sentient beings in the world to attain liberation from such phenomena as birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction—this is what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva being able to act as a refuge for the world.
“Subhūti! How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he is able to act as a dwelling place for the world?”
"It is said that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains awakening, they teach the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings by means of non-attachment.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"What is meant by 'non-attachment'?
The Buddha said, "Subhūti!..."

If form is not bound, then form is not clung to; if form is not clung to, then form is not bound. Because form is not bound, form is neither born nor extinguished; because form is neither born nor extinguished, there is nothing to which one clings. Since there is nothing to which one clings, there is neither bondage nor liberation.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this: if consciousness is not bound, then consciousness is not attached; if consciousness is not attached, then consciousness is not bound. Because consciousness is not bound, consciousness neither arises nor ceases. Because consciousness neither arises nor ceases, there is no attachment. Because there is no attachment, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
All those dharmas are likewise thus; they are entirely without attachment in any cognition or vision. Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he teaches the Dharma to all sentient beings in this manner; this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva being able to act as a dwelling place for the world.
“Subhūti! How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he is able to act as the ultimate path for the world?”
It is said that when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains awakening, they speak thus for the sake of all sentient beings:
"If form is ultimate, it is not form; if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimate, they are not consciousness."
"Because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are thus, all phenomena are likewise.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately [empty], and all dharmas are likewise so, then would those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas not all fail to attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi?
"Why is this? Because within all dharmas there is no discrimination.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! It is so, it is so!
Because all those dharmas are without differentiation and no differentiator, by virtue of this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

Therefore, all dharmas are supreme, most profound, subtle, and difficult to enter; they abide in tranquility, being without attainment, without realization, without movement, and without transition. Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he preaches the Dharma to all sentient beings in this manner; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva being able to act as the ultimate path for the world.
“Subhūti! How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he is able to act as a vast island for the world?”
Furthermore, why is this called an island?
Subhūti, it is like a piece of land in the water where the current is cut off; therefore, it is called an island.
All phenomena are likewise thus. Because the prior limit of form is severed, its subsequent limit is also severed;

because the prior limits of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are severed, their subsequent limits are also severed; and so on, until because the prior limits of all phenomena are severed, their subsequent limits are also severed. Since they are severed in this way, all phenomena are entirely severed; yet this characteristic of severance is not a characteristic of inversion, but is the tranquility of nirvāṇa.

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he preaches the Dharma to all sentient beings in this manner; this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is able to act as a vast island for the world.
“Subhūti! How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they are able to act as a great light for the world?”

It is said that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, throughout the long night, extensively employs great skillful means for the sake of sentient beings, desiring to extract from them the arrows of ignorance and cause them to transcend the suffering of birth and death; by means of the light of all-knowledge, they shatter the darkness of delusion. This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva being able to act as a great illumination for the world.
“Subhūti! How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they are able to act as a good guide for the world?”

It is said that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains awakening, they teach all sentient beings that the intrinsic nature of form is neither produced nor extinguished; they teach that the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither produced nor extinguished; they teach that the intrinsic nature of the dharmas of ordinary beings is neither produced nor extinguished; they teach that the intrinsic nature of the dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is neither produced nor extinguished; they teach that the intrinsic nature of the dharmas of bodhisattvas is neither produced nor extinguished; they teach that the intrinsic nature of the dharmas of all buddhas is neither produced nor extinguished; and so on, up to teaching that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is neither produced nor extinguished.

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings in this manner; this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who can act as a good guide for the world.
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when attaining unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, act as a true refuge for the world?”

That is to say, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains bodhi, they declare that form tends toward emptiness; they declare that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness tend toward emptiness; and they declare that all dharmas tend toward emptiness.

Thus all dharmas neither come nor go, just as that space neither comes nor goes; they are without action and without marks, without abiding and without location, abiding in the dharma of non-abiding, and without arising or ceasing.

Furthermore, all dharmas neither come nor go; they are without action and without marks; they have no abiding and no location; they abide in the dharma of non-abiding; they are without arising and without cessation.
For this reason, there is neither non-conceptualization nor a conceptualizer. Why is this?

Because form abides in emptiness, it neither comes nor goes; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness abide in emptiness, they neither come nor go; and so on, until: because all phenomena abide in emptiness, they neither come nor go.
In this regard, how is it so? The realm of emptiness is the realm of all phenomena; this realm is without turning. The realm of signlessness is the realm of all phenomena;
this realm is without turning. The realm of wishlessness is the realm of all phenomena; this realm is without turning.
The realm of non-action is the realm of all phenomena; this realm is without turning. The realm of non-arising is the realm of all phenomena;
this realm is without turning. The realm of no-realm is the realm of all phenomena; this realm is without turning. The realm of no-nature is the realm of all phenomena;
this realm is without turning. The realm of dreams is the realm of all phenomena; this realm is without turning.
The realm of non-turning: the realm of self is the realm of all phenomena, and this realm is non-turning;
the realm of selflessness is the realm of all phenomena, and this realm is non-turning; the realm of the limitless is the realm of all phenomena, and this realm is non-turning;
the realm of tranquility is the realm of all phenomena, and this realm is non-turning; the realm of nirvāṇa is the realm of all phenomena, and this realm is non-turning.
All dharmas tend toward this tendency which is without turning; the tendency that is without arising is the tendency toward which all dharmas tend, and this tendency is without turning;
the tendency that is without returning is the tendency toward which all dharmas tend, and this tendency is without turning;

the tendency that is without going is the tendency toward which all dharmas tend, and this tendency is without turning; the tendency that is without movement is the tendency toward which all dharmas tend, and this tendency is without turning.
The realm of form is the realm of all dharmas; this realm is unchanging. The realms of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the realms of all dharmas;

these realms are unchanging. The realm of the fruit of arhatship, the realm of the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood, and the realm of the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi are the realms of all dharmas; these realms are unchanging.
Furthermore,
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they proclaim to all sentient beings that all dharmas thus tend toward emptiness.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is most supreme and profoundly deep; who will be able to believe and understand it according to reality?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have already matured their roots of goodness under past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and who have long cultivated the profound and supreme practices of a bodhisattva, they will be able to have faith and understanding in this profound Prajñāpāramitā."
Subhūti asked: "What are the characteristics of one who is able to have faith and understanding?
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! If the nature of being free from greed, hatred, and delusion is the characteristic of faith and understanding, then one who possesses this characteristic is able to have faith and understanding in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* attained by a bodhisattva mahāsattva also proceeds in this manner. Having attained this manner, he proclaims it to all sentient beings as it truly is, so that all sentient beings may also attain this manner.”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “It is so, it is so, Subhūti!”

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise such a course; once bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have attained this course, they proclaim it to all sentient beings as it truly is, so that all sentient beings may also attain this course.

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he preaches the Dharma to all sentient beings in this manner; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva being able to act as a true refuge for the world.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma, Dharma-Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, Imperially Conferred Purple Robe, Court Gentleman for Ceremonial Service and Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, during the Western Heaven Translation Era, under Imperial Decree. Chapter Fifteen, Part Two: On the Holy Ones. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva performs what is exceedingly difficult: for the sake of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, he dons the armor of diligence and makes great adornments, universally causing all beings to attain Great Nirvāṇa, yet the characteristic of a "sentient being" is utterly unobtainable.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “So it is, so it is! Subhūti!”

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva performs what is exceedingly difficult: for the sake of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, he dons the armor of diligence and makes great adornments, universally causing all beings to attain Great Nirvāṇa, yet the characteristic of a "sentient being" is utterly unobtainable.

Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not don the great armor for the sake of the liberation or bondage of form; he does not don the great armor for the sake of the liberation or bondage of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor does he don the great armor for the sake of the liberation or bondage of the stage of the śrāvaka, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, or the stage of the Buddha.
"Why is this? Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perform adornment for the sake of adorning all phenomena; this is called performing the great adornment.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, this is precisely what constitutes the great adornment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.”
Although the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice this profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not give rise to grasping or attachment toward three things.
What are these three?
"Namely, the stage of the śrāvaka, the stage of the pratyekabuddha,
and the stage of the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Subhūti!"
As you have said, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in such a manner, it is a great adornment.

Yet, Subhūti, although these bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not give rise to grasping or attachment toward the level of a śrāvaka, the level of a pratyekabuddha, or the level of a buddha. Subhūti!
"What meaning do you see that leads you to speak thus?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The Prajñāpāramitā is most supreme and profoundly deep; there is not even the slightest dharma that can be cultivated, for there is nothing to be cultivated and no one who cultivates. Why is this?

Because there is no dharma that can be produced within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, there is nothing to be cultivated. To cultivate space is to cultivate *prajñāpāramitā*; not to cultivate any dharma is to cultivate *prajñāpāramitā*; to cultivate non-attachment is to cultivate *prajñāpāramitā*; to cultivate the boundless is to cultivate *prajñāpāramitā*; to cultivate non-cultivation is to cultivate *prajñāpāramitā*; and to cultivate non-appropriation is to cultivate *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying: “So it is, so it is!
This Prajñāpāramitā is subtle and profoundly deep.”
Subhūti! Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are able to practice should be tested and their characteristics indicated by means of this Dharma.

If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not give rise to craving or attachment toward this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and has no expectations, who does not follow the discourses of others, whose mind is pure and does not give rise to divergent beliefs, and who—upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught—is not startled, not terrified, does not retreat or fall away, does not doubt or hesitate, does not regret or sink into despondency, but instead feels great joy and possesses pure faith and understanding, one should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. They have already heard this profound Dharma in the presence of previous Buddhas, and furthermore, they have questioned its meaning therein.

"By virtue of these causes and conditions, I am now able once again to hear this most profound Dharma, without being startled or terrified, and even with a heart that gives rise to joy, faith, and understanding.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, is not startled or terrified, how should they contemplate this profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to contemplate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) should contemplate it by following the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta).”
Subhūti asked: "What is meant by 'contemplating with a mind that accords with all-knowledge'?
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! If one contemplates in accordance with space, one contemplates in accordance with the mind of omniscience.
What is meant by ‘contemplating in accordance with space’?
Subhūti! One who contemplates in accordance with space has nothing to contemplate.
Because it is thus, it is called "contemplating the Prajñāpāramitā in accordance with the mind of omniscience."
Why is this? Subhūti, the immeasurable is omniscience.

If the immeasurable is formless, and without feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; without attainment or realization; without the dharma of the path or the fruit of the path; without wisdom or cognition; without arising or ceasing; without formation or disintegration; without contemplation or an object of contemplation; without action or an agent; without going or coming; without direction or destination; and without abiding yet not non-abiding—this is the immeasurable.

If one perceives this immeasurability, one falls into the numerical category of the immeasurable; if one does not perceive this immeasurability, it is like the immeasurability of space, and all-knowledge is likewise immeasurable.

Such immeasurability is neither attained nor realized; therefore, it cannot be attained through form, nor through feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it cannot be attained through the perfection of generosity, nor through the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.
In this regard, what is it?

It is that form itself is omniscience; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness themselves are omniscience; the perfection of generosity itself is omniscience; and the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom themselves are omniscience.

At that time, Mahābrahmā, the lord of the Sahā world, together with the assembly of devas from the realm of form, and Śakra, the king of devas, together with the assembly of devas from the realm of desire, came to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, they each prostrated with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side. Each addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is most supreme and profoundly deep; its limits and depths cannot be reached, and it is difficult to see and difficult to understand.”
For what purpose did the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, take his seat at the site of enlightenment, realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and teach this profound Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha addressed the Brahma King, Śakra, and the sons of the gods, saying:
“So it is, so it is! The Prajñāpāramitā is most supreme and profoundly deep; its limits and depths cannot be reached, and it is difficult to see and difficult to understand.”

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, having perceived this meaning within this profound Prajñāpāramitā, sat upon the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and, having realized the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, proclaimed this profound Prajñāpāramitā.
"O sons of the gods!
Although the Tathāgata has attained awakening, there is no one who attains it, nor is there anything to be attained;
although he speaks of the Prajñāpāramitā, there is no speaker, nor is there any dharma that can be spoken."

Why is this? My Dharma is profoundly deep and not something that can be fully expounded. Just as space is profoundly deep, so too is this Dharma profoundly deep; because I am profound, this Dharma is profoundly deep; because all dharmas have no coming, this Dharma is profoundly deep; because all dharmas have no going, this Dharma is profoundly deep.
At that time, Brahmā, Śakra, and the various devaputras again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One! It is rare, Sugata!”
The various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) taught by the Buddha regarding the world are difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
Why is this? Worldly phenomena involve attachment, whereas the Dharma taught by the Buddha is free from attachment; therefore, all phenomena are detached from all forms of attachment.
Chapter 16: On Suchness (Tathatā) At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Dharma taught by the Buddha accords with all phenomena being free from all hindrances; yet all phenomena are ultimately ungraspable, just as space is free from the characteristics of hindrance.”

"World-Honored One! Because all dharmas are like space, no phrases can be apprehended; because all dharmas are equal, dualistic dharmas cannot be apprehended; because all dharmas are unarisen, the dharma of arising cannot be apprehended; because all dharmas are unceasing, the dharma of cessation cannot be apprehended; because all dharmas are signless, the grasping of signs cannot be apprehended; because all dharmas have no location, no locations whatsoever can be apprehended."
At that time, Brahmā Śakra and the various devaputras together addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Elder Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata.”
"Why is this? Because, Elder Subhūti, all dharmas that are taught are entirely empty.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti addressed the Brahma King, Śakra, and the various devaputras, saying:

"As for what you have said—that Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata—it should be known that because he acts in accordance with suchness (tathatā), and since suchness is without birth, Subhūti is therefore born after the Tathāgata."
O sons of the gods!
Just as the Tathāgata’s suchness neither comes nor goes, so too Subhūti’s suchness neither comes nor goes;
just as the Tathāgata’s suchness is fundamentally unarisen, so too Subhūti’s suchness is fundamentally unarisen.

Why is this? The *tathatā* (suchness) of the Tathāgata is the *tathatā* of all dharmas; the *tathatā* of all dharmas is the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata; and the *tathatā* of all dharmas is also the *tathatā* of Subhūti, for these various *tathatās* are without arising.
Therefore, Subhūti, he is born following the Tathāgata within this dharma of suchness (*tathatā*), yet that suchness is not suchness.
O sons of the gods!
Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata neither abides nor does not abide, so too the suchness of Subhūti neither abides nor does not abide.

Just as the Tathāgata’s suchness is neither unconditioned nor non-unconditioned, neither conceptualized nor non-conceptualized, so too, Subhūti, suchness is neither unconditioned nor non-unconditioned, neither conceptualized nor non-conceptualized.

Because Subhūti’s suchness is without action and not without action, without discrimination and not without discrimination, the Tathāgata’s suchness is likewise without action and not without action, without discrimination and not without discrimination, and is without obstruction.
Because they are without obstruction, all dharmas are neither active nor inactive, neither conceptualizing nor non-conceptualizing, and are free from all obstructions. Why is this?
The suchness of the Tathāgata and the suchness of all phenomena are one and the same suchness.
This suchness is non-dual and indivisible; it is without characteristics and without differentiation.

That non-dual suchness is neither suchness nor non-suchness; that which is neither suchness nor non-suchness is suchness without duality or division, without characteristics and without conceptual differentiation. Therefore, Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata.

"O sons of the gods! The Tathāgata’s non-acting suchness is not a non-acting suchness; the non-existent suchness is not a non-existent suchness. This suchness is without duality and cannot be divided into two parts; it is without marks and without discrimination. Therefore, Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata."
"O sons of the gods!

Just as the Tathāgata’s suchness is at all times constant, uninterrupted, and indestructible, so too is Subhūti’s suchness at all times constant, uninterrupted, and indestructible; and the suchness of all phenomena is likewise at all times constant, uninterrupted, and indestructible."

The Tathāgata’s suchness is signless, immovable, and unattainable; Subhūti’s suchness is likewise signless, immovable, and unattainable; the suchness of all dharmas is likewise signless, immovable, and unattainable. Therefore, Subhūti is born after the likeness of the Tathāgata.
"O sons of the gods!

The Tathāgata’s true suchness (tathatā) is not different from the true suchness of all phenomena; Subhūti’s true suchness is not different from the true suchness of all phenomena. Those all phenomena are not different from true suchness, yet they are not [separate] true suchness; that which is not [separate] true suchness is precisely the true suchness of all phenomena."
In this way, suchness is without coming and without going, non-dual and undifferentiated; therefore, Subhūti is born following the Tathāgata. O Devaputras!

Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is not of the past, future, or present, so too the suchness of Subhūti is not of the past, future, or present, and the suchness of all dharmas is also not of the past, future, or present; therefore, Subhūti is born following the Tathāgata.

O sons of the gods! The *tathatā* (suchness) of the Tathāgata is the *tathatā* that neither comes nor goes nor abides. The *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is the *tathatā* of the past, which does not go; the *tathatā* of the past is the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata, which does not go. The *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is the *tathatā* of the future, which does not come; the *tathatā* of the future is the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata, which does not come. The *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is the *tathatā* of the present, which does not abide; the *tathatā* of the present is the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata, which does not abide. The *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is the *tathatā* of the past, future, and present; the *tathatā* of the past, future, and present is the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata.

Whether it be the suchness of the Tathāgata, the suchness of the past, future, or present, or the suchness of Subhūti—these various suchnesses are non-dual, indivisible, signless, and without differentiation; the suchness of all phenomena is likewise non-dual, indivisible, signless, and without differentiation.
O sons of the gods!

Whether it be the suchness of the Tathāgata, the suchness of the bodhisattva stages, or the suchness of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi—these various suchnesses are non-dual and indivisible, signless and non-conceptual, utterly unapprehendable, for they are all merely conceptualized by means of names.
Subhūti again addressed the devaputras, saying:

"You should know that Subhūti, who is born after the Tathāgata, is not born after form; he is not born after feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; he is not born after the fruit of a srotāpanna, nor born after the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, nor born after the fruit of an anāgāmin, nor born after the fruit of an arhat, nor born after the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, nor born after the fruit of a Buddha."
Why is this? All phenomena are unarisen, yet it is not that there is nothing arisen; all phenomena are unattainable, yet it is not that there is nothing attained.
O sons of the gods!
"For this reason, Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata.
When Subhūti spoke these words on the Dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*), this great earth shook in six ways with eighteen aspects, namely:

shaking, universal shaking, and total universal shaking; trembling, universal trembling, and total universal trembling; leaping up, universal leaping up, and total universal leaping up; crashing, universal crashing, and total universal crashing; bursting, universal bursting, and total universal bursting; roaring, universal roaring, and total universal roaring.
Having manifested these eighteen signs, the great earth immediately returned to its former state.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"The Dharma of True Suchness is most supreme, profoundly deep, subtle, and difficult to understand.
The Buddha said to the Venerable Śāriputra: "So it is, so it is!"
"The Dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) is most supreme, most excellent, profound, subtle, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter.

When the Buddha praised this Dharma of True Suchness, three hundred bhikṣus in the assembly, no longer grasping at any phenomena, realized the exhaustion of outflows and attained the well-liberated mind.
Five hundred bhikṣuṇīs distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye;
five thousand devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti);
and six thousand bodhisattvas, no longer grasping at any dharmas, realized the exhaustion of outflows and attained the well-liberated mind.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, knowing that those six thousand bodhisattvas had realized the liberation of the mind through the exhaustion of outflows, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“By what causes and conditions have these bodhisattvas, while practicing the bodhisattva path, now attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind within this assembly?
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

You should now know that these bodhisattvas have, in the past, personally approached and made offerings to five hundred buddhas, and have each practiced the dharmas of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and so forth.

Although they practice these various dharmas of cultivation in this manner, because they do not receive the protection and mindfulness of the skillful means of the Prajñāpāramitā, for this reason they instead realize this fruit [of the śrāvaka].
Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who,

although they cultivate the gateways of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness while practicing the bodhisattva path, will attain the fruit of a śrāvaka— meaning they realize the limit of reality— if they do not receive the protection and mindfulness of the skillful means of the prajñāpāramitā.

Śāriputra! It is as if there were a bird in this world whose body was large, measuring one yojana up to five yojanas, yet whose wings were not yet fully formed so that it could not fly far; and it wished to cast itself down from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to reach the ground of Jambudvīpa.
Then, while on its way, that flying bird conceived this thought in its mind:
"I now wish to return to the Heaven of the Thirty-three," or it might think:
"May I reach the land of Jambudvīpa with my body unharmed and free from all suffering and affliction.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
And as for that flying bird wishing to return to the heavens, would it be possible for it to return?
Would it be possible for it to reach the land of Jambudvīpa with its body uninjured, just as it desires?
Śāriputra said: “No, World-Honored One! Why is this? Because...”
"Furthermore, since that flying bird’s body is already large and its wings are not yet fully formed, its body will surely be injured or it will even die.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "The Bodhisattva is also like this."

Furthermore, even if there are those who can resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and have extensively cultivated all practices for as many *kaṅkha-ga-śa* eons as there are grains of sand, being able to practice generosity with total relinquishment, maintain the precepts, accept patience, exert diligence without slackening, and abide in the tranquility of meditative concentration; and even if they can again give rise to the great mind and great vows for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, if they do not receive the protection and mindfulness of the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, such bodhisattvas will inevitably fall to the level of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who, although they recollect the roots of goodness consisting of the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, because these bodhisattvas recollect them by grasping at signs, they are unable to know and unable to see those roots of goodness consisting of the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."

Because they do not know and do not see, when they hear it said that all dharmas are empty, these bodhisattvas grasp at the characteristics of sounds and thereby give rise to faith and understanding; they then dedicate this merit of grasping at characteristics toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Such bodhisattvas will inevitably fall into the stage of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"Why is this? Because they do not obtain the protection and mindfulness of the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there may be bodhisattvas who, despite having extensively cultivated various practices for a long time, if they distance themselves from those spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) and do not receive the protection and mindfulness of the skillful means of the Prajñāpāramitā, such bodhisattvas will be unable to achieve the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
Therefore, if bodhisattvas wish to accomplish the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should practice this skillful means of the prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra: “So it is, so it is!

If bodhisattvas wish to accomplish the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should draw near to those spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), for only then can they practice this skillful means (upāyakauśalya) of the Prajñāpāramitā.”
"For this reason, one is able to accomplish the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Brahmā-rāja, Śakra, and all the devaputras addressed the Buddha together, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“The Prajñāpāramitā is profound; Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is difficult to attain.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Brahma King, Śakra, and the various devaputras, saying: “So it is, so it is!”
The Prajñāpāramitā is profound, and Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is difficult to attain.

For those who lack wisdom, exert inferior diligence, give rise to inferior faith and understanding, lack skillful means, and associate with evil friends, it becomes even more exceedingly difficult to realize Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Regarding the Buddha’s statement that *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is difficult to attain—according to my understanding of the meaning of what the Buddha has said, *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is not difficult to attain.”
Why is this? All phenomena are empty; there is no phenomenon that can be apprehended, nor is there anyone who can apprehend it.
The Buddha has proclaimed that all phenomena are empty so that something may be severed; yet even the phenomena that are to be severed are themselves empty.

Regarding that *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, whether it be the dharmas attained or the dharmas employed, whether it be knowledge or understanding—all are entirely empty, with nothing to be attained and nothing to be realized.
"Therefore, Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is not difficult to attain.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is difficult to attain because there is nothing to be attained; it is difficult to attain because there is no one who attains; it is difficult to attain because there is no conceptual discrimination."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:

"If, as you have said, anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is not difficult to attain, then those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and seek awakening should not experience any regression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Why is that? Because you say that awakening (bodhi) is not difficult to attain. Subhūti said:
"Venerable Śāriputra! Does form regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti. Subhūti asked: "Do feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti. Subhūti said:
"Is there any phenomenon apart from form that regresses from unexcelled, perfect,
and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, "No, Subhūti."
Subhūti said: "Apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, is there any dharma that regresses from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti. Subhūti said:
"Does the suchness of form regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Śāriputra replied, "No, Subhūti."
Subhūti said: "Does the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness ever regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti. Subhūti said:
"Is there any dharma apart from the *tathatā* of form that could regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Śāriputra replied, "No, Subhūti."
Subhūti said: “Apart from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, is there any dharma that regresses from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
Śāriputra said: "No, Subhūti. Subhūti said:
“Is there anything in form that is realized in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Śāriputra replied, “No, Subhūti.”
Subhūti said: “Do feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness have anything to be realized regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra said:
"No, Subhūti. Subhūti asked: "Apart from form, is there any dharma that realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti. Subhūti said:
"Is there any dharma apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that can be realized in unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, "No, Subhūti."
Subhūti said: "Is there anything realized in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by the suchness of form? Śāriputra said:
"No, Subhūti. Subhūti asked: "Is there anything realized in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti. Subhūti said:
"Is there any dharma apart from the suchness of form that can be realized in unexcelled, perfect,
and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, "No, Subhūti."
Subhūti said: "Apart from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, is there any dharma that realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti. Subhūti said:
"Does form have any realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, "No, Subhūti."
Subhūti said: "Do feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have any realization of unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti. Subhūti said:
"Is there any dharma apart from form that can be fully awakened to in unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, "No, Subhūti."
Subhūti said: "Apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, is there any dharma that awakens to or realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti. Subhūti said:
“Does the suchness of form have anything that is realized in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Śāriputra replied, “No, Subhūti.”
Subhūti said: "Does the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have anything to be awakened to or realized regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti. Subhūti said:
"Is there any dharma apart from the *tathatā* of form that can be fully awakened to in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Śāriputra replied, "No, Subhūti."
Subhūti said: "Apart from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, is there any dharma that is awakened to in regard to anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti. Subhūti said:
"Up to and including all dharmas and the suchness of all dharmas— can one regress from unexcelled, complete,
and perfect enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, "No, Subhūti."
Subhūti said: "Śāriputra, what do you think?"
If there were any dharma that could regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, that dharma would have a place of abiding.
Since all dharmas are without abiding, what dharma could possibly regress?
“Śāriputra! Can true thusness (tathatā) undergo retrogression? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti! Subhūti said: "Śāriputra!..."
"In this way, when all phenomena are truly sought, they cannot be found; thus, there is no phenomenon that can regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra said to the Venerable Subhūti:
"According to the meaning of what the Venerable One has said, there is no bodhisattva who regresses from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
“Subhūti! If it is as you say, then according to what the Buddha has taught, would there not be no distinction between those who seek the three vehicles?
