"At present, I am only in the stage of training; it is not yet the time for realization. Therefore, I do not abide in samāhita, nor do I deeply collect the mind and bind it to the object."

Because that bodhisattva mahāsattva is protected by the power of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), although they do not realize emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they do not fall back from the factors of awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*); nor do they exhaust their outflows (*āsrava*) while abiding in a mind of cessation (*nirvāṇa*). Therefore, although the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the gate of liberation of the concentration on emptiness, they do not realize emptiness; and although they enter the gate of liberation of the concentration on signlessness (*animitta*), they do not realize signlessness, nor do they abide in signs.
Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess profound wisdom and are fully endowed with roots of goodness, such that they are able to form this thought:
"Now is the time for training; it is not the time for realization."

Therefore, although they contemplate emptiness, they encounter no obstruction; and although they abide in the samādhi of emptiness, they do not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) therein, because they are protected by the power of the prajñāpāramitā.

“Subhūti! Suppose there were a person whose physical appearance was upright and handsome, who was most preeminent in valor, firm in diligence, and possessed of wealth, happiness, and sovereignty; whose speech for himself and others was meaningful and beneficial; who was unimpeded in eloquence and clear in wisdom; who knew the proper time, the direction, and the place, as well as the destination and the course of action; who had mastered both good and evil and clearly understood calculation; who was highly accomplished in all arts and crafts; who was brave, robust, and powerful enough to withstand enemy armies; and who, moreover, thoroughly understood every kind of worldly affair—such a person would be loved by others, gazed upon with affection, approached, and held in respect and reverence.”
By virtue of these causes and conditions, this person will obtain great benefit in all their endeavors; their mind will become harmonious, supple, serene, and joyful.

At one time, due to some minor circumstance, this person, together with their parents, wife, children, and kinsmen, passes through a vast wilderness—a most terrifying and perilous path—where there are robbers, non-human beings, and other such creatures.
At that time, all his kinsmen were struck with terror; their hair stood on end and they trembled. The man immediately said to his parents and kinsmen:
"You, my kinsmen, do not give way to fear. I possess a skillful means by which I can bring about peace and happiness, enabling you to pass beyond all perils."
He immediately manifested many people, wielding various sharp weapons and implements, to protect his retinue as they passed through this perilous difficulty.
All those thieves, non-humans, and their like were completely dispersed and fled, unable to cause any further harm or harassment.
Once those attendants have overcome these hardships, they will reach their destination—whether it be a province, a city, or a village—in peace, security, and prosperity. Why is this?
Because this person possesses wisdom and insight, is most preeminent in valor, has achieved great power, and is firm and non-regressive; therefore, thieves and bandits cannot withstand him.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this: out of compassion and with the aim of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they constantly practice the four immeasurable states of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Because they are protected by the power of the Prajñāpāramitā and possess skillful means, they dedicate all roots of goodness toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Thus, although they cultivate the gates of liberation—the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they do not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva transcends all afflictions and their derivatives, transcends all evil Māras and those who assist them, and transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; yet, while abiding in samādhi, he does not exhaust his outflows.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are fully endowed with all powers and possess firm diligence, being protected by the power of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Bodhisattva does not abandon any sentient being, universally causing them all to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva takes all sentient beings as the object of focus to enter the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and further enters the supreme samādhi of objectless loving-kindness (*apraṇihita-maitrī*), cultivating the supreme *pāramitās*.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the liberation door of the emptiness samādhi, within this state he does not realize the signless, nor does he fall into the realm of signs."
Subhūti! It is as if a flying bird travels through space without falling to the ground; though it moves through space, it neither relies upon space nor dwells in space.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this: although they practice emptiness and study emptiness, practice signlessness and study signlessness, and practice wishlessness and study wishlessness, as long as they have not yet fulfilled the Buddha-dharmas, they will never fall into [the mere state of] emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness.

Subhūti! It is as if there were a person who, having studied the art of archery under a master, became thoroughly proficient and skillful; he then shoots upward into the air, and as soon as the first arrow is released, he immediately releases the next, so that the arrows follow one another in succession for as long as he desires, and none of them fall.

The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: desiring to accomplish the roots of goodness for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and being protected by the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*, he will never realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as long as the roots of goodness for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* are not yet accomplished. Only when the roots of goodness have been accomplished and he has attained the perfection of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does the Bodhisattva then realize the limit of reality.

Therefore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and cultivates the perfection of wisdom, they should thus contemplate the profound, true reality of all phenomena; yet, even after having contemplated them, they do not realize [nirvāṇa] therein.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

What the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas undertake is exceedingly difficult, most supremely difficult; for although they practice emptiness, study emptiness, and enter the samādhi of emptiness, they do not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) within it.”
“World-Honored One!
This is most rare, this is most rare!
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:

"So it is, so it is! Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices emptiness, enters the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), and dwells within emptiness, they do not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) therein. This is most difficult, supremely difficult; this is rare, supremely rare."
Why is this? Subhūti! That bodhisattva has made such a most supreme great vow:
"I shall deliver all sentient beings; I shall not abandon any sentient being.

Having made this vow, the bodhisattva immediately enters the liberation door of the emptiness samādhi, the liberation door of the signlessness samādhi, and the liberation door of the wishlessness samādhi.
Although the bodhisattva enters these gates of liberation, he does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) therein.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva has already attained the protection of the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), he is able to form this thought:
"I do not abandon any sentient beings.
Until the Buddha-dharmas are fully perfected, one shall never realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) of emptiness therein. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to enter the profound emptiness, they should enter the gate of liberation of the emptiness samādhi, the gate of liberation of the signless samādhi, and the gate of liberation of the wishless samādhi.
If a bodhisattva wishes to enter these samādhis and gates of liberation, they should give rise to this thought:
"Throughout the long night, all sentient beings are attached to the mark of a sentient being and give rise to views of objective attainment."
‘Once I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall proclaim the essential Dharma for sentient beings to sever these marks.
Thereupon, he enters the liberation door of the emptiness samādhi, the liberation door of the signlessness samādhi, and the liberation door of the wishlessness samādhi.

By means of such a mind and the power of prior skillful means, the bodhisattva does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) within those samādhis, nor do they diminish or lose the dharmas of the various samādhis of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have already attained the protection of the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they further increase all their wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*); their faculties (*indriya*) become sharp and penetrating, and their powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and path (*mārga*) are likewise fully increased.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Again, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to enter the liberation door of the *śūnyatā-samādhi*, he should give rise to this thought:

'Throughout the long night [of saṃsāra], all sentient beings have given rise to the notion of a self (*ātman*) and become attached to that which is apprehended. Once I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I shall proclaim the essential Dharma for the sake of these sentient beings to sever their attachment to the notion of a self.'"
He immediately enters the liberation door of the emptiness samādhi.

Because of such a mind and the power of his prior skillful means, the bodhisattva does not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), nor does he diminish or lose the dharmas of the various samādhis—compassion, joy, and equanimity.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have already attained the protection of the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they further increase all wholesome dharmas; their faculties become sharp and penetrating, and their powers, factors of awakening, and the path are likewise all enhanced.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Again, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to enter the gate of liberation that is the samādhi of signlessness, he should give rise to this thought:

'Throughout the long night, all sentient beings are attached to the signs of existence and harbor perceptions of signs. Once I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall proclaim the essential Dharma for the sake of these sentient beings to sever their attachment to signs.'"
He immediately enters the liberation door of the signless samādhi.

Because the bodhisattva possesses such a mind and the power of prior skillful means, he does not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), nor does he diminish or lose the dharmas of the various samādhis—compassion, joy, and equanimity.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have already attained the protection of the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they further increase all wholesome dharmas; their faculties (*indriya*) become sharp and penetrating, and their powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and path (*mārga*) are likewise fully increased.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Again, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to enter the liberation door of the samādhi of wishlessness (*asaṃskṛta-samādhi*), he should give rise to this thought:

'Throughout the long night [of saṃsāra], all sentient beings are attached to the notion of permanence, the notion of pleasure, the notion of self, and the notion of purity; they give rise to such inverted perceptions as these, which are the characteristics of conditioned activity.'"

"After I have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall proclaim the essential Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, namely: that this is impermanent and not permanent, this is suffering and not happiness, this is non-self and not self, and this is impure and not pure."
"In this way, one should cause the notions of permanence, pleasure, self, and purity to be severed, and become detached from the signs of conditioned activity.
Thus, he entered the liberation door of the signless samādhi.

By means of such a mind and the power of prior skillful means, the bodhisattva does not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), nor does he diminish or lose the dharmas of the samādhis of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have already attained the protection of the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they further increase all wholesome dharmas; their faculties (*indriya*) become sharp and penetrating, and their powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and path (*mārga*) are likewise fully enhanced.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to this thought: 'All sentient beings, throughout the long night, are attached to the signs of existence (*bhava-nimitta*).

That is to say, they previously practiced with the notion of attainment and now practice with the notion of attainment; they previously practiced with the notion of permanence and now practice with the notion of permanence; they previously practiced inverted practices and now practice inverted practices; they previously practiced with the notion of combination and now practice with the notion of combination; they previously practiced with the notion of unreality and now practice with the notion of unreality; they previously gave rise to wrong views and now give rise to wrong views; they previously committed various faulty actions and now commit various faulty actions.'"
All sentient beings, at all times and in all places, act in this manner.

Because I am protected by the power of the *prajñāpāramitā* and am endowed with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), I shall thus diligently practice with vigor until I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. At that time, I shall preach such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, enabling them to enter into the profound true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena—namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), non-arising (*anutpāda*), non-birth (*ajāti*), and the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a mind and possesses such wisdom, yet should fall back into arising conditioned dharmas and dwell within the three realms, such a thing is impossible."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the path of correspondence, he should ask another bodhisattva:
'If one wishes to accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, how should one train in emptiness?'"

How should one generate the mind so that one enters emptiness without realizing emptiness, and enters signlessness, wishlessness, non-action, non-arising, non-birth, and the absence of intrinsic nature, yet without realizing signlessness up to the absence of intrinsic nature, and is thus able to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*?
"If a bodhisattva should say:

'One who wishes to accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should merely contemplate emptiness, contemplate signlessness, wishlessness, non-action, non-arising, non-birth, and the absence of intrinsic nature.'"
"One who answers in this way abandons all sentient beings and has not yet perfected skillful means.

It should be known that such a bodhisattva has not yet received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from a previous Buddha, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and has not yet dwelled on the stage of non-retrogression."

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva is unable to proclaim the unique characteristics of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor is he able to provide correct instruction and correct answers regarding the Dharma asked about.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should one recognize a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

You should know that those non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whether they have heard this profound dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* or not, are able to provide correct demonstrations and correct answers regarding whatever questions are posed.”
"One who possesses these marks is an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"Bodhisattvas mostly practice for enlightenment and are rarely able to provide correct answers. The Buddha said, "Subhūti!"
There are few who abide in non-retrogression; for this reason, they are unable to answer correctly.
Subhūti! If there were those who already abide in non-retrogression, they would be able to answer correctly.

It should be known that this bodhisattva’s roots of goodness are bright, pure, and fully endowed with skillful means, such that they cannot be shaken or destroyed by any in the world—whether devas, humans, or asuras.
This bodhisattva is able to skillfully observe that all phenomena are like dreams, yet within this state does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Subhūti,
you should know that this is the mark of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma (Shi Hu), Imperially Appointed Grand Officer for the Propagation of the Dharma, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and Bestowed with the Purple Robe, during the Western Heaven Translation Era. Chapter Twenty: Skillful Means, Part Two. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"I shall now further explain the various marks and characteristics of non-retrogressive Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. You should listen attentively and apply your mind with proper attention."
Subhūti said: “Excellent, World-Honored One!
I wish and desire to hear it.”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even in a dream, does not take pleasure in the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor gives rise to a mind that dwells within those three realms.”
"Subhūti! One who possesses these marks should be known as having the characteristics of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within a dream, sees hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, humans, and devas in a great assembly respectfully surrounding the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, as they listen to his preaching of the Dharma.
Subhūti! If one sees such signs in a dream, you should know that this is the mark of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within a dream, sees his own body dwelling in mid-air preaching the Dharma to others, and sees himself emitting great radiance, manifesting in the form of a bhikṣu to go to various other world-systems to perform buddha-works and preach the Dharma;
Subhūti! If one sees such signs within a dream, you should know that this is the mark of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within a dream, sees a province, city, or village entirely consumed by fire and utterly destroyed, with various evil insects and beasts scattering and fleeing in all directions, and all the people therein becoming greatly terrified and giving rise to a mind of suffering and distress.
Having seen this, the bodhisattva is neither startled nor terrified.
Upon waking from the dream, he reflects:
"The three realms have no reality; they are all entirely like a dream."
"May I, when I attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, preach this Dharma for the sake of sentient beings. Subhūti,
if one sees such signs within a dream, it should be known that this is the mark of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while in a dream, sees sentient beings within the hells undergoing various sufferings."
Having seen this, the bodhisattva reflects:
"May it be that when I attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, my buddha-field shall be pure and free of hells, such that even their names are not heard, let alone being visible."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while in a dream, sees various hungry ghosts suffering from hunger and thirst,
and having seen them, reflects as follows:"
“May it be that when I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, my Buddha-field shall be pure and free of hungry ghosts, such that even their names shall not be heard, let alone be seen.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within a dream, sees various animals undergoing extremely heavy suffering,
and having seen this, the bodhisattva reflects thus:"
"May it be that when I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, my Buddha-field shall be pure and free of animals, such that even their names are not heard, let alone seen."
"Subhūti! If one sees such signs within a dream, you should know that this is the mark of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in various regions, should see a state, city, or village suddenly consumed by fire, upon seeing this, he should immediately say:

"Just as the signs I previously saw in my dream are no different from these, if I have already attained abiding in the stage of non-retrogression, by the power of this truthful speech, may this fire be spontaneously extinguished and no longer spread to other regions."

"Subhūti! If, after that bodhisattva has spoken these words, the fire should immediately extinguish itself, you should know that this bodhisattva has already received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from former Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and has already dwelled in the stage of non-retrogression."

If, after a bodhisattva has spoken these words, the fire does not go out, it should be known that this bodhisattva has not yet received the prediction of enlightenment and has not yet been established in the stage of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a fire cannot be extinguished and subsequently continues to burn other locations, passing from one house to another and from one village to another, such that the fire spreads in this manner without being put out, you should know that in a previous life the sentient beings of that place committed the grave offense of destroying the Dharma; they are now experiencing the remaining retribution of that karma in this present life.
Subhūti! By these causes and conditions, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fulfill their vows accordingly, you should know that this is the mark of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If there are men or women who have been possessed or bewitched by non-human spirits, at that time the Bodhisattva, having seen this situation, shall speak these words:

'If I have already received the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi from the former Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyak-saṃbuddhas; if my profound mind is pure for the sake of accomplishing Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; if I have distanced myself from the minds of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas and my conduct is pure, then I shall certainly attain what is to be attained in Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and it is not something that cannot be attained.'"

Furthermore, as for the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who currently dwell and teach the Dharma in the immeasurable, incalculable worlds of the ten directions—those Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, there is nothing they do not know, nothing they do not see, nothing they do not understand, nothing they do not realize, and nothing they do not attain.

If these Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know that my profound resolve is certain to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, then by the power of this truthful speech, may those non-human beings depart and leave me far behind, and may the man or woman possessed by them quickly attain liberation.

If, when a bodhisattva speaks these words, that non-human being does not depart immediately and the one possessed by it does not attain liberation, you should know that this bodhisattva has not yet received the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi from a previous Buddha, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and has not yet established themselves on the stage of non-retrogression.

Subhūti! If, when a bodhisattva speaks these words, that non-human being immediately departs from afar and the one possessed by them attains liberation, you should know that this bodhisattva has already received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from former Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and has already attained firm abiding on the stage of non-retrogression.

Chapter Twenty-one: Distinguishing the Characteristics of Māra Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattvas who have newly entered the Great Vehicle and, seeing a man or woman possessed by a non-human spirit (*amanuṣya*), speak as follows:

"If I have already received the prophecy of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from previous Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, then by the power of this word of truth, may that non-human spirit depart and leave far behind, and may that man or woman who is possessed quickly attain liberation."

Having spoken these words, at that time the evil Māra concealed his form and came to where the Bodhisattva was; secretly employing his magical power, he immediately caused the non-human beings to abandon him and depart.
Why is this? Because the power of the various Māra-demons surpasses that of non-humans, it is by virtue of this that human power cannot prevail; thus, they abandon [the effort] and depart.
At that time, the Bodhisattva was unable to perceive that this was the power of Māra, but thought only this:
"I have already received the prediction of enlightenment from previous Buddhas and am able to abide securely on the stage of non-retrogression. Why is this?
Because whatever I vow, it is immediately accomplished."
"Because those bodhisattvas have not yet received their prediction, they lack such power.

In this regard, the bodhisattva gives rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and various forms of conceit; through such conceit, his arrogance increases, and because of this arrogance, he treats other bodhisattvas with contempt and disdain, claiming for himself that he has already received a prediction from a former Buddha, while all others have not yet received a prediction from a Buddha.

Due to these causes and conditions, they remain far removed from the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom, spontaneous wisdom, all-encompassing wisdom, and the wisdom of all-knowledge, and so on, up to being far removed from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If a bodhisattva does not associate with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) in this regard, they will not receive the guidance of wholesome dharmas; being protected and assisted by evil associates, and lacking skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) within their own body and mind, their pride (adhimāna) becomes increasingly firm. Due to these causes and conditions, they are bound by Māra and cannot attain liberation, falling into one of two stages: either the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha.

Subhūti! Those who possess such characteristics are bodhisattvas who have newly entered the Great Vehicle; because they have seen and heard but little, they are unable to draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Failing to be protected by the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*, their pride increases due to minor causes and conditions, leading them even to distance themselves from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti! For this reason, you should know that this too is called a demonic deed of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are certain evil Māras who further corrupt and disturb Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas by means of names and conditions.
What are these names and conditions?
That is to say, evil Māras manifest various strange forms and may at times come to where those Bodhisattvas dwell, speaking to them as follows:

“Bodhisattva, you should know that your father’s name was such-and-such, your mother’s name was such-and-such, and the names of your other relatives and friends were each as follows; even down to your great ancestors of seven generations back, their names were each as follows. You were born in such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a place, in such-and-such a country, in such-and-such a city, within such-and-such a clan, and your family name was such-and-such.”
Furthermore, whether one’s nature is gentle or fierce, slow or quick, and whether one’s faculties are sharp or dull—the evil Māra can immediately describe each of these. He will also say:

"In your previous lives, you also practiced the dhūta virtues, namely: observing the *aranyaka* rule, always begging for food, wearing rag-robes, not drinking liquids after a meal, always eating in a single sitting, always following the practice of sitting wherever a seat is spread, wearing only the three robes, dwelling in a *śītavana* (cemetery), sitting at the foot of a tree, sitting in an open space, always moderating your food intake, and always sitting without lying down. You fully cultivated such dhūta virtues."

Furthermore, you are moderate in speech, content with little, and far removed from worldly clamor; when you do speak, your words are gentle and pleasing, and you even decline such things as oil for anointing your feet.

In previous lives, you have fully cultivated these various merits, and in this life as well, you possess such merit that you see the Dharma and know the Dharma. You have already received the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi from the former Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyak-saṃbuddhas, and you abide securely on the stage of non-retrogression.
Why is this? It is because you already possess all such merits.
Since you are fully endowed with these marks of merit, you should know that you have already received a prediction of enlightenment from previous Buddhas.
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva immediately thought to himself:
"I have already received the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi from that former Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha; I am one who abides in non-retrogression."
"Why is this? Because what is now being said regarding my possession of such dhūta merits is truly no different [from yours].

At that time, Māra, having known the thoughts in his mind, further manifested various other forms—namely, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, brahmins, householders, and even the Bodhisattva’s parents, brothers, kinsmen, and friends—and having manifested them accordingly, they all stood before the Bodhisattva and spoke these words:
"You have already received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from the former Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and you abide on the stage of non-retrogression."
Why is this? Because you have already fully perfected such marks and characteristics of merit. Subhūti!

When that bodhisattva heard such words from those emanated beings, he was unable to realize they were emanations of Māra. Immediately, he gave rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and various forms of conceit. Due to this conceit, his arrogance increased; because of this arrogance, he treated other bodhisattvas with contempt and disdain, claiming for himself that he had already received a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) from a former Buddha, while asserting that all other bodhisattvas had not yet received such a prediction from the Buddha.

Due to these causes and conditions, they become distant from the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom, spontaneous wisdom, all-encompassing wisdom, and the wisdom of all-encompassing wisdom, and even become distant from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If a bodhisattva does not associate with spiritual friends in this regard, they will not receive the guidance of wholesome dharmas; being protected and assisted by evil associates, and lacking skillful means within their own body and mind, their pride of overestimation (adhimāna) becomes even more firm and solid.
This bodhisattva will fall into one of two stages: either the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha.

Subhūti, regarding the true characteristics of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva that I have previously described, this bodhisattva is unable to accomplish or abide in them; failing to obtain the protection and assistance of the power of the prajñāpāramitā, for these reasons and conditions, they are bound by Māra.
Subhūti! For this reason, you should know that this too is called a demonic deed of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
Furthermore, there are evil Māras who, by means of names and conditions, corrupt and disturb Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. How is this so?
It is that an evil Māra may at times manifest in the guise of a bhikṣu and come to where a bodhisattva is, speaking these words:
"When you attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, your name shall be such-and-such.

Now, the name spoken by that bhikṣu was no different from the name the bodhisattva had originally aspired to obtain upon attaining *bodhi*. Because that bodhisattva lacked wisdom and further failed to possess skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), upon hearing these words he immediately thought:
"How wonderful is what this bhikṣu has said! The name I shall have when I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is no different and no distinct from my original vow; I now have no further doubts."
At that time, having formed this thought, the Bodhisattva accepted with faith the words spoken by the bhikṣus emanated by Māra.

Due to these causes and conditions, he became possessed by Māra; being possessed by Māra, he gave rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and various forms of conceit. Because of this conceit, his arrogance increased; because of his arrogance, he treated other bodhisattvas with contempt and disdain, claiming for himself that he had already received a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) from a previous Buddha, while asserting that all other bodhisattvas had not yet received such a prediction from the Buddha.

By reason of these causes and conditions, they remain far removed from the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom, spontaneous wisdom, all-encompassing wisdom, and the wisdom of all-knowledge, and even remain far removed from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If a bodhisattva does not associate with spiritual friends in this regard, they will not obtain the wholesome dharmas that provide guidance; being protected and assisted by evil associates, and furthermore lacking skillful means within their own body and mind, their pride of overestimation becomes increasingly firm.
This bodhisattva will fall into one of two stages: either the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha.

Subhūti, the true characteristics of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva that I have previously described, this bodhisattva is unable to accomplish or abide in; nor does he obtain the protection and assistance of the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*. For these reasons, he is bound by Māra.

Subhūti! This bodhisattva should repent and relinquish the various forms of pride that previously arose. Even if the bodhisattva is able to repent of such thoughts, they will still fall into the cycle of birth and death for a long time. However, if at a later time they encounter a spiritual friend who provides guidance, they will once again, by virtue of the *prajñāpāramitā*, gradually be able to advance toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because the transgression of a bodhisattva who gives rise to various forms of pride is extremely grave.
For example, if a bhikṣu commits one or two of the four root offenses, which are the most extreme and heavy sins, he is no longer a śramaṇa and no longer a son of the Śākya.
If a bodhisattva gives rise to various forms of conceit on account of names and designations, the offense they incur is likewise so great. Subhūti!

Setting aside these four root offenses for a moment, you should know that all five crimes of immediate retribution (ānantarya) are most extremely deep and heavy; yet if a bodhisattva gives rise to various forms of conceit on account of names and designations, the offense they incur is even more deep and heavy. Such a bodhisattva is called one who lacks great skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), and is unable to properly perceive and understand the works of Māra.

Subhūti! Therefore, you should know that those evil Māras can, by means of such subtle causes and conditions, perform demonic deeds to corrupt and disturb Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas; a Bodhisattva should recognize these for what they are, and having recognized them, remain far removed from them.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva grows weary of that clamor and desires to dwell in seclusion, various evil Māras will manifest in transformed appearances and come to where the bodhisattva is, speaking these words:

'If you wish to dwell in seclusion, you should go to mountain crags, beneath trees, or to empty, silent wildernesses; practicing in such a way is true seclusion, and this practice of seclusion is praised by the Buddha.'"
"Subhūti! I do not say that for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to dwell in mountain crags, beneath trees, or in empty, silent wildernesses constitutes true seclusion.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwelling among mountain crags, beneath trees, or in empty, secluded wildernesses is not said to be ‘distantly removed,’ then what characteristics must they possess to be called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who is truly ‘distantly removed’?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom possesses skillful means, and practices great loving-kindness and great compassion for the sake of all sentient beings, remaining far removed from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, then even if he dwells near a village, it is called 'seclusion'; or if he dwells among mountain crags, beneath trees, or in empty, silent wildernesses, it is also called 'seclusion'."
Subhūti! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to remain far removed from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, that is true seclusion; such seclusion is what I authorize.
A bodhisattva should constantly cultivate such true practice of seclusion throughout the day and night.

Subhūti, if— as the evil Māra praises— a bodhisattva merely dwells among mountains, cliffs, beneath trees, or in empty, silent wildernesses as one who practices seclusion, yet despite such seclusion is unable to distance himself from the mindsets of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, that is not true seclusion.
Although they cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*, they cannot fulfill the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).

You should know that such individuals are practitioners of confused conduct; their actions of body, speech, and mind are not purified, and they lack wisdom and skillful means, as well as the practice of great compassion.
Because their own three types of karma are impure, they instead give rise to a mind of contempt toward those who dwell near a village.
Subhūti, although that bodhisattva dwells near a village, he does not engage in confused conduct.
Why is this? Because they are able to remain far removed from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Their physical, verbal, and mental actions are entirely pure; possessing wisdom and skillful means, they are endowed with the practice of great compassion. Though they may dwell near a village, they are truly secluded.

If one develops contempt for those who thus practice genuine seclusion and renunciation, it should be known that although such a bodhisattva may have attained dharmas such as meditative concentration, liberation, supernormal powers, wisdom, and samādhi, they nevertheless lack skillful means.

Subhūti! Although a bodhisattva may dwell in remote places such as wildernesses or desolate regions hundreds of yojanas away, even if they spend a year, a hundred years, or even hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of years practicing the conduct of seclusion, if it exceeds this [proper duration], it will ultimately yield no benefit.

They do not understand the practice of true seclusion as I have explained it; they are unable to dwell with firm stability in the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and lacking skillful means, they take mere physical stillness to be true seclusion.
If those who seek the Buddha-way are greedily attached to and rely upon [such things], I do not permit such distancing from me, nor can it bring joy to my heart. Why is this?
"In the practice of detachment as I have described it, one does not perceive such a practitioner of detachment as being 'truly detached.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
There are certain evil Māras who, seeing one dwelling in a secluded place practicing the path of detachment, immediately go to that person's location and speak these words from the midst of the sky:
"Excellent, excellent!
"Good son! That which you practice is the true practice of detachment; because the Tathāgata praises your cultivation of this practice, he causes you to swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Having heard the voice in the sky praising him thus, the bodhisattva comes from those places of empty, silent wildernesses and the like to a village. There he sees other bodhisattvas who are gentle, compliant, and practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*), who have distanced themselves from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and whose three karmas are pure; yet he immediately gives rise to contempt and speaks these words:
"You are practitioners of worldly clamor; what you practice is not the practice of seclusion."

"Subhūti! Those bodhisattvas who dwell in emptiness and stillness take the practice of true seclusion to be the practice of worldly clamor, and take the practice of worldly clamor to be the practice of true seclusion. Because of these faults and evils, they instead treat those who deserve respect with contempt, and instead treat those who do not deserve respect with reverence."
Why is this? He thinks to himself:
"I dwell in places such as empty, quiet, and desolate wildernesses; there are non-human beings who come because they think of me, and they come to assist me."
"Since you dwell near a village, how could non-human beings come to assist you with mindfulness?
Having thought this, he gave rise to a mind of contempt toward other bodhisattvas.

Subhūti! You should know that such a person is a caṇḍāla among bodhisattvas, one of transgressions among bodhisattvas, and one of defiled conduct among bodhisattvas. This is a bodhisattva in name only; he is also called a "thief-dwelling śramaṇa," a "thief in the form of a śramaṇa," an "impure follower of the Dharma," and one who does not abide by the proper Dharma.

Because of these characteristics, one should know that this is one who has only recently resolved to attain enlightenment; for this reason, they are not revered by the gods, humans, and others of all the worlds.
Why is this? Subhūti, I say that such a person is one of overweening pride. Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not associate with such persons. Furthermore, Subhūti,

if bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not abandon all sentient beings, cherish omniscience, have deeply resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and desire to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, they should not associate with such people as these.
Subhūti! Those who seek awakening should always be aware of all demonic activities and, having become aware of them, remain far removed from them.

At all times, they should constantly give rise to a mind of weary detachment and fear toward the three realms; solely for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they should guide and show sentient beings the true path, causing all beings to fulfill the fruit of correctness and abide in the true nature of phenomena.
Furthermore, giving rise to the mind of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity toward all sentient beings, the Bodhisattva constantly makes this vow:
"May I, at all times and in all places, remain far removed from all such demonic activities; should they ever arise even momentarily, may I swiftly cause them to be extinguished."
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can train in this way, this is the power of the superknowledges and wisdom of that bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti!"
It should be understood that such passages as these all explain the true characteristics of remoteness regarding the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s recognition of the works of Māra.
Chapter Twenty-Two: On Spiritual Friends (Kalyāṇamitra), Part One. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
“If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, with a profound mind, desires to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should draw near to and revere spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, with a profound resolve, desire to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. If they are able to cherish and delight in spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), what constitutes a bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s spiritual friend?”
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! You should know that all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, are the spiritual friends of bodhisattvas.”

Why is this? Because the Buddhas are able to expound the dharmas of bodhisattva practice and the various pāramitās, and instruct bodhisattvas on how to enter the prajñāpāramitā; therefore, the Tathāgatas are the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) of bodhisattvas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is the good spiritual friend of a bodhisattva. Why is this?

The perfection of wisdom is the ultimate locus of all perfections; because the perfection of wisdom serves as the bodhisattva’s spiritual friend, all six perfections likewise become the bodhisattva’s spiritual friends.

Furthermore, the six pāramitās are the great teachers of bodhisattvas; the six pāramitās are the correct path to be traversed; the six pāramitās are the light of the world; the six pāramitās are the great Dharma-torches; the six pāramitās are the great Dharma-illumination; the six pāramitās are true protection; the six pāramitās are the destination to which one returns; the six pāramitās are the dwelling house; the six pāramitās are the ultimate path; the six pāramitās are the continents and islands; the six pāramitās are the father and the mother; indeed, even the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is accomplished entirely through the six pāramitās.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past—who have already attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and have entered parinirvāṇa—all those Tathāgatas were born from the six pāramitās."
All future Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas who shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—those Tathāgatas likewise arise from the six pāramitās.

Furthermore, the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas who are currently present throughout the immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions, teaching and transforming sentient beings, and who have now attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—they too have all arisen from the six pāramitās.
Furthermore, the all-knowing wisdom (*sarvajñā*) of all Buddhas of the three periods of time also arises from the six *pāramitās*. Why is this?

When the Buddhas were originally practicing the bodhisattva path, they all cultivated these six *pāramitās*, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), the four immeasurable practices (*apramāṇa*), the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), and even all the Buddha-dharmas; thereby, they attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. All these Buddha-dharmas arise from the six *pāramitās*.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s wisdom—spontaneous wisdom, inconceivable wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, unequaled wisdom, and wisdom equal to the unequaled—likewise arises from these six pāramitās.

Subhūti! For this reason, the six pāramitās are the spiritual friends of bodhisattvas; the six pāramitās are the great teachers of bodhisattvas; they are the right path to be traversed, the light of the world, the great Dharma-torch, the great Dharma-illumination, true protection, the place of refuge, the dwelling house, the ultimate path, the great island-continent, the father and the mother, even unto the birth of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, they should train in these six pāramitās."
If one wishes to train in these perfections, one should train accordingly in this Prajñāpāramitā, understand its meaning, reflect upon it as it truly is, and contemplate it as it truly is.
Why is this? Because the perfection of wisdom acts as the precursor to the five perfections, revealing and clarifying them.
Furthermore, if the five perfections were separated from the perfection of wisdom, they would not receive the name "perfection."
Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes not to give rise to reliance on others and not to follow the words of others, they should practice and study this perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are the characteristics of the prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, the mark of non-attachment is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).”
Subhūti said: "Is there any causal condition by which all phenomena, like the perfection of wisdom, are also characterized by non-attachment?"
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! There is a causal condition such that, just as the prajñāpāramitā has the characteristic of non-attachment, all dharmas likewise have the characteristic of non-attachment.”
Why is this? Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are empty and detached.

Therefore, Subhūti, because all phenomena are empty of the characteristic of non-attachment and are detached, the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise empty of the characteristic of non-attachment and is detached.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are empty and detached, why does the Buddha say that all sentient beings have defilement and purity?”
"Bhagavān! Within the dharma of emptiness there is neither defilement nor purity; within the dharma of detachment there is neither defilement nor purity. Bhagavān!"

One cannot attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of this very dharma of emptiness or the dharma of detachment; nor can one attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of any dharma other than this dharma of emptiness or the dharma of detachment.
“World-Honored One!
I am currently unable to understand such a meaning; I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will explain it for me.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, what do you think? Do all sentient beings, throughout the long night, cling to a self and what belongs to a self? Subhūti replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
Sentient beings have for a long night been attached to 'self' and 'what belongs to self.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, what do you think? Are ‘self’ and ‘what belongs to self’ empty? Subhūti replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
'Self' and 'what belongs to self' are empty.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, what do you think? Because sentient beings are attached to ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ do they transmigrate through birth and death? Subhūti replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
Because sentient beings are attached to 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' they revolve in birth and death.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! You should know that as for all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), they are merely designated as 'defiled' because sentient beings experience them and become attached to them.

If sentient beings neither experience nor become attached to them, then no defilement can be found, nor is there anyone who experiences defilement. Therefore, there is neither self (*ātman*) nor what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*). Because there is neither self nor what belongs to a self, it is designated as 'pure' (*viśuddha*)."
If sentient beings do not accept or cling [to anything], there is no purity to be found, nor is there anyone who attains purity.
Subhūti, for this reason,
within the emptiness of all phenomena and the detachment from all phenomena, one speaks of "defilement" and one speaks of "purity."
“Subhūti! Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom should practice in this manner.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Rare indeed, World-Honored One!
You have well explained this meaning: that within the emptiness of all phenomena and the detachment from all phenomena, one speaks of defilement and purity without experiencing or clinging to them.”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) should practice in this way.
World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices in this manner, this constitutes not practicing form (rūpa), and not practicing feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), or consciousness (vijñāna).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they will cause all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and others—to universally revere and submit to them, and they will not be moved or disturbed by them.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices in this manner, they do not mix with the practices of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor do they dwell in the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Why is this? Because such a practitioner practices by practicing non-practice and dwells by dwelling in non-dwelling; they are able to enter the Buddha-nature, the Tathāgata-nature, the nature of self-arisen wisdom, and the nature of all-knowledge.
“World-Honored One!
Such a practitioner is supreme and unsurpassed, being in accord with the sublime practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Therefore, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice diligently in this manner throughout the day and night, they will be able to draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and will even swiftly achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīlagupta, Dharma Master and Imperially Appointed Trial Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree. Chapter Twenty-Two, Part Two: On Spiritual Friends. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying: "So it is, so it is!"

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they practice in this manner, this constitutes not practicing form, and not practicing feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
A practitioner who acts in this way will be universally revered and submissive to by all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and others—and cannot be disturbed or moved by them.
A practitioner who acts in this way does not mingle with the practices of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor do they abide in the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Practicing in this manner, they practice without anything to practice and abide without anything to abide; thus they are able to enter the Buddha-nature, the Tathāgata-nature, the nature of self-arisen wisdom, and the nature of all-knowledge.
A practitioner who acts in this way is supreme and unsurpassed, being in accord with the sublime practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice diligently in this manner throughout the day and night, they will be able to draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and will even swiftly achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose every single sentient being within Jambudvīpa were to attain a human body, and all were to resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Having made this resolution, they would, for as long as they lived, honor, revere, and make offerings to the Buddhas; furthermore, they would universally practice extensive giving toward all, and dedicate the merit of such giving toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
“Subhūti! By this cause and condition, would these people obtain much merit? Subhūti replied:
“Very much so, World-Honored One!
Very much so, Sugata!
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! Although these people obtain much merit through such causes and conditions, it is not equal to a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, for even a single day, gives rise to right mindfulness associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Because that bodhisattva gives rise to right mindfulness associated with the perfection of wisdom, they are able to serve as a great field of merit for all sentient beings.”

Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas are able to give rise to a mind of impartial compassion; among all other sentient beings, there is no such mind as that of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, with the sole exception of the Tathāgata, whose mind of compassion is fully perfected.

Why is this? Because the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have already perfected the inconceivable Dharma, yet they never depart from loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Subhūti! How is it that a bodhisattva can act as a great field of merit for sentient beings? Subhūti!

It is said that because a bodhisattva is endowed with right wisdom by virtue of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), having attained this wisdom, they perceive all sentient beings as being in prison, suffering under their bonds.

At that time, because the Bodhisattva is protected and assisted by the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he immediately uses his purified divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) to universally observe immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings. He sees sentient beings who have committed acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*), who are destined to undergo the retribution of suffering, fallen into the net of various views (*dṛṣṭi-jāla*), and unable to escape.

Having contemplated in this way, the bodhisattva deeply gives rise to a mind of great loving-kindness and a mind of great compassion, feeling pity for all sentient beings; with the radiance of this great loving-kindness and great compassion, he universally illuminates everything.
That bodhisattva forms this thought:
"I shall act as a great refuge for all sentient beings, extensively liberating all sentient beings from their various sufferings."
Having formed this thought, he dwells neither in this mark nor in any other mark.
Subhūti, this is called the great light of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; it is that which can act as a great field of merit for sentient beings.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices in this manner, they will not regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and shall be worthy of receiving the offerings of faith from all the world, namely food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine.

Although the bodhisattva accepts gifts, because they practice the perfection of wisdom with single-minded devotion, the giver, the receiver, and the gift itself are all rendered pure; thus, they draw near to omniscience.

Therefore, Subhūti! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish not to receive in vain the faithful offerings of their lands; if they wish to lead and show sentient beings the path of right practice; if they wish to rescue and deliver sentient beings from the bonds of the triple world; if they wish to extricate and save sentient beings from the suffering of saṃsāra; and if they wish to open and guide the pure eye of wisdom for sentient beings—they should give rise to right mindfulness associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). If they give rise to such mindfulness, they will be in accord with the discourse of the perfection of wisdom.

Why is this? Because whatever a bodhisattva speaks accords with the mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and whatever they mindfully contemplate accords with their speech; thus, they do not depart from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should not, throughout the day and night, be separated from this right mindfulness associated with the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti, it is as if, for example, there were a person who obtained a great, unprecedented maṇi-jewel; having obtained this jewel, his heart was filled with great joy, but later, at another time, due to some cause or condition, he lost this jewel.
Subhūti! Because of these conditions, that person’s mind will give rise to grief, distress, sorrow, suffering, and remorse, constantly thinking:
"For what reason have I now lost this great treasure?"
"In this way, his contemplation proceeds without interruption.

Subhūti, it is the same for a bodhisattva: the great Dharma-treasure is what is called the *prajñāpāramitā*. Because a bodhisattva has obtained this great Dharma-treasure of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they constantly give rise to right mindfulness associated with the *prajñāpāramitā* and never depart from the mind of omniscience."
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are empty and detached by virtue of their own nature, then all thoughts are likewise empty and detached.”
"Why does the Buddha say that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is never separated from mindfulness associated with the perfection of wisdom? The Buddha said, "Subhūti!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus know that because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature and detached, all mental recollections are likewise empty and detached, this is precisely the right mindfulness associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and it is not to be separated from the mind of omniscience.
"Why is this? Because in the emptiness of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is neither increase nor decrease.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since there is neither increase nor decrease within the emptiness of the *prajñāpāramitā*, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva cause the *prajñāpāramitā* to increase?”
"How does one attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, there were increase or decrease therein, then within the emptiness of the *prajñāpāramitā* there would likewise be increase and decrease."

Subhūti, if there is neither increase nor decrease in emptiness for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, then there is likewise neither increase nor decrease in the emptiness of the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti!
Because there is nothing to be increased or diminished within emptiness, the bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of this dharma of non-increase and non-decrease.

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having heard this teaching, is neither startled nor terrified, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Subhūti asked: “Is the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā* itself the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha said:
"No, Subhūti. Subhūti said: "Is it by means of the mark of emptiness that the perfection of wisdom practices the perfection of wisdom?"
The Buddha said, "No, Subhūti. Subhūti said:
“Is there any dharma apart from the emptiness of the *prajñāpāramitā* that can practice the *prajñāpāramitā*? The Buddha said, “No, Subhūti.”
Subhūti asked: "Can emptiness practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said:
"No, Subhūti. Subhūti said: "Apart from emptiness, is there any dharma that can practice the perfection of wisdom?"
The Buddha said, “No, Subhūti. Subhūti said:
“Can emptiness practice emptiness? The Buddha said, “No, Subhūti.”
Subhūti asked: "Can form practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said:
"No, Subhūti. Subhūti asked: "Can feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness practice the perfection of wisdom?"
The Buddha said, “No, Subhūti. Subhūti said:
"Is there any dharma apart from form that can practice the perfection of wisdom? The Buddha said, "No, Subhūti."
Subhūti asked: "Apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, is there any dharma that can practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said:
"No, Subhūti. Subhūti said: "How, then, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice this practice of the perfection of wisdom?"
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti! Do you perceive any dharma that can practice the perfection of wisdom?”
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! Do you see this prajñāpāramitā as the sphere of practice for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said, "Subhūti!
"If a dharma is non-apprehendable, then that dharma is invisible. Within this, is there any arising that can arise, or any cessation that can cease?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One."
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva thoroughly understands such characteristics as these, they immediately attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). A bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses this patience immediately receives the prediction (vyākaraṇa) of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).”

Subhūti! This is called the Tathāgata’s practice of fearlessness. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they will immediately attain the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom, vast wisdom, the most supreme beneficial wisdom, and the wisdom of all-knowledge.
"A practitioner who acts in this way is one who practices without a locus.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"Can one receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of this non-arising dharma? The Buddha said, "No, Subhūti."
Subhūti asked: "By means of what dharma shall one receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! Do you perceive any dharma that can be granted the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said, "Subhūti!
"Do you see any such thing as 'unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment' that is the object of this prediction? Subhūti replied,
"I do not see any dharma that is predicted, nor do I see any dharma that constitutes the act of bestowing a prediction."
Why is this? Because all dharmas are unattainable,
World-Honored One!
For this reason, I know that all dharmas are without realization, and within them there is no one who realizes; all dharmas are without attainment, and within them there is nothing to be attained.
Chapter 23: The Chapter on the Praise by Śakra Devānām Indra. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra rose from his seat within the great assembly and approached the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, the Prajñāpāramitā is most supreme and profoundly deep; it is difficult to see and difficult to hear, and furthermore, it is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
The Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying: “Kauśika, it is so, it is so!”
The Prajñāpāramitā is most supreme and profoundly deep; it is difficult to see, difficult to hear, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter.

Kauśika! Just as space is profoundly deep, so too is the Prajñāpāramitā profoundly deep; because space is empty, the Prajñāpāramitā is also empty; because space is detached, the Prajñāpāramitā is also detached; because space is difficult to see, the Prajñāpāramitā is also difficult to see; because space is difficult to understand, the Prajñāpāramitā is also difficult to understand.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are those who obtain this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and who listen to, receive, read, recite, explain it to others, or even transcribe it, one should know that such persons are fully endowed with the most supreme roots of goodness.”
The Buddha said, "Kauśika! So it is, so it is!"

If there are those who obtain this profound Dharma-gate of the Perfection of Wisdom, and who listen to it, receive it, recite it, explain it to others, or even transcribe it—I declare that such persons have already been able to fulfill the most supreme roots of goodness.
Kauśika! What do you think?

Suppose all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa were to attain human bodies, and each individual were to fully practice the ten wholesome actions. Would those sons and daughters of good family obtain much merit on account of this?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
“Very many, World-Honored One! Very many, Sugata!”
The Buddha said, "Kauśika!

Although those sons and daughters of good family acquire much merit, it does not equal that of a person who, regarding this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, listens to, receives, recites, reads, explains it to others, or even writes it down; the former does not approach one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousand *koṭi-nayuta* parts, nor any part calculated by number or analogy, nor even an *upaniṣad* part."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly who, having heard these words, said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:

"If there be a son or daughter of good family who, upon briefly hearing this profound Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā, is able to give rise to pure faith for even a single thought-moment, you should know that such a son or daughter of good family surpasses your honor."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to those bhikṣus:

"If a son or daughter of good family generates pure faith for even the duration of a single thought-moment, they would still surpass me; how much more so if they are able to extensively hear, receive, read, recite, explain to others, and even write it down."
Furthermore, how much more so for those who, having heard and received it, train as taught, practice as taught, and apply themselves to cultivation.
You should know that such sons and daughters of good family, practicing the bodhisattva path, surpass all those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras alike.
"O Bhikṣus!
Not only does he surpass all those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras—but he also surpasses the srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, and their pratyekabuddhas."

Not only does he surpass those from the stage of stream-enterer up to the pratyekabuddha, but he also surpasses other bodhisattvas who practice giving while being devoid of the perfection of wisdom and lacking skillful means.

Not only does he surpass those bodhisattvas who practice such giving, but he also surpasses other bodhisattvas who maintain pure ethical discipline while lacking skillful means and being remote from the perfection of wisdom.

Not only does he surpass those bodhisattvas who maintain such ethical discipline, but he also surpasses other bodhisattvas who practice patience while lacking skillful means and being devoid of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Not only does he surpass those bodhisattvas who possess such patience, but he also surpasses other bodhisattvas who, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom and lacking skillful means, exert diligence.

Not only does he surpass those bodhisattvas who possess such diligence, but he also surpasses other bodhisattvas who, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom and lacking skillful means, practice meditative concentration.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having heard this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, are able to train according to what is taught and practice according to what is taught, and are thus able to fulfill skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*); for this reason, they surpass all those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras, as well as śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and other bodhisattvas.

It should be known that this bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom skillfully; this bodhisattva is able to draw near to all-knowledge and does not remain far from the Buddhas; this bodhisattva will mature their roots of goodness and shall sit at the site of enlightenment; this bodhisattva is able to sever the suffering of the afflictions of sentient beings.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can train in this manner, this constitutes training in the bodhisattva-dharma and not training in the dharmas of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; this is training in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, the four world-protecting great kings (Caturmahārājika) shall come to where the bodhisattva is and speak these words:
"O son of good family!..."
"You should apply yourself with diligence to swiftly study this Prajñāpāramitā and swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
When you sit upon the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), we four kings shall each hold a precious bowl and present it to you."
"World-Honored One!

It is not only the Four World-Protecting Kings who appear before these bodhisattvas and speak thus; I, too, constantly go to where those bodhisattvas dwell to provide protection and assistance, let alone the other sons of heaven."
Why is this? It is because it is most rare for a bodhisattva to be able to train in the *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, and having trained, to be able to practice it.

While sentient beings in the world are beset by various sufferings and afflictions, the bodhisattva has already been able to distance himself from all suffering and brings about great benefit and happiness in every place.
“World-Honored One!
This is the present-life merit for a bodhisattva who trains in the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda had this thought:
“Did this Lord Śakra, King of Devas, speak these words through his own eloquence,
or was he sustained by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha?
At that time, Lord Śakra, King of Devas, perceiving their thoughts through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke to them, saying:
“Venerable One!
You should know that all that I have spoken is established by the majestic spiritual power of the Blessed One.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:

"So it is, so it is! That which the Lord of the Devas, Śakra, has thus joyfully proclaimed should be known as being entirely through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and his protective mindfulness."
Chapter Twenty-Four: On Overweening Pride At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:

"You should know that when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the *prajñāpāramitā* and practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, all the evil Māras within the entire trichiliocosm give rise to doubts, thinking:
'Will this bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing this *prajñāpāramitā*, realize the fruit of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha midway? "
"Will they indeed proceed resolutely until they reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? "Ānanda!

Whenever those evil Māras see that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, is proceeding resolutely toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Māras immediately become sorrowful and distressed, as if an arrow had pierced their hearts."

"Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and courses in the perfection of wisdom, various evil Māras come to the bodhisattva’s presence to disturb and distract his mind. By means of their demonic power, they manifest signs such as thunder, hail, wind, and rain throughout all directions, desiring to cause the bodhisattva fear and distraction, even to the point of causing him to fall away from the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for even a single thought-moment."
"Ānanda! You should know that evil Māra is not necessarily able to disturb all bodhisattvas.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Which bodhisattvas are tormented by Māra?
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! If a bodhisattva, in a previous life, had previously heard this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, yet despite having heard it, did not give rise to faith and understanding;”
Ānanda! You should know that when such a bodhisattva exists, evil Māras will come to harass and disturb them, as those Māras seek to find an opportunity against them. Furthermore, Ānanda!
If, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this Dharma gate of the profound Prajñāpāramitā, a doubt arises in their mind:
"Does this Dharma gate of the Prajñāpāramitā actually exist?"
"Is there no such Dharma-gate as this Prajñāpāramitā?
Ānanda! You should know that when this occurs, an evil Māra will come to harass and disturb them, for those Māras have found their opportunity.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva distances himself from virtuous friends and associates with evil friends, because of associating with evil friends, he will not give rise to faith and understanding upon hearing this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Moreover, he will be unable to inquire about its meaning, but will instead think:
'How can I possibly practice this *prajñāpāramitā* now?'"
"Ānanda! You should know that when such a bodhisattva exists, an evil Māra will come to harass and disturb them, seeking an opportunity against them.
Furthermore, Ānanda!"
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accepts those false teachings and acts in accordance with them, those evil Māras, having learned of this matter, will feel joy in their hearts and think:
"This person assists me; he will also cause others to come and assist me, thereby fulfilling my aspirations and conforming to my intentions."
"Ānanda! You should know that when such a bodhisattva exists, an evil Māra will come to harass and disturb them, seeking an opportunity to take advantage of them.
Furthermore, Ānanda!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having heard this profound Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, says to other bodhisattvas:
"This *prajñāpāramitā* is so profound and difficult to understand that I myself cannot fathom its source or bottom; what use is there for you to practice it further?"
"However, you should listen to, receive, and practice what has been taught by the Buddha in other sūtras; you will certainly find the flavor of the Dharma therein.
When that bodhisattva had spoken thus, the other bodhisattvas immediately conceived a mind of distancing themselves from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Ānanda! You should know that when such a statement is made, an evil Māra will come to cause disturbance, seeking an opportunity against those [who speak thus].
Furthermore, Ānanda!"
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva forms such a thought as this:
"I am one who practices genuine seclusion, whereas other bodhisattvas do not practice seclusion."
