Immediately, when the evil Māra knew this thought, he was filled with great joy, delight, and exhilaration. Why is this?
Because as soon as that bodhisattva gives rise to such a thought, he immediately falls away from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; and because of such a fall, the mind of Māra rejoices.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

There may be various evil Māras who come to where a bodhisattva dwells and praise the bodhisattva’s name, clan, and lineage, as well as their dhūta virtues and even the various characteristics of their meritorious qualities."

Having heard this praise, the bodhisattva becomes attached to it; consequently, he gives rise to overweening pride and various forms of conceit, becoming arrogant and haughty while disparaging other bodhisattvas. Due to these causes and conditions, his afflictions increase.

However, because this bodhisattva is beset by the power of Māra, all those who hear his speech will believe and accept it; having accepted it, they will train and practice exactly as he has taught. Yet, for those who see or hear him training and practicing in such a manner, these actions are not genuine. Because they are not real, they give rise to perverted minds, and due to these minds, their physical, verbal, and mental activities are all impure.
By these causes and conditions, they are able to increase the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Seeing this benefit, that host of evil Māras is filled with great joy, delight, and exultation, and immediately thinks:
"Now my palaces are truly not empty, for by those causes and conditions they are able to flourish."

"Ānanda! You should know that such a bodhisattva is unable to fulfill the characteristics of merit; they are not practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), nor are they one who dwells in the stage of non-retrogression."
Why is this? Because a mind of overweening pride gives rise to various faults.
Such a bodhisattva will have evil Māras come to harass and disturb them, as those Māras seek to find an opportunity to exploit them.

"Furthermore, Ānanda! If a person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle and a person belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle should engage in mutual strife and contention, mutually uttering harsh words and treating one another with contempt, derision, and abuse."
At that time, the evil Māra, having understood this matter, immediately thought to himself:

"Although that person of the Bodhisattva vehicle has, by reason of these causes and conditions, become distant from omniscience, that which he has distanced himself from is neither great nor long-lasting."

If a person of the Bodhisattva vehicle quarrels with another person of the Bodhisattva vehicle, mutually uttering harsh words, treating them with contempt, or reviling and slandering them, at that time the evil Māra, having learned of this matter, will be greatly delighted, joyful, and exultant, and will think:
"By these causes and conditions, these persons of the Bodhisattva vehicle will for a long time remain far removed from that omniscience."

"Furthermore, Ānanda! If there is a bodhisattva who has not yet received a prophecy of enlightenment, and he gives rise to a mind of resentment toward another bodhisattva who has already received such a prophecy, he will suffer a retrogression and loss according to the extent of that mental state. For every single thought of retrogression, he loses one kalpa; subsequently, he must complete the full number of kalpas corresponding to those thoughts. However, if he does not abandon the mind of omniscience, or if he encounters a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), he will once again don the armor of diligence."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If such an offense were committed, would the Buddha permit its repentance?"
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!

Within my Dharma, I teach the method for the expiation of offenses; likewise, among the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, I have each taught their respective methods for the expiation of offenses.”

Ānanda! You should know that if a person of the bodhisattva vehicle quarrels with another person of the bodhisattva vehicle, mutually uttering harsh words, treating one another with contempt, reviling, and disparaging them, and having done so, neither repents nor relinquishes it, but instead harbors resentment and binds the mind with it—of such a person, I do not say there is a method for purifying their offense.

Ānanda! If those who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle should quarrel with one another, or even revile and disparage each other, yet subsequently repent and relinquish their animosity, I shall expound for them the method for the purification of offenses.
Ānanda! Furthermore, a bodhisattva should form this thought:

"I shall practice loving-kindness and forbearance toward all sentient beings. Even if they should give rise to evil and come to insult or humiliate me, I shall not produce even a single thought of anger, much less retaliate against them. Should I momentarily give rise to a heart of resentment or hatred, it would be a profound and great failure."

Why is this? I shall act as a great bridge for all sentient beings to enable them all to cross over; I shall always maintain a virtuous intention toward all those beings, and even if I hear harsh words, I will not give rise to anger. I shall be equal toward both myself and others: I shall not transfer my own faults onto others, and regarding the faults of others, I shall always feel regret and apprehension as if they were my own.
Why is this? It is because I desire to cause all sentient beings everywhere to attain great peace and happiness.
If there are sentient beings who are full of anger and affliction, I vow that when I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I shall deliver and liberate them.
Whenever I see anyone seeking enlightenment in any place, at that time I gaze upon them with joy; my face is bright and serene, free from any expression of frowning.
"My mind is firm and unshakable by any anger or affliction.
Ānanda, if a person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle can give rise to such a thought, you should know that they are one who practices the conduct of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not give rise to thoughts of contempt toward those who are śrāvakas, nor indeed should they give rise to thoughts of contempt toward any sentient beings whatsoever."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva dwell together with other bodhisattvas?”
The Buddha said: “Ānanda!
When Bodhisattvas dwell together, they should regard one another as they would the Buddha, thinking: ‘This is our Great Teacher; we are borne on the same vehicle and travel the same path.’”
Whatever that bodhisattva mahāsattva studies, I likewise study; abiding impartially within the Bodhisattva Vehicle, I practice and train according to the Dharma of the bodhisattvas as it truly is.
If their study is mixed and not that which I have studied, yet if their study is pure and can be brought into accord with all-knowledge according to reality, I shall likewise study in that same way.
Ānanda! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is able to train in this way is one with whom you should study and with whom you should dwell together.
One who trains in this way will certainly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma, Dharma-transmitting Master, Imperially Conferred Purple Robe, Court Honorary Official of the Third Rank, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, under Imperial Decree. Chapter Twenty-five: On Training At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Bhagavān, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to study all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) train? The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies exhaustively, he studies all-knowledge; if he studies by way of detachment, he studies all-knowledge.

If he studies in a manner that is without arising, without cessation, without origination, without defilement, and without intrinsic nature—studying like space, the dharma-realm, and tranquility—he studies all-knowledge.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the study of detachment up to the study of the quiescence of the dharma-realm, thereby studying omniscience, how should such persons act?”
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti! If you speak in this manner, how could such people perform any action?"
Subhūti, what do you think?
Since the Tathāgata is named "Tathāgata" because he has realized suchness (tathatā), does that suchness have an end or is there anything produced by it?
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One! Why is this?
"Just as the mark of inexhaustibility is also without activity," the Buddha said, "Subhūti!"

What do you think? Since the Tathāgata is named "Tathāgata" because he has realized suchness (tathatā), does this suchness have arising and ceasing, origination and cessation, defilement, attainment, or realization?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! It is just the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in all-knowledge. Subhūti!”
Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not exhaust the characteristic of suchness;
training in this manner is training in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), training in this manner is training in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*),
training in this manner is training in the stage of a Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*), and training in this manner is training in the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four [fearlessnesses] of a Buddha.
The fearlessnesses and all other Buddha-dharmas, up to and including the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*):
one who trains in this manner can reach the further shore of all training; one who trains in this manner is universally able to subdue Māra and his hosts;
one who trains in this manner swiftly attains the state of non-retrogression; one who trains in this manner swiftly sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). As...
One who trains in this way trains in the Wheel of Dharma with its three turnings and twelve aspects;
one who trains in this way trains in the practice of their own conduct; one who trains in this way trains in the dharma of acting as a refuge for others;

one who trains in this way trains in great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; one who trains in this way trains in delivering the realm of sentient beings.
One who trains in this way trains in the non-interruption of the Buddha-lineage; one who trains in this way trains in opening the gate of the Deathless. Subhūti!
This vast learning is the supreme learning; ordinary, inferior persons are unable to learn in this way.
Only those who can discipline all sentient beings, who wish to act as a refuge for all sentient beings, and who wish to transcend the realm of all sentient beings, are able to learn in this manner.

One who trains in this manner does not fall into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals; is not born into the realm of asuras; is not born in border regions; is not born into the caste of caṇḍālas, nor into low-born lineages, nor into various base castes of craftsmen and the like.
One who trains in this manner does not lose a single eye nor become blind in both; nor does one suffer from squinting, deafness, muteness, hunchback, or lameness.

He is neither ugly nor coarse, neither physically deformed nor possessing unusual features; furthermore, he is free from diseases such as scabies, sores, abscesses, or consumption. His sense faculties are unimpaired and his human form is perfectly complete; his voice is clear and elegant, beloved by all.

Subhūti! Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this way does not take the lives of others, does not steal the property of others, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, nor use divisive speech, harsh words, or idle chatter; he does not give rise to covetousness, does not harbor malice or anger, does not abide in wrong views, does not live by wrong livelihood, does not practice the methods of wrong livelihood, does not keep a retinue of those who break the precepts, and does not associate with those who follow what is not the Dharma. He is not reborn in the long-lived heavens (*dīrghāyuṣka-deva*), and although he enters the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), he is not reborn according to those absorptions.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva is able to accomplish skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
What kind of skillful means does the bodhisattva accomplish?

This refers to the skillful means born from association with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); therefore, although a bodhisattva enters the various meditative absorptions (dhyāna), they are not reborn according to those absorptions.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this manner will attain the purity of the ten powers, the purity of the four fearlessnesses, and even the purity of all buddha-dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Since the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is originally pure, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva further attain the purity of the ten powers, the purity of the four fearlessnesses, and even the purity of all Buddha-dharmas?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “So it is, so it is! Subhūti!”

The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is primordially pure; within this primordially pure intrinsic nature of all phenomena, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in accordance with reality, without being startled, without being terrified, without retreating, and without sinking.
Subhūti! Those foolish ordinary beings do not know and do not see such dharmas; because they do not know and do not see them, they have no realization.

Therefore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva exerts diligent effort in training therein; having trained himself, he causes other ordinary beings to train in this Dharma according to the principle, so that they may know it truly and see it truly.
By training in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the purity of the ten powers, the purity of the four fearlessnesses, and even the purity of all buddha-dharmas.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this manner is able to fully comprehend the mental activities and the objects of the minds of all sentient beings. Subhūti!
For example, the great earth produces little Jāmbūnada gold, while there are many thorns, pebbles, sand, grasses, trees, and the like.

It is the same with all sentient beings: among the multitude of beings, few are able to take delight in practicing and studying the Prajñāpāramitā, whereas many take delight in practicing and studying the dharmas of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Subhūti! Furthermore, it is as if among a multitude of sentient beings, few cultivate the karma of a wheel-turning monarch, while many cultivate the karma of various minor kings. Subhūti!

It should be known that among the multitudes of sentient beings, those who practice the path of the *prajñāpāramitā* are few, while those who practice the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are many; it is likewise so.
"Subhūti! Furthermore, among the assembly of sentient beings, few cultivate the meritorious karma of Śakra, while many cultivate the karma of those various devaputras. Subhūti!"

It should be known that among the multitudes of sentient beings, those who practice the *prajñāpāramitā* are few, while those who practice the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are many; it is likewise so.
Subhūti! It is just as among a multitude of sentient beings, few cultivate the meritorious karma of that Brahmā King, while many cultivate the karma of those various Brahmā assemblies. Subhūti!

It should be known that among the assembly of sentient beings, those who do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* are few, while those who do regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* are many; it is exactly like this.

Subhūti! For this reason, you should know that among the multitude of sentient beings, few are able to resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; of those few who have resolved their minds, even fewer are able to practice in accordance with the truth; of those few who are able to practice, even fewer are able to cultivate practices associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*; and of those few who are able to cultivate such associated practices, even fewer are able to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without falling back.
Subhūti! Therefore, if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to be among the very least of the few, they should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies this perfection of wisdom, they will not give rise to a defiled mind, nor a mind of doubt, nor a mind of malice or envy, nor a mind of stinginess, nor a mind of broken precepts, nor a mind of anger or resentment, nor a mind of laziness, nor a mind of distraction, nor a mind of delusion."
Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice and study this perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
This perfection of wisdom can protect all perfections, can receive all perfections, can grasp all perfections, can accumulate all perfections, and can encompass all perfections.
Subhūti! Just as the sixty-two views are subsumed within the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), so too are all the pāramitās subsumed within the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Subhūti! Furthermore, just as all the faculties of a person are entirely subsumed within the life-faculty, so too are all wholesome dharmas subsumed within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Subhūti! Furthermore, just as when the life-faculty of a person ceases, all the other faculties also cease, so it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattva: when wisdom ceases, all wholesome dharmas likewise cease accordingly.
Subhūti! Therefore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to protect the various pāramitās, or wishes to encompass the various pāramitās, they should practice and study this prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to be the most preeminent in merit among all sentient beings and to serve as their leader, they should practice and study this Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, the Buddha said:
"Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the sentient beings in the trichiliocosm many?"
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Even the sentient beings within this Jambudvīpa alone are already countless; how much more so are all the sentient beings in the trichiliocosm?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings in this trichiliocosm were each to practice and abide on the bodhisattva stages; and suppose there were a person who, for the duration of their entire life, provided offerings of food and drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and other articles of comfort to all these bodhisattvas throughout the trichiliocosm.”
"Would this person, by reason of these causes and conditions, obtain much merit? Subhūti replied,
"Very much, World-Honored One!"
"Very much so, Sugata! The Buddha said, "Subhūti!..."

If, moreover, there should be someone who is able to practice this Prajñāpāramitā for even the duration of a single snap of the fingers, the merit they obtain would be twice as great as that of the former.
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā brings vast benefit to all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and is further able to protect and assist them in their attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Subhūti! For this reason, if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to be the most supreme and unsurpassed among all sentient beings; if they wish to serve as a refuge for all sentient beings; if they wish to enter exclusively into the realm of the Buddhas; if they wish to be fully endowed with the dharmas of the Buddha’s merits; if they wish to attain the playful supernormal powers of a Buddha; if they wish to perform the great lion’s roar of a Buddha; if they wish to reach all the spheres of a Buddha’s activity; or if they wish to preach the Dharma universally in great assemblies throughout the trichiliocosm.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish such merits and benefits as these, they should study this Prajñāpāramitā.
"It is impossible that one who studies this Prajñāpāramitā would be unable to fulfill all merits and benefits.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“Does a bodhisattva mahāsattva also fully possess the merits and benefits of the śrāvakas? The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas likewise study these dharmas of the śrāvakas and likewise fulfill the benefits of the śrāvaka’s merits.
Subhūti, although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study in this way, know in this way, and obtain such benefits, they do not give rise to a mind of dwelling or attachment therein.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva likewise teaches those Śrāvaka dharmas, yet does not grasp at these dharmas.

Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva trains in this manner, he can act as a great field of merit for all the world, including its gods, humans, and asuras; moreover, the field of merit created by the Bodhisattva is supreme and most excellent, surpassing all fields of merit belonging to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

Subhūti! One who trains in this manner practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), draws near to all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), does not abandon the perfection of wisdom, and does not depart from the perfection of wisdom.
One who trains in this manner does not fall away from omniscience, remains far removed from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and draws near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva should form this thought:
"This is the prajñāpāramitā; this is called the prajñāpāramitā; by studying this prajñāpāramitā, I shall attain all-knowledge (sarvajñatā)."
“Subhūti! If one discriminates in this way, it is not called training in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to discrimination regarding the perfection of wisdom—having no cognition, no vision, and no attainment—and because they do not discriminate in this way, have no cognition or vision, and have no attainment, this is called training in the perfection of wisdom.”
Chapter 26: The Parable of the Illusion At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had this thought:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this *prajñāpāramitā* can already surpass all sentient beings, how much more so one who has realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"

Therefore, you should know that if there is anyone who delights in omniscience, that person attains great and wholesome benefit and leads a truly virtuous life; how much more so for one who can resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. You should know that such a person is universally revered and loved by all sentient beings, and is capable of universally taming and guiding all sentient beings.
After Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had formed this thought, he immediately manifested mandārava flowers, filling the palms of his hands and scattering them over the Buddha.
Having scattered the flowers upon the Buddha, he joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!

If there are those who resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, may they all universally attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; may they universally fulfill all Buddha-dharmas, fulfill the dharmas corresponding to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), fulfill the dharmas of spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), and fulfill the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*). May all sentient beings universally cross the shore of birth and death and realize the path to *nirvāṇa*; may they gather the minds of sentient beings and cause them all to be universally fulfilled.
“World-Honored One!

I see that within birth and death there are various kinds of suffering. I do not wish for those who have first resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* to undergo any regression in even a single thought-moment; nor do I wish for those who have already attained stable abiding in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* to give rise to regression in even a single thought-moment. For this reason, I desire to cause all beings universally to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
Why is this? Those who are able to resolve their minds bring vast benefit and compassion to all the worlds—devas, humans, asuras, and so forth.

Having themselves attained liberation, they further give rise to such a mind toward all sentient beings: to cause all who are not yet liberated to be universally liberated; to cause all who have not yet crossed over to be universally delivered; and to cause all who have not yet entered nirvana to universally attain nirvana.
“World-Honored One!

If there are good sons or good daughters who, toward a bodhisattva who has first resolved for enlightenment, give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy regarding all their meritorious dharmas; or if they give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward a bodhisattva who has long practiced and cultivated; or if they give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward a bodhisattva who dwells in non-retrogression; or if they give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward a bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood—among such good sons and good daughters who are able to give rise to these minds of sympathetic joy, which one should be said to obtain the greater merit?”
The Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:

“Kauśika! Even Sumeru, the king of mountains, may be weighed and its measure known; yet the merit obtained by those sons and daughters of good family through these various minds of sympathetic joy cannot be weighed, nor can its measure be known.”

“Kauśika! Furthermore, while the four great continents may be weighed and their limits known, the merit obtained by those sons and daughters of good family through these various acts of sympathetic joy cannot be weighed and its limits cannot be known.”

Kauśika! Furthermore, while a small chiliocosm may be weighed and its limit known, the merit obtained by those sons and daughters of good family through these various minds of sympathetic joy cannot be weighed, nor can its limit be known.

Kauśika! Furthermore, while a medium-sized thousandfold world-system may be weighed and its limits known, the merit obtained by those sons and daughters of good family through these various acts of sympathetic joy cannot be weighed, nor can its limits be known.

Kauśika! Furthermore, while the three-thousandfold world system may be weighed and its limit known, the merit obtained by those sons and daughters of good family through these various minds of sympathetic joy cannot be weighed, nor can its limit be known.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If there are those who cannot give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward bodhisattvas from those at the stage of initial resolve up to those in their final birth before buddhahood, you should know that such persons are possessed by evil Māras and are the retinues of Māra; they have passed away from the realm of those Māras and come to be born here."
Why is this? It is because these minds of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-citta*) are capable of destroying all evil Māras.

Furthermore, if there are persons who can give rise to these minds of sympathetic joy, those persons should dedicate the merit of that sympathetic joy toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; by means of this dedication, they are able to increase their progress toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Therefore, you should know that those who are able to give rise to such minds of sympathetic joy are never separated from the Buddha, never separated from the Dharma, and never separated from the Sangha; they increase all supreme merits.
The Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: “So it is, so it is! Kauśika!”

If there is anyone who can give rise to such thoughts of sympathetic joy, that person will not be separated from the Buddha, not be separated from the Dharma, and not be separated from the Saṅgha, and will increase all supreme merits.
Furthermore, Kauśika!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family can give rise to such minds of sympathetic joy, you should know that this son or daughter of good family will swiftly encounter a Buddha.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Sugata!”
Those sons or daughters of good family who are able to give rise to such thoughts of sympathetic joy will swiftly encounter a Buddha.
Furthermore, by the power of these roots of goodness from sympathetic joy, wherever they are born, they will be respected, honored, and praised by others.

These sons and daughters of good family will have pure faculties of the eye, not beholding unwholesome forms; pure faculties of the ear, not hearing unwholesome sounds; pure faculties of the nose, not smelling unwholesome odors; pure faculties of the tongue, not tasting unwholesome flavors; and pure faculties of the body, not being defiled by improper tactile objects.
Furthermore, they shall not fall into the evil realms, but will be reborn in the human or heavenly paths. Why is this?

Because these sons and daughters of good family have accomplished immeasurable and innumerable roots of goodness through sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*); because they always delight in benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings; and because by being able to give rise to this mind of sympathetic joy, they are able to increase their practice for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, gradually attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"After these sons and daughters of good family have attained Bodhi, they will extensively deliver immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, causing them all to enter Nirvana.
The Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying: "Kauśika!"
All that you have said is due to the majestic power and protective mindfulness of the Tathāgata.

If good sons or good daughters can give rise to such minds of sympathetic joy, these good sons and good daughters will deeply plant roots of goodness; by means of these roots of goodness, they will extensively bring great benefit to immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings.
"By means of these causes and conditions, one is able to increase all wholesome dharmas and gradually attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Since the mind is like an illusion, how can one attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of this mind?
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"What do you think? Do you perceive a mind that is like an illusion?"
Subhūti said, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! Do you perceive any characteristic of an illusion that can be apprehended? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
I do not perceive a mind that is like an illusion, nor do I perceive any illusory characteristics that can be apprehended.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! Can you, by means of this mind or these marks, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said, "Subhūti!

What do you think? If one does not perceive a mind that is like an illusion and the characteristics of an illusion, apart from this mind and these characteristics, do you see any dharma by which one can attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One!
Apart from the mind that is like an illusion and its illusory marks, one does not perceive any dharma that can attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

"Bhagavān! If there were any dharma that could be perceived apart from the mind that is like an illusion and apart from illusory marks, that dharma could likewise not be said to exist or not to exist. Therefore, within the ultimate detachment of all dharmas, one cannot say they exist, nor can one say they do not exist."
If all dharmas are ultimately detached, then unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening is also ultimately detached, and the perfection of wisdom is also ultimately detached.

Because all dharmas are ultimately detached, there is no dharma that can be cultivated and no dharma that can be attained; because all dharmas are unattainable, even *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* cannot be attained.
Because this is ultimately detached, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also ultimately detached.
World-Honored One!
It is by means of the perfection of wisdom that the bodhisattva mahāsattva attains unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment.
Yet the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is ultimately detached, and unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) is also ultimately detached.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, how can that which is detached attain that which is detached?
The Buddha praised Subhūti, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”

So it is, so it is! All dharmas are ultimately detached; the perfection of wisdom is also ultimately detached; unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment is also ultimately detached; and the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also ultimately detached.

Furthermore, because the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas understand, in accordance with reality, that this perfection of wisdom is ultimately detached within these dharmas, it is therefore not the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti! Therefore, although all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment by means of the perfection of wisdom, therein there is no dharma that can be grasped and no dharma that can be obtained.
Because there is neither grasping nor attainment, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, it is not by means of abandoning that which is abandoned.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, it is extremely difficult for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to practice this profound meaning.”
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, it is so, it is so!”
This profound meaning is extremely difficult for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to practice. Subhūti!
If a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices this profound meaning yet does not realize the fruits of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha along the way, that is truly difficult indeed.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, that which is undertaken by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not difficult.”
Why is this? Because all dharmas are neither to be attained nor realized.

Since there is nothing to be attained and nothing to be realized, within this there is no one who realizes, no object to be realized, and no dharma used for realization; therefore, what the bodhisattva mahāsattva does is not difficult.

"Bhagavān! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this teaching, is not startled, not terrified, does not recoil, and does not sink in despair, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
Although they practice in this way, they do not perceive themselves as practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Because they do not perceive the characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā* being practiced in this manner, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and are able to remain far removed from the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; this is the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
World-Honored One!
It is as if space does not form this thought:
"This is distant; this is near."
Why is this? Because space is without discrimination.
The perfection of wisdom is likewise; it does not form such a thought:
"Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is near to me; the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha are far from me.
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is free from conceptual discrimination.
Furthermore, it is like a person conjured by illusion who does not think:
"That magician is near to me, while the other spectators are far from me. Why is this?
Because a person conjured by illusion is devoid of discrimination, so too is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); it does not form such a thought as:
"Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is near to me, while the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha are far from me."
Why is this? Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is free from conceptual discrimination.
Furthermore, it is like various reflections which do not form such thoughts:
"That which is the cause of the shadow is near to me; that which is not its cause is far from me. Why is this?
Because the shadow has no discrimination.
The Prajñāpāramitā is likewise; it does not form the thought:
"Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is near to me, while the stages of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha are far from me."
Why is this? Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is non-conceptual.
Furthermore, it is just as the Tathāgata has neither hatred nor affection toward any sentient beings.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has severed all hatred and attachment.
The Prajñāpāramitā is likewise; it is without hatred and without attachment.
Why is this? Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is not a dharma of aversion or attachment.
Furthermore, it is like the Tathāgata, who is free from all conceptual discrimination.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has severed all conceptual discrimination.
Prajñāpāramitā is likewise; it is free from all conceptual discrimination.
Why is this? Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is without conceptual discrimination.
Furthermore, it is like a person created by a Buddha who does not form such thoughts:
“Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is near to me; the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha are far from me.
Why is this? Because a person created by transformation is without discrimination.
The perfection of wisdom is also like this; it does not form such a thought as:
"Unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is near to me, while the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are far from me."
Why is this? Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is without conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*).

It is also like a person created by the Buddha through transformation (*nirmāṇapuruṣa*), who is able to accomplish all tasks as they are performed; yet, although these tasks are accomplished, there is no conceptual discrimination.
Why is this? Because an emanated person is without conceptual discrimination.
The Prajñāpāramitā is likewise; if one practices all dharmas accordingly, they can all be accomplished.
Why is this? Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is free from conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*).

It is like a master craftsman who, through skillful means, uses mechanical wood to create the forms of men and women; these can accomplish whatever task they are made to perform, yet despite what they accomplish, they remain without conceptual discrimination.
Why is this? Because it is produced by skillful illusion,
World-Honored One!

The perfection of wisdom is likewise: if all phenomena are practiced according to their respective applications, they can all be accomplished; yet, although there is that which is accomplished, there is no conceptual discrimination.
"Why is this? Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is without conceptual discrimination.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heavens, Imperial Honorary Court Gentleman, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, and Purple-Robed Subject Shi Hu, by imperial decree. Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Meaning of Firmness. Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Meaning of Firmness. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this profound perfection of wisdom, they are practicing the meaning of firmness.
Subhūti said, “So it is, so it is!”
"Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this profound perfection of wisdom, they are practicing the meaning of firmness.
At that time, a host of one thousand devaputras from the desire realm had this thought:
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, practice this profound prajñā-pāramitā.

Although they fully comprehend the characteristics of all phenomena and enter into the nature of all phenomena, they do not abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) realized by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; for this reason, they are worthy of veneration.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, knowing their thoughts, addressed them, saying:
"O sons of the gods!
It would not be difficult for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* not to realize the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."

Why is this? If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dons the armor of diligence, desiring to deliver immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, causing them all to dwell securely in great parinirvāṇa—this is a difficult task.

Why is this? Because sentient beings are ultimately detached and non-existent; because they are non-existent, the characteristic of a sentient being cannot be apprehended. Therefore, sentient beings cannot be delivered.
O sons of the gods!
If a bodhisattva wishes to deliver sentient beings, he wishes to deliver empty space. Why is this?
Because space is detached, sentient beings are also detached; because space is non-existent, sentient beings are also non-existent; ultimately, no sentient being can be apprehended.
That all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas desire to deliver those who are to be delivered is a difficult task. O devaputras!
It is just as if a person were to fight against empty space; the Buddha’s teaching that the characteristics of sentient beings are ungraspable is likewise so.

Why is this? Because sentient beings are detached, form is also detached; because sentient beings are detached, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also detached; because sentient beings are detached, even all dharmas are likewise detached.
"O sons of the gods!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such a teaching, is not startled, not terrified, does not retreat, and does not sink into despondency, you should know that this one is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"For what reason and by what causes does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this teaching, not become startled, not become terrified, not retreat, and not sink into despondency?"
Subhūti said: "Because all dharmas are detached, they do not sink. Why is this?"
“World-Honored One!
‘Sinking’ cannot be apprehended, the phenomenon of sinking cannot be apprehended, and the place where one sinks also cannot be apprehended.
For these reasons, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this teaching, they are not startled, not terrified, do not retreat, and do not sink.”
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, it is so, it is so!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this teaching, is not startled, not terrified, does not retreat, and does not sink, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this prajñāpāramitā, they will always be honored, revered, prostrated to, and praised by Mahābrahmā, Śakra Devendra, Maheśvara, and the hosts of all other devaputras of the desire realm.”
The Buddha said: “Subhūti!

Not only do Mahābrahmā, Śakra Devendra, Maheśvara, and the other hosts of devaputras in the desire realm revere, respect, prostrate to, and praise them, but all the devaputra hosts of the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahma, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha heavens likewise constantly revere, respect, prostrate to, and praise these bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently dwelling and teaching the Dharma in the infinite, incalculable worlds of the ten directions constantly observe this bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom with their Buddha-eye, and they also constantly protect and keep them in mind through their Buddha-majesty.

Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they immediately attain non-retrogression from anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, and the hosts of evil Māras find no opportunity to interfere.

Subhūti! Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were each transformed into various evil Māras; even this host of Māras would still be unable to find any opportunity to harm that bodhisattva mahāsattva who is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti! Let alone this trichiliocosm.

As previously described, even if all sentient beings in as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were each transformed into evil Māras, that host of Māras would still be unable to find any opportunity to harm a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti! You should know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom accomplishes two dharmas, such that all māras cannot find an opportunity to exploit them.
What are these two? They are:
contemplating that all phenomena are empty, and not abandoning any sentient beings. These are the two dharmas, Subhūti.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas which, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes them, prevent the various māras from finding an opportunity to exploit him.
What are these two? They are:
being able to act according to one’s word, and being praised by all Buddhas. These are the two dharmas.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, various sons of the gods will constantly come to his presence, gaze upon him with reverence and pay him homage, saying:
"O son of noble family!"
"You should swiftly practice this Prajñāpāramitā and swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Why is this?
O son of good family!"

Because you practice this *prajñāpāramitā*, you are able to serve as a refuge for sentient beings who have no refuge; to deliver those who have no savior; to provide a place of return for those who have no return; to serve as a dwelling for those who have no shelter; to provide a destination for those who have no destination; to serve as an island for those who have no island; to show the ultimate path to those who do not know the ultimate path; to show the right path to those who do not know the right path; and to provide light for those who dwell in darkness.
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) achieve such merits as these.

Subhūti, furthermore, when the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in the immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions, surrounded by assemblies of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, proclaim the Dharma, they constantly praise all the merits of these bodhisattvas, as well as their names, clans, physical appearances, and majestic powers.

Subhūti! Just as I now gather this assembly and preach the Dharma, I constantly praise the merits, names, clans, physical forms, and majestic powers of the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu in the Buddha-field of Akṣobhya, as well as those of all the other bodhisattvas practicing the holy life in that field.

Subhūti! It is likewise in all the buddha-fields; whenever those various buddhas preach the Dharma in their assemblies, they also constantly praise the merits, names, clans, physical forms, and powers of those who practice the *prajñāpāramitā* in my own land, as well as other bodhisattvas who cultivate pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, when the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
expound the Dharma, do they universally praise all the merits, names, clans, physical characteristics, and majestic powers of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?”
The Buddha said, “No, Subhūti! When the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, expound the Dharma, there are some bodhisattva-mahāsattvas whom they praise and others whom they do not praise.”
Subhūti asked: "Which bodhisattvas are those who offer praise?
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! All those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the stage of non-retrogression are constantly praised by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Subhūti said:
“If one has not yet abided in the stage of non-retrogression, are they praised by the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones? The Buddha said, “Subhūti!...”

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, although they have not yet established themselves on the stage of non-retrogression, are nonetheless constantly praised by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Who are they?

They are those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who study the path and dharmas practiced by the Tathāgata Akṣobhya when he was originally a bodhisattva; such bodhisattvas, though they have not yet established themselves on the stage of non-retrogression, are also constantly praised by all the Buddhas.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the dharmas of the path practiced by the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu, that bodhisattva, although not yet established in the stage of non-retrogression, is constantly praised by all Buddhas.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), has faith and understanding that all phenomena are unborn, yet has not yet realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); and if they have faith and understanding that all phenomena are quiescent, yet within the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika-bhūmi) have not yet attained mastery over the quiescence of all phenomena—such a bodhisattva is also constantly praised by all Buddhas.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is praised by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, they will certainly abide in the stage of non-retrogression, remain far removed from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and will definitely receive the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For what reason do Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas receive the joint praise of all those Buddhas?
It is because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are able to practice this Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, does not doubt, does not regret, does not find it difficult, and does not become despondent, then that bodhisattva mahāsattva shall hear this Dharma-gate of *prajñāpāramitā* in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya, as well as in the presence of the bodhisattvas in his land. Having heard it, they will believe and understand it; having believed and understood it accordingly, they will attain the stage of non-retrogression."

Subhūti! If those who hear this Dharma-gate and give rise to faith and understanding obtain such merit as this, how much more so for those who, according to their faith and understanding, abide in accordance with the principle and act in accordance with the principle, dwelling in all-knowledge just as they abide in Suchness?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since no dharma can be apprehended apart from suchness (tathatā), by what dharma should one abide within suchness?”
"By what dharma should one attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
and by what dharma can it be explained?
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! As you have said, apart from suchness (tathatā), no dharma can be apprehended. By means of what dharma would one abide within suchness?
By means of what dharma would one attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
By what dharma can it be explained? It is so, it is so, Subhūti!
Apart from suchness, no dharma can be apprehended; even within suchness, abiding in suchness itself cannot be apprehended, let alone one who abides in suchness.
Within suchness, even *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not exist, let alone one who realizes it. Therefore, there is nothing to be realized, no realizer, and no dharma by which to realize.
"If even in the middle there is no dharma to be found, how much less could there be one who preaches the Dharma?
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The perfection of wisdom is most supreme and profound.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to accomplish unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, hears this teaching—that there is no dharma to abide in, no dharma to realize, and no dharma to expound—and yet does not doubt, does not regret, does not find it difficult, and does not become despondent therein, you should know that what this bodhisattva mahāsattva undertakes is exceedingly difficult.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
“Kauśika! As you have said, it is indeed most difficult for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to hear this profound Dharma and neither doubt, nor regret, nor find it hard, nor become despondent.”
"Kauśika! Within the emptiness of all phenomena, what phenomenon could there be that might give rise to doubt, regret, or difficulty?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:

"Whatever the Venerable One delights in expounding is all based on emptiness, yet therein he encounters no obstruction; it is just as when an arrow is shot upward into the void and its flight meets no resistance—the unimpeded nature of the Venerable One’s exposition is likewise so."
After Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had spoken thus, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is what I have said in accordance with the Tathāgata’s teaching and is it a response that accords with the Dharma?”
The Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying: “Kauśika, it is so; it is so!”
What you have said is in accordance with what the Tathāgata has taught; it is called the correct teaching. Your response is in accordance with the Dharma; it is called the correct answer. Kausika!

Whatever Subhūti delights in expounding all arises from emptiness. Since even the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be one who practices the perfection of wisdom?
Since even *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be one who realizes *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Since even omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be one who realizes omniscience?
Since even suchness cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be one who abides in suchness?
Since even the dharma of non-arising cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be one who realizes non-arising?
If even a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be one who seeks awakening?
If even the ten powers cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be one who possesses these powers?
Since even the four fearlessnesses cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be one who has achieved them?
Since even dharmas cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be one who preaches the Dharma?
Kauśika! Subhūti thus delights in practicing the seclusion of all dharmas and practices the path of non-apprehension of all dharmas.

Compared to the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* by the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, Subhūti’s such practice does not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousandth part, a *koṭi*-th part, a hundred-thousand-*koṭi*-th part, a hundred-thousand-*koṭi*-nayuta-th part; it does not equal any part calculated by number, nor any part expressed by analogy, nor even a part as small as an *upaniṣad*.

Kauśika! With the exception of the practice of the Tathāgata, among all other practices of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice this Prajñāpāramitā, it is the most supreme, the greatest, the most excellent, the most wondrous, the unsurpassed among the unsurpassed, the unequaled and equal to the unequaled; it cannot be equaled by any Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha.

Therefore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to be the most supreme, the greatest, the most excellent, and the most wondrous among all sentient beings— the unsurpassed among the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled— they should study this perfection of wisdom, the practice of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Chapter 28: The Chapter on the Circumstances of Scattering Flowers, Part One. At that time, there was again a multitude of devaputras from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, each holding māndārava flowers and mahāmāndārava flowers, who came to where the Buddha was and scattered these flowers over him.

At that moment, sixty thousand bhikṣus within the assembly rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and stood reverently before the Buddha with palms joined.

At that time, through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, each of the bhikṣus naturally had their palms filled with *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers; they then scattered these flowers over the Buddha.
Having scattered flowers over the Buddha, they all spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
We all cultivate this Prajñāpāramitā and all practice such unsurpassed and supreme conduct."

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately emitted a great radiance from the opening of his mouth—various colored lights such as blue, yellow, red, and white—which illuminated immeasurable and boundless Buddha-fields up to the Brahma realm. Having shone everywhere, the light returned, circled the Buddha three times, and re-entered through the crown of the World-Honored One’s head.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"By what cause and by what condition has this radiance been emitted?"
"If there were no causes and conditions, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha would not emit this light.
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:

"You should now know that these sixty thousand bhikṣus will all attain Buddhahood in the future Star-Constellation Eon (Tārakakalpa), appearing in the world with the same name: Saṃkusumita Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
The lifespan of all these Tathāgatas is exactly equal at twenty thousand kalpas, and the duration of their True Dharma remaining in the world is likewise twenty thousand kalpas.
Furthermore, the assemblies of śrāvakas within the congregations of these Buddhas are also equal in their respective numbers.

Ānanda! You should know that from this time forward, wherever these sixty thousand bhikṣus are born, they shall leave the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma. In whatever direction—whether royal cities or villages—they shall everywhere expound the True Dharma for the sake of others. In each world where they preach the Dharma, various wonderful flowers of five colors shall constantly rain down as an offering. These bhikṣus will bring great benefit in every place they go, until finally they attain perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, Ānanda! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva desires to practice that supreme conduct, they should practice this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, Ānanda!

If there are those who can practice this Prajñāpāramitā, you should know that they have all passed away from the human realm, or else have passed away from the realm of the gods of the desire realm and subsequently been reborn here.
Why is this? Because the human realm and the gods of the Heaven of Contentment find it easy to practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, Ānanda!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this perfection of wisdom, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is constantly observed by all the Buddhas.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having received, upheld, recited, memorized, contemplated, and even transcribed this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā*, further explains it to others according to reason, instructs them according to reality, benefits them as is appropriate, and generates joy in them according to principle.

One who practices in this manner should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has deeply planted roots of goodness under the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and not under śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Why is this? Because the roots of goodness of the *prajñāpāramitā* are supreme.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva receives, upholds, reads, recites, memorizes, contemplates, explains to others, or even transcribes this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will constantly draw near to the Buddhas of the present and hear and receive the True Dharma.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this Dharma-door of the Perfection of Wisdom and does not oppose, resist, disparage, or slander it, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already planted roots of goodness under previous Buddhas.
Why is this? Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice this prajñāpāramitā, they are able to accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Therefore, Ānanda! I now entrust this true Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā to you among the assembly of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras. You should, regarding this true Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā, mindfully receive, uphold, proclaim, and disseminate it, so that it may endure for a long time without being extinguished.
Ānanda! Among all the dharmas I have taught, only the Prajñāpāramitā must not be forgotten or lost.
If there is anyone who receives and upholds this dharma-gate, yet errs or forgets even a single word or phrase, their transgression is extremely grave; such a person does not bring joy to my mind.
If one forgets or loses other dharmas, the offense is light.
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is subtle, wondrous, and profoundly deep.

If there are those who do not give rise to respect or reverence for this Dharma-gate, and are unable to gaze upon it, pay homage to it, or make offerings to it, you should know that such persons do not give rise to respect or reverence for the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, nor are they able to gaze upon them, pay homage to them, or make offerings to them; such persons do not bring joy to my mind.
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present; she gives birth to all Buddhas and to omniscience.
Therefore, Ānanda, I now entrust this true Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā to you. When this true Dharma is on the verge of being extinguished,
you should receive, uphold, proclaim, and disseminate it so that it does not perish.

Furthermore, regarding all the words, phrases, and syllables of this Dharma, you should clearly memorize them so as not to forget or lose them; you should contemplate and practice them with correct mental attention, extensively explain their meaning to others, and exhort them to receive, uphold, recite, and transcribe it.
Why is this? Because this Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-body of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

If there are those who give rise to a heart of joy toward me, and who revere, honor, gaze upon, and make offerings to me, such persons should, by means of that very same mind, revere, honor, gaze upon, and make offerings to this Dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. This is equivalent to making offerings to me, and it is likewise equivalent to making offerings to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

If there are those who love and do not forsake me, they should likewise love and not forsake the Prajñāpāramitā, recollecting, upholding, proclaiming, and disseminating it so that it shall never be extinguished.

Ānanda! I now entrust you with these causes and conditions for this commission; I shall speak of them briefly for now, but were I to explain them in detail, even in one kalpa, or more than one kalpa, or even for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, I could not finish speaking of them.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
All the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, act as Great Teachers among the multitudes of devas, humans, and asuras in all worlds.
The Prajñāpāramitā is likewise so; among all the multitudes of gods, humans, and asuras in all worlds, it serves as the Great Teacher.
Why is this? Because this Prajñāpāramitā possesses great causal conditions, capable of providing great benefit to all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

If there are persons who do not depart from this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā, and who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, remember, contemplate, explain it to others, and even transcribe it—this is precisely my practice of teaching and transformation.

Such a person is then not separated from the Buddha, not separated from the Dharma, and not separated from the Sangha; they are able to protect and assist the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present.
Why is this? Because all the unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas is born from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Ānanda! The unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all past Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, has arisen entirely from this Prajñāpāramitā.
If the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all future Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas also arises from this Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones who currently reside and teach the Dharma in the immeasurable, incalculable worlds of the ten directions, also arises from this very Prajñāpāramitā.

Therefore, Ānanda! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should skillfully study the various pāramitās; for one who studies these pāramitās is studying the prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is able to give birth to all the other *pāramitās*.
Furthermore, this *prajñāpāramitā* is the mother of all bodhisattvas, for it is able to give birth to all bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, the various pāramitās are also able to give birth to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Why is this?
Because all the pāramitās arise from within the prajñā-pāramitā; thus, the various pāramitās produced by this prajñā-pāramitā are also able to assist in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should skillfully train in the various pāramitās.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
You should listen attentively; I now entrust this True Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā to you for a second and third time."
You should remember and uphold this, taking care not to forget it.
When this Dharma is about to perish, you should protect, assist, proclaim, and disseminate it so that it does not come to an end.
Ānanda! This Prajñāpāramitā is the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas. Why is this so?

All the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past extensively expounded this inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of all sentient beings, causing all beings to universally attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The future Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas will likewise expound this inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of the Prajñāpāramitā for all sentient beings, so that all sentient beings may universally attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Furthermore, the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who currently reside and teach the Dharma in the immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions, likewise proclaim this inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of all sentient beings, so that all sentient beings may universally attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

If a person of the Śrāvaka vehicle were to universally proclaim the Śrāvaka Dharma for all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm according to their needs, causing them all to realize the fruit of Arhatship, that benefit would not be in vain.
Ānanda! Regarding all the merit of those arhats consisting of their giving, their observance of precepts, and their cultivation of concentration—what do you think? Is this not much?
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“Very many, World-Honored One! Very many, Sugata!”
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!

Although that merit is vast, it does not equal the merit obtained by a bodhisattva who, through this single dharma corresponding with the *prajñāpāramitā*, correctly expounds it for the sake of all sentient beings; that bodhisattva mahāsattva obtains far more merit.”

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within this Dharma-gate of the Prajñāpāramitā, can expound it correctly for other bodhisattva mahāsattvas even for a single day, they shall obtain manifold greater merit.
Ānanda! Let alone for a single day; if one can [practice] from dawn until the time for the meal;
and setting aside the period from dawn until the time for the meal, if one can [practice] for even a single *le-ke* (ghaṭikā);
Setting aside this single *ghaṭikā*, if one can [teach] for even a single *muhūrta*;
setting aside one *muhūrta*, if one can [teach] for even a single *lava*;

setting aside one *lava*, if one can [teach] for even a single *kṣaṇa*—if, during such a single *kṣaṇa*, one correctly expounds this Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* for other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, it should be known that the merit obtained by that bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise many times greater.
Ānanda! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus bestow the Dharma upon sentient beings, it cannot be compared or equated with the roots of goodness or the merit of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

[Translated by Imperial Decree by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heavens, Chao Feng Da Fu, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Dharma-Transmitting Master, and Purple-Robed Subject Shi Hu. Chapter Twenty-Eight, Part Two: The Section on the Circumstances of Scattering Flowers. At that time, when the World-Honored One was preaching this True Dharma of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he manifested signs of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) within the great assembly; and among those gathered, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...
Bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and upāsakas.
Upāsikās, devas, and nāgas.
yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras.
Garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
Through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, humans and non-humans alike suddenly beheld the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya within this assembly.

He was like the great ocean—profound, stable, and immovable—surrounded by immeasurable and innumerable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who were endowed with inconceivable and manifold merits. There were also Arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions; whose minds were well-liberated and whose wisdom was well-liberated; who, like great dragon kings, had accomplished what was to be done and laid down their heavy burdens; who had attained their own benefit and exhausted the fetters of existence; who possessed unimpeded right knowledge and mastery over their minds; and who were fully endowed with all virtues. Furthermore, there were great Śrāvakas and immeasurable, innumerable Bhikṣus.
Bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
as well as the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings— surrounded by such a multitude— they were able to see all the signs of adornment and other features of the Buddha-land of Akṣobhya.
Although this assembly had given rise to a sense of wonder at these signs and took delight only in gazing upon them, they all remained unaware of where they had come from.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One withdrew his supernormal power, and suddenly this assembly no longer saw the Tathāgata Akṣobhya nor those various signs.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"Since this great assembly no longer sees the Tathāgata Akṣobhya nor his various marks, you should know that all dharmas are likewise so: they do not confront the eye; they are dharmas that cannot be confronted, dharmas that cannot be seen. Therefore, they come from nowhere and go nowhere."
Why is this? Ānanda! All phenomena have no knower, no seer, no creator, and no doer.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are like space, being without discrimination.
All phenomena are profoundly deep and inconceivable; they are like illusory beings who do not grasp at any phenomena, for they lack any solid substance.
All phenomena are likewise without anything to be grasped. Ānanda!
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice in this manner, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), yet within it there is no dharma to which they may become attached.
If one trains in this way, one trains in the perfection of wisdom; one who trains in this way is able to reach the further shore of all trainings.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should study this prajñāpāramitā.

Why is this? Because this training in the perfection of wisdom is the most supreme, the greatest, the most excellent, and the most wondrous among all trainings; it is unsurpassed among the unsurpassed, peerless, and equal to the unequaled. It is able to benefit and bring peace and happiness to the entire world, acting as a protector for those who have no protector.
Those who train in this manner are approved by all Buddhas and praised by all Buddhas. Ānanda!

Having trained in this Dharma, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to press the earth with their toes and cause the trichiliocosm to tremble; even the lifting and lowering of their feet can all manifest various signs of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
Why is this? Because all Buddhas are fully endowed with immeasurable and innumerable supreme merits.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
Because all Buddhas have studied this Prajñāpāramitā, they have attained unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena of the past, future, and present. Therefore, Ānanda!

I declare that the training in the perfection of wisdom is the most supreme, the greatest, the most excellent, the most sublime, the unsurpassed among the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled.
Ānanda! You should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is immeasurable, inexhaustible, and without limit; if anyone wishes to measure the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are measuring empty space.

Why is this? Because space is immeasurable, the Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable; because space is inexhaustible, the Prajñāpāramitā is inexhaustible; because space is boundless, the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless.
Ānanda! I do not say that the prajñāpāramitā has any limit. Why is this?
"If names, phrases, and syllables are finite dharmas, and the Prajñāpāramitā is not names, phrases, or syllables, then it is indeed limitless.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason, Ānanda, does the Buddha say that the *prajñāpāramitā* is immeasurable? The Buddha said: "Ānanda!"

Because the perfection of wisdom is inexhaustible, it is immeasurable; because the perfection of wisdom is detached, it is immeasurable. Since it is inexhaustible and detached, phenomena cannot be apprehended; within that which cannot be apprehended, how could there be any measure?
Therefore, I say that the *prajñāpāramitā* is immeasurable. Ānanda!
All past Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas were born from this *prajñāpāramitā*; thus, this *prajñāpāramitā* is inexhaustible.
All future Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are born from the Prajñāpāramitā, and this Prajñāpāramitā is likewise inexhaustible.

All those Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas who currently reside and teach the Dharma in the infinite, asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions are born from this Prajñāpāramitā; and this Prajñāpāramitā is likewise inexhaustible.
Ānanda! I, too, am born from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and this perfection of wisdom is likewise inexhaustible.
For this reason, the perfection of wisdom has been inexhaustible, will be inexhaustible, and is now inexhaustible.
Why is this? Because if one can exhaust all of space, one can likewise exhaust the Prajñāpāramitā. Therefore, Ānanda!
"The Prajñāpāramitā is inexhaustible.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti had this thought:
"The meaning of what the Buddha has spoken is extremely profound; I shall question the Buddha regarding it."
Having formed this thought, he immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Is the Prajñāpāramitā inexhaustible?"
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is inexhaustible.”
"Why is this? Because all dharmas are unarisen; like space, they are inexhaustible.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are unarisen, how can the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) arise?
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! Because form is inexhaustible, the perfection of wisdom arises in this way; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inexhaustible, the perfection of wisdom arises in this way.”
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands in this way, then the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) arises in this manner.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should contemplate that because ignorance (avidyā) is inexhaustible, the perfection of wisdom arises in this manner.

Because in this way, form is inexhaustible, consciousness is inexhaustible, name-and-form is inexhaustible, the six sense bases are inexhaustible, contact is inexhaustible, feeling is inexhaustible, craving is inexhaustible, grasping is inexhaustible, becoming is inexhaustible, birth is inexhaustible, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair are inexhaustible, the *prajñāpāramitā* arises in this manner.

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all dependently originated phenomena through such inexhaustible dharmas, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); they do not abide in the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but will certainly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and dwell securely in omniscience (sarvajñatā).

When a bodhisattva sits at the site of enlightenment, they should contemplate dependently arisen phenomena in this manner. Having contemplated them thus, they do not fall into the two extremes, nor do they abide in a middle way; this is the unique quality of a bodhisattva. One who contemplates in this way attains the wisdom of all-knowledge.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, that bodhisattva mahāsattva would be unable to accomplish such skillful means, nor would they be able to know:
"How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom?"
