How is it that the inexhaustible dharma gives rise to the perfection of wisdom?
How is it that the inexhaustible dharma contemplates all conditioned origination? Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is non-retrogressive regarding unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they are able to accomplish such skillful means and are also able to understand that the practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is the practice of the perfection of wisdom; they give rise to the perfection of wisdom through such inexhaustible dharmas, and they contemplate all dependently originated phenomena through such inexhaustible dharmas.

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all things arising through conditions in this way, they do not perceive any dharma that does not arise from causes and conditions; nor do they perceive any dharma that is permanent, ultimate, or solid; nor do they perceive any dharma that has an agent or a recipient.

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they contemplate inexhaustible phenomena and give rise to the perfection of wisdom in accordance with reality.

When one contemplates all dependently arisen phenomena through such inexhaustible dharmas, one does not perceive form; one does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Furthermore, one does not perceive ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair.

One does not perceive this buddha-field, nor does one perceive that buddha-field; one does not perceive any dharma that constitutes this buddha-field, nor does one perceive any dharma that constitutes that buddha-field.
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, Māra’s mind becomes greatly terrified, filled with sorrow and distress.
Subhūti! It is just as if someone were to lose their parents and experience extreme grief, sorrow, and mental anguish; the suffering that arises in the mind of Māra is likewise.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
is it only a single Māra who experiences mental distress?"
"Are many evil Māras all thus afflicted with distress?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, all the evil Māras throughout the trichiliocosm will have their minds filled with sorrow and distress, each unable to remain settled in his seat."

Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this perfection of wisdom, they cannot be shaken by any in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and so forth—and no evil māras can find an opportunity to exploit them.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should practice this prajñāpāramitā.

Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice this Prajñāpāramitā, they are able to bring to perfection the pāramitā of generosity, the pāramitā of ethical discipline, the pāramitā of patience, the pāramitā of diligence, and the pāramitā of meditative concentration.
Having thus fulfilled all the pāramitās, one is then able to fulfill all wholesome dharmas and become endowed with all skillful means and the power of aspiration.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to encompass all skillful means, they should practice this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, they should contemplate inexhaustible phenomena and give rise to the perfection of wisdom in accordance with reality.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and contemplates in this manner, they should give rise to this thought:

"All those Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, who currently reside and teach the Dharma in the immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions, as well as the omniscience of all those Buddhas—all arise from this Prajñāpāramitā."
"Just as the Dharma attained by all Buddhas, I too shall fully attain it. Subhūti,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom gives rise to such a thought for even the duration of a finger-snap, they surpass the merit of other bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice giving for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
You should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already attained abiding in the stage of non-retrogression and is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas. Subhūti,
you should know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is able to give rise to such a mind for even the duration of a finger-snap is endowed with all such meritorious qualities.

Furthermore, if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva can give rise to such a mind for even a single day, or even beyond a single day, it should be known that this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas; wherever they are born, they will be born in Buddha-fields where they possess all merits and are praised by all Buddhas, extensively performing great benefit and happiness for sentient beings in all places.

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are able to give rise to such a mind and further contemplate the inexhaustible Dharma. One who gives rise to the perfection of wisdom in accordance with reality is, for example, like the Bodhisattva Gandhahastin, who practiced the perfection of wisdom and cultivated the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya; we bodhisattvas are likewise so.
Chapter Twenty-nine: Following Knowledge Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should follow and know the characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
It should be known that just as all phenomena are unimpeded, so too is the perfection of wisdom;
it should be known that just as all phenomena are non-conceptual, so too is the perfection of wisdom.
All phenomena are indestructible; one should know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise.
All phenomena are without the mark of agency; one should know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise.
All phenomena are without self and without representation, to be realized through wisdom; one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise.
All phenomena exist only as provisional names; one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise.
All phenomena are conceptualizations of language; since this very language is non-existent and unattainable, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise.
All dharmas are ineffable; one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise.
Form is immeasurable; one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are immeasurable; one should know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise so.
All phenomena are immeasurable; one should know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise so.
All phenomena are signless; one should know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise.
All phenomena are characterized by thorough penetration; one should know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise.
All phenomena are pure by nature; one should know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise.
All phenomena are quiescent; one should know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise.
All phenomena are without cessation and are identical to annihilation; one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also thus.
All phenomena attain *nirvāṇa* and are identical to *tathatā*; one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also thus.
All phenomena have neither coming nor going, neither arising nor that which arises; ultimately, arising cannot be apprehended. One should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise.
All dharmas have neither self-characteristic nor other-characteristic; one should know that the prajñāpāramitā is also thus.
All noble ones and sages are pure by nature; one should know that the prajñāpāramitā is also thus.
All phenomena relinquish all vows; one should know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise.
All phenomena have no direction and no location; one should know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise.
Why is this? Because form is without direction and without location, its intrinsic nature is pure; one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without direction and without location, their intrinsic nature is pure; one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise.
All phenomena have the nature of joy and bliss; one should know that the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is likewise.
All phenomena are neither defiled nor free from defilement; one should know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise.
All phenomena are neither craving nor free from craving; one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise.
Form is neither defilement nor free from defilement, being pure by its very nature; one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither objects nor free from objects; their intrinsic nature is pure. One should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also thus.
All phenomena are without attachment; one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also thus.
Bodhisattvas realize all phenomena through the Buddha’s wisdom; one should know that the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is likewise so.
All phenomena are empty, signless, and wishless; one should know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise so.
All dharmas are a great and excellent medicine, with a mind of loving-kindness as their foremost; one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise.
All dharmas abide in the practices of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise.
All phenomena abide in pure conduct, free from all faults; know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also like this.
The great ocean is boundless; know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also like this.
Just as Mount Sumeru is magnificent, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise.
Just as form is boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are boundless; one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also thus.
The radiance of the solar orb shines boundlessly; one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also thus.
All sounds are boundless; one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise.
The accumulation of all Buddha-dharmas is boundless; one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise.
Just as the merit and wisdom produced by the realm of all sentient beings are boundless, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise.
Just as the element of earth is boundless, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise.
The water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element are boundless; one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise.
Wholesome and unwholesome phenomena are boundless; one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise.
The treasury of all Buddha-dharmas is boundless; one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise.
All dharmas are boundless; one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise.
Emptiness is boundless; one should know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise.
The mind and mental factors are boundless; one should know that the perfection of wisdom is likewise.
The range of mental activity is boundless; one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise.
The accumulation of all dharmas is immeasurable; one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise.
All dharmas are immeasurable and unapprehendable through samādhi; one should know that the prajñāpāramitā is also thus.
Wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are immeasurable; one should know that the prajñāpāramitā is also thus.
All dharmas are like the lion’s roar; one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also thus.
All dharmas are indestructible; one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also thus.
Why is this? Form is like the great ocean; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like the great ocean.
Form is adorned like Mount Sumeru; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are adorned like Mount Sumeru.
Form is like the light of the solar disc, radiating boundlessly; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like the light of the solar disc, radiating boundlessly.
Form is like all sounds, which are boundless; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like all sounds, which are boundless.

The suchness of form is as boundless as the gathering of all Buddha-dharmas; the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is as boundless as the gathering of all Buddha-dharmas.
The suchness of form is as boundless as the realm of sentient beings; the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is as boundless as the realm of sentient beings.
Form is as boundless as the earth element; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are as boundless as the earth element.

Form is as boundless as the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are as boundless as the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
Form is characterized by being detached from accumulation; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are characterized by being detached from accumulation.
Form is characterized by being detached from conjunction; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are characterized by being detached from conjunction.
Form is as infinite as the samādhi of all dharmas; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are as infinite as the samādhi of all dharmas.

Form, the detachment from form, the intrinsic nature of form, and the suchness of form constitute the Buddha-dharma; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, the detachment from consciousness, the intrinsic nature of consciousness, and the suchness of consciousness constitute the Buddha-dharma.
The characteristic of form is boundless; the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are boundless.
The emptiness of form is boundless; the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is boundless.
Form is boundless within the mind and mental factors; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are boundless within the mind and mental factors.
Form is non-arising within the sphere of mental activity; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are non-arising within the sphere of mental activity.
Form cannot be apprehended within wholesome or unwholesome dharmas; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended within wholesome or unwholesome dharmas.
Form is like the lion’s roar; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like the lion’s roar.
Form is ultimately indestructible; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately indestructible.
By this principle, all phenomena are indestructible, and the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise so.

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus follow and know the prajñāpāramitā, they will have nothing to practice, nothing to do, and nothing to realize within that prajñāpāramitā; it is not something that can be reached through thought, observation, or deliberation.

He remains far removed from all mental engagements of flattery and deception; far removed from all mental engagements of indolence; far removed from all mental engagements of stinginess and envy; far removed from mental engagements of grasping at a self; far removed from mental engagements of self and other; far removed from notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, and so forth; far removed from worldly fame and gain; far removed from the factors such as the five hindrances; and even far removed from all improper mental engagements.

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they attain that which is difficult to attain among all dharmas; they are thus able to fulfill all merits, take birth in the buddha-fields, and achieve unsurpassed wisdom.

Chapter Thirty: Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva, Part One Furthermore, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who wish to seek the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) should practice the holy life and diligently seek the perfection of wisdom just as the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sadāprarudita did in the past within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ghoṣadatta-rāja.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what skillful means did the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita seek this Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"You should now know that when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita formerly sought the Prajñāpāramitā, he did not fear the length of time, did not dwell on worldly affairs, did not cherish his own body or life, and took no pleasure in worldly fame, profit, or offerings. He gave rise to no attachment toward any worldly things, but with single-minded intent sought the Prajñāpāramitā, contemplating skillful means within the forest."
At that time, a voice arose in the air, saying:
"Good son! You should travel eastward to seek this Prajñāpāramitā."

When you go there, let neither body nor mind give rise to weariness; do not think of sleep, do not think of food or drink, do not think of day or night, do not think of cold or heat, and do not think of any obstructive matters whatsoever.

Furthermore, do not attend to internal phenomena or external phenomena; do not attend to what is before you, nor to what is behind; do not attend to the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above, or below.
Moreover, while walking, you must not look to the left or right, but maintain single-minded mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
When contemplating in this way, one should not move within form; one should not move within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
If one moves within the five aggregates, one does not practice the Buddha-dharma; such is the practice of saṃsāra.
If one practices the conduct of birth and death, one is not practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, and one does not achieve the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Therefore, you should now abandon such signs and seek it with single-minded devotion.
"Subhūti! At that time, having heard this voice from the air, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita replied to the voice from the air, saying:
'I shall now act exactly as instructed.'"
"Why is this? Because I wish to act as a great light for all sentient beings and desire to gather all the Buddha-dharmas.
At that moment, a voice from the air again praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!

When you travel eastward in search of this *prajñāpāramitā*, you should have faith and understanding that all phenomena are empty, signless, and wishless. You should abandon all signs and remain far removed from the view of a self, the view of a person, and the view of a sentient being. You should distance yourself from evil associates and draw near to virtuous friends; as for those whom you draw near, you should honor, respect, and make offerings to them."
A spiritual friend is one who can explain for you that all phenomena are empty, signless, wishless, unarisen, unceasing, and without intrinsic nature.
If you give rise to such a mind of respect, reverence, and making offerings, you shall before long hear the Prajñāpāramitā.

Whether you hear it from within a scriptural volume or from a Dharma teacher, wherever you hear the Prajñāpāramitā, you should conceive of that person as the Great Teacher; you should honor, revere, serve, and make offerings to them. This is what it means to recognize kindness and repay one's debt of gratitude.
One should form this thought: "This is my true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).

Because I have heard this Prajñāpāramitā, I shall not regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi); I shall draw near to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; I shall not be separated from the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; I shall be born in Buddha-fields and not be born in fields where no Buddha resides; I shall remain far removed from all calamities and not be born in places of hardship."
"Good son! You should follow the Dharma Master for the sake of seeking such merit and benefit; you should not follow the Dharma Master for the sake of worldly wealth, profit, or reputation."
Furthermore, because of their mind that values the profound Dharma, they should honor, revere, serve, and make offerings to the Dharma-preacher, regarding them as the Great Teacher.

They should always remain aware of all demonic activities; for at times, due to certain conditions, an evil Māra may offer to the Dharma-preacher excellent and sublime objects of the five senses—forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and tangibles—as acts of worship.
That teacher of the Dharma, by means of skillful power, partakes in these five desires; at that time, you should not give rise to an impure mind to create an obstacle, but should instead think:

"Because I lack such skillful power, while this Dharma teacher—desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings and to cause them to plant roots of goodness—partakes in these five desires, there is not even the slightest dharma that can act as an obstacle for this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva."
“Good son! At that time, you should abide securely in the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
What is called the true reality of all phenomena?
It is said that all dharmas are neither defiled nor pure.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty; therein there is no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span. All dharmas are like dreams, like illusions, like shadows, and like echoes; such is called the true mark of all dharmas.
If you abide in this manner, you will before long hear the Prajñāpāramitā.
Son of good family!
Furthermore, you should recognize the works of Māra; for sometimes, due to the influence of Māra, the teacher of the Dharma may give rise to feelings of aversion toward the listener of the Dharma.

At that time, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, you should not give rise to even a momentary thought of opposition or obstruction; rather, you should increase your respect, affection, and reverence toward that Dharma teacher.
"You shall, before long, hear the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, having heard the voice in the sky providing this instruction, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita immediately proceeded eastward as directed to seek the Prajñāpāramitā.
Not long after traveling eastward, he had this thought:
"Why did I not ask the voice in the sky just now how far I must travel to the east, and to what place I shall arrive?"
"From whom shall I hear the Prajñāpāramitā?
Having had this thought, he became sorrowful and wept; remaining right there, he further reflected:

"I shall remain here for one day, two days, or even up to seven days, such that neither my body nor my mind feels weariness; I shall not think of sleep, nor of food and drink, nor of cold and heat, nor of day and night, but shall focus my single mind solely on the Prajñāpāramitā."

It is, for example, like a person who has an only son; their love and affection for him are so profound that when he suddenly passes away, at that moment the parents have no other thought but great anguish, sorrow, and weeping.
Subhūti! The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita was likewise; at that time, he had no other thoughts, but thought only: "When and in what place shall I hear the Prajñāpāramitā from whom?"

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma, Dharma-transmitting Master and Imperially Conferred Purple Robe, Subject Shi Hu, under Imperial Edict. Chapter Thirty, Part Two: Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva. At that time, the Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"When that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita was thus grieving and weeping, suddenly he saw the form of a Tathāgata standing before him, who spoke these words of praise:
'Excellent, excellent!'"

"Good son! When the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas were originally practicing the bodhisattva path, they sought the prajñāpāramitā just as you do now; their diligent seeking was exactly like yours, without any difference."

Therefore, you should further increase your diligence, courage, and steadfastness. From here, travel five hundred *yojanas* to the east; there is a great city named Saṃghagandha. Its sevenfold walls are twelve *yojanas* in length and breadth—vast, pure, exquisite, and magnificent. The population is dense, peaceful, secure, and prosperous. Five hundred streets connect everywhere; the bridges and fords are level and straight, beloved by all people. These sevenfold walls are adorned with the seven precious jewels. Upon each wall is a multi-storied pavilion made of Jāmbūnada gold, surrounded on all sides by rows of trees made of the seven jewels, and further encircled by seven layers of *tāla* trees.

Those rows of trees made of the seven treasures each bore various kinds of precious flowers and fruits; between every tree, various jewels were interspersed, and nets of precious gems reflected one another in intricate lattices, completely covering the city above. From these hung strings of precious bells, whose sound when stirred by the wind was most delightful, like the exquisite sounds produced by the five types of musical instruments—pure, subtle, harmonious, and elegant, bringing joy and satisfaction to all who heard them.

On all four sides of that city, flowing springs and bathing pools are perfectly pure and complete; within them are various boats adorned with the seven treasures, and the water in the pools is naturally temperate in both warmth and cold, as is pleasing to people.

Within these ponds are various colored flowers, namely the utpala, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka, as well as other diverse flowers of exquisite color and fragrance; indeed, all the wonderful flowers existing throughout the entire trichiliocosm are fully present there.

On its four sides, the city has five hundred gardens; within each garden are five hundred ponds, each one *krośa* in length and breadth, adorned with the seven precious jewels and most delightful to behold.

Within these various ponds there are also various wonderful flowers of exquisite color and fragrance, namely the utpala, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers. Each individual flower is as large as a chariot wheel; the blue ones emit a blue light, the yellow ones a yellow light, the red ones a red light, and the white ones a white light.
Within each pond, moreover, various exotic birds such as white cranes, ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks gather and sport upon them.

These gardens and bathing pools are where the people of the city roam and enjoy themselves at will, unencumbered by any attachments; this is solely due to what has been induced by the prior karma of sentient beings.

Because those sentient beings have practiced the perfection of wisdom throughout the long night and have attained pure faith and understanding in this profound dharma-gate, they have obtained such a most excellent karmic fruition.
"Good son! In that City of Fragrance there is a great high terrace, and upon it is the palace where the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmodgata resides."

The dimensions of that terrace were exactly one yojana in length and breadth; it was adorned with seven tiers of walls made of the seven precious substances, exceptionally magnificent and beautiful, surrounded on all sides by seven rows of trees, and further encircled by seven *tāla* trees.
Within that palace there were four great gardens: the first was named Constant Joy, the second Sorrowless, the third Delightful, and the fourth Adorned with Flowers.

Within each garden there are eight great ponds: the first is named Bhadra, the second Bhadrottama, the third Nandana, the fourth Nandottama, the fifth Sukha, the sixth Suxhottama, the seventh Niścaya, and the eighth Avaḥa.

The four sides of each of those ponds are adorned with the four precious substances: gold to the east, silver to the south, lapis lazuli to the west, and crystal to the north; their bottoms are made of rose quartz, covered with golden sand.
Beside each pond there are eight stairways adorned with the seven precious gems; these are formed into tiers of various jewels, and between the tiers stand rows of *jambu-river gold* plantain trees.

Within those various ponds there are also various flowers of exquisite colors and fragrances, namely the *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses; furthermore, various exotic birds such as white cranes, ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks gather and sport upon them.

On each side of those individual ponds, there are trees of exquisite fragrant flowers; their scent is like that of sandalwood, and they are endowed with perfect color and flavor. When the wind blows, their blossoms fall into the waters of the ponds.

The palaces, gardens, groves, ponds, and pools were thus magnificently adorned. Within those palaces resided the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, together with a retinue of sixty-eight thousand court ladies; they enjoyed themselves amidst such gardens, groves, ponds, and pools, delighting in the pleasures of the five senses and sporting with sovereign ease.
All the people within the City of Universal Fragrance, whether men or women, likewise enter the gardens such as Ever-Joyful and the ponds such as Worthy to sport and enjoy themselves.
After that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata had finished his recreation, he taught the Prajñāpāramitā three times each day within his own palace.
Furthermore, all the people within the city of Saṃghāṭa gathered in a great assembly place inside the city and prepared a great Dharma throne for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
The four legs of that throne were made of four precious substances— gold, silver, vaidūrya, and crystal— and it was further adorned with various...

It was adorned with various pearls and necklaces as its embellishments; the seat stood half a krośa in height, upon which were spread carpets and *kauśika* cloths, further decorated with exquisite fine cotton fabrics of various kinds.
Around the perimeter of the seat, flowers of five colors were scattered, and various wonderful incenses were burned, making it exceptionally beautiful and sublime.
Pure and lovely— the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata sat upon his Dharma-throne,
surrounded by a respectful assembly of the fourfold community of gods and humans gathered in one place. Out of reverence for the Dharma,
each person burned incense and scattered flowers as an offering to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
At that time, the Bodhisattva extensively proclaimed the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of all the devas and the fourfold assembly of humans.

Having taught it according to their capacities, among them were those who upheld it, those who recited it, those who contemplated it, those who transcribed it, those who practiced according to the teaching, and those who became non-retrogressive from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"Good son! Within that assembly where the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmodgata teaches the Dharma, there are such merits and benefits as these. Therefore, you should now travel eastward to where the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmodgata resides; from him you shall hear the Prajñāpāramitā, and that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva will be able to instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden you with this Dharma."
Go east now, disregarding day and night; with courageous diligence and single-minded effort, you shall before long certainly hear the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita felt joy, gladness, and exultation in his heart.

It was as if a person were struck by an arrow and suffered intense pain; at that moment, the person would have no other thought but to wonder when he might obtain a great, excellent medicine to receive healing and be delivered from such suffering and distress.

Subhūti! The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita was likewise thus, without any other thought, thinking only: "When shall I be able to behold, pay homage to, and draw near to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata?"
Having heard the Prajñāpāramitā from him,
he then focused his mind one-pointedly on that place, clearly contemplating the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata and reflecting upon the Prajñāpāramitā.

When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita engaged in such reflection, he gave rise to the perception of non-reliance toward all phenomena and attained immeasurable and innumerable gateways to samādhi, namely:
the samādhi of contemplating the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; the samādhi of the non-apprehension of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
the samādhi of the arising of wisdom regarding the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; and the samādhi that destroys the ignorance regarding all phenomena.
The *samādhi* of the indestructible vision of all phenomena, the *samādhi* of producing light for all phenomena,
the *samādhi* of being free from the darkness of delusion regarding all phenomena, the *samādhi* that shatters ignorance concerning all phenomena,
the *samādhi* of being free from obscurity regarding all phenomena, and the *samādhi* of the non-apprehensibility of the characteristics of all phenomena.
The *mudrā* samādhi, the *scattered-flower* (*puṣpavikīrṇa*) samādhi, the *all-phenomena-lack-of-self-characteristic* (*sarvadharmanairātmyalakṣaṇa*) samādhi,
the *devoid-of-illusion* (*nirmāṇavigata*) samādhi, the *arising-like-a-mirror-image* (*pratibimbodaya*) samādhi,
the *language-of-all-sentient-beings* (*sarvasattvabhāṣā*) samādhi, the *dust-free* (*viraja*) samādhi, and the *joy-of-all-sentient-beings* (*sarvasattvapramoda*) samādhi.
The samādhi of skillful speech that accords with all sentient beings; the samādhi of the arising of various languages, scripts, and phrases;
the samādhi of fearlessness; the samādhi of intrinsic nature; the samādhi of attaining liberation through the removal of hindrances;
the samādhi of non-defilement; and the samādhi adorned with names, phrases, and syllables.
The *mudrā*, the *samādhi* of impartially contemplating all phenomena, the *samādhi* of all phenomena being free from the marks of objective spheres,
the *samādhi* of the unimpeded limit of all phenomena, the *samādhi* like space, the *samādhi* of the diamond analogy,
the *samādhi* of the King of Pure Marks, and the *samādhi* of being without defeat.
The Samādhi of Attaining Victory, the Samādhi of Non-retrogressive Contemplation, the Samādhi of Certainty in the Dharma-realm,
the Samādhi of Quiescence in the Dharma-realm, the Samādhi of Peaceful Security, the Samādhi of the Lion’s Roar,
the Samādhi of Surpassing All Sentient Beings, the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement, and the Samādhi of Purity.
The samādhi of [the Lotus], the Lotus-Adornment Samādhi, the Severing of Craving Samādhi, the Samādhi Following All that is Firm,
the Supreme Samādhi of All Dharmas, the Samādhi of Attaining the Powers and Fearlessnesses of Supernormal Knowledge,
the Samādhi of Penetrating All Dharmas, and the Destruction of All Dharmas.
The Seal Samādhi; the Samādhi of Seeing All Dharmas as Undifferentiated; the Samādhi of Being Free from All Views;
the Samādhi of the Great Dharma Radiance; the Samādhi of All Dharmas Being Free from Characteristics;
the Samādhi of Liberation from All Attachments; the Samādhi of All Dharmas Being Without Sloth; the Profound...
The Samādhi of the Radiance of Profound Dharma, the Samādhi of Equal Height, the Samādhi of the Inalienable,
the Samādhi of Shattering the Realm of Māra, the Samādhi of Supreme Excellence in the Three Realms,
the Samādhi of the Gateway of Radiance, and the Samādhi of Beholding All Tathāgatas.

“Subhūti! That Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita entered such gateways of samādhi as these. Within those samādhis, he beheld the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds throughout the ten directions, each of whom was teaching the Prajñāpāramitā to various Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.”
All these Tathāgatas comforted and praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita,
saying: "Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!"
"You are able to diligently seek the Prajñāpāramitā.
When we formerly practiced the bodhisattva path and sought the Prajñāpāramitā, it was no different from what you have now attained—these various samādhis and so forth."
Now that you have attained these various samādhis, you are able to penetrate the Prajñāpāramitā and skillfully abide in the dharma of non-retrogression.
Having attained these various samādhis, we immediately realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Within these samādhis, we observed that their intrinsic nature is such that no dharma can be perceived.
Having emerged from all these samādhis, one gives rise to the perception of non-abiding regarding all phenomena.
Son of good family!
This non-abiding dharma is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Within this dharma of non-abiding, we have attained golden bodies with various radiances; we are fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor characteristics; we have attained the inconceivable, unsurpassed wisdom and insight of a Buddha, accomplished all the merits and virtues of the Buddha-dharmas, and reached the other shore of all dharmas.
Good son! Even the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, cannot measure, praise, or describe the limits of such merits; how much less so can the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?

Therefore, you should now apply yourself even more to this Dharma with reverence, respect, affection, and delight, seeking it with diligent effort; for by virtue of this principle, Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi will not be difficult to attain.
Furthermore, son of good family!
You should now cultivate extreme reverence, respect, and affection for spiritual friends. Why is this?
"A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is protected and assisted by spiritual friends will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita addressed the Tathāgatas, saying:
"Who shall be my true spiritual friend?"
"I pray that all Tathāgatas will instruct and guide me.
At that moment, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, said to him:
"O son of good family!

You should know that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata is your spiritual friend; for throughout successive lifetimes, that Bodhisattva has constantly instructed and transformed you, enabling you to master the skillful means of the Prajñāpāramitā, to study all Buddha-dharmas, and to bring you to the fulfillment of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"You should recognize his profound kindness and keep in mind the need to repay it. Good son!

If you, as a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, wish to repay the kindness of the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, even if for one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, or even a hundred thousand kalpas you were to honor him by carrying him upon your head and shoulders, and were to provide him with all manner of articles of pleasure—including every superior and exquisite form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch within the trichiliocosm—you would still not have repaid even a small fraction of his kindness."
Why is this? It is because of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata that you have been enabled to enter the various gates of samādhi and to master the skillful means of the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Therefore, you should know that their kindness is profound and heavy.
When the Tathāgata had spoken these words, he suddenly vanished.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita emerged from his samādhi; no longer seeing those Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, he was overcome with grief and distress, and remained there weeping.
He then had this thought:
"From where did the Tathāgata come just now?
Where has he gone?"

He has preached the Dharma for me; that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata is truly rare. That Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already attained dhāraṇīs and the five supernormal powers, and has already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past; he is my true and virtuous spiritual friend.

Throughout successive lifetimes, they have constantly taught and benefited me; therefore, I should now increase my reverence, respect, affection, and joy toward them, and thus go to visit, pay homage to, attend upon, and make offerings to them in order to hear and receive the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, when asked where the Tathāgata had come from and where he was going, I thought to myself:

"I am currently so impoverished that I possess nothing at all. I cannot provide gold, silver, precious gems, clothing, bedding, banners, pennants, jeweled canopies, incense, flowers, lamps, or ointments; indeed, I cannot even afford a single flower. With what, then, shall I make this offering?"
"If I were to go empty-handed, my mind would not be at ease.
Thus he grieved and contemplated, devising a plan.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita had formed this thought, he did not immediately proceed eastward; instead, he entered another city along the way and stayed quietly within it, reflecting:

"I wish to travel eastward for the sake of seeking the Dharma; to make offerings to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmodgata will be of great benefit. I should now sell my own body, and with whatever price is obtained, purchase incense and flowers to take there myself and offer them to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmodgata."

Why is this? Since time immemorial, for the sake of desire as a causal condition, I have undergone bodies of birth and death within saṃsāra, passing through immeasurable suffering and transmigrating through the various realms of existence; though I have destroyed my body, it has never brought any benefit, nor have I ever sacrificed my own life for the sake of this pure Dharma. Therefore, I now have no sense of stinginess in seeking the Dharma.
Having reflected thus, he immediately went to a crowded public place within the city and proclaimed:
"I am now selling my body. Who will buy me?"
"Who will buy me?
At that time, when the various Māras learned of this matter, they immediately thought to themselves:

"Now the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, out of his love for the Dharma, has sold his own body, wishing to purchase incense and flowers to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata in order to seek the Prajñāpāramitā."

For what reason are all bodhisattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom able to accomplish unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, remaining as immovable as the great ocean, such that we, the māras, are unable to destroy or disturb them?
"Because of those causes and conditions, my domain is empty; therefore, I should now employ skillful means to destroy his resolve for the Way.

At that time, after the evil Māra had thought thus, as the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita was uttering these words, he immediately used his demonic power to conceal all the people within the city, ensuring that none of them heard the sound of the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita’s proclamation.
“At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita made this proclamation three times, yet no one would buy him.
The Bodhisattva then felt sorrow and distress in his heart, weeping as he said: ‘Alas, alas! How bitter!’”
"I have sold my own body to make an offering to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, yet now there is no buyer; therefore, I know that my body is deeply tainted by sin.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having learned of this matter, thought to himself:
"I should go to where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita is and test whether his mind is firm and his deep resolve for the Dharma is such that he can truly renounce a body like this."

After Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had formed this thought, he immediately transformed his body into that of a brahmin, approached and stood before the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, and asked him:
"For what reason are you now so sorrowful, weeping, and afflicted with distress?"
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva said, "I now wish to sell this body, yet there is no one to buy it; for this reason, I remain here weeping.
The brāhmaṇa said:
"What do you intend to do with the body you are selling?
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva replied,

"Out of my love for the Dharma, I am now selling my own body to purchase incense and flowers, desiring to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata in order to seek the Prajñāpāramitā."
"However, because my merit is meager, this body of mine cannot be sold.
Then, the brahmin said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, "I do not require a person for any labor;
rather, I am about to perform a great sacrifice and need human heart, human blood, and human marrow. Could you possibly give these to me now?"
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita leapt for joy and thought to himself:
"At this moment, I have attained the most supreme benefit; I shall certainly hear the Prajñāpāramitā and fulfill my aspiration."
"If this brahmin is willing to take my heart, blood, and marrow, I should joyfully grant each one to him.
Having formed this thought, he immediately said to the brahmin:
"Whatever you require, O worthy one, I shall offer it to you."
The brahmin asked, "What is the price you desire for it?
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva replied:
"Whatever you require, I shall immediately grant it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita took up a sharp blade and pierced his right arm to draw blood; he then intended to break the bone of his right thigh to extract the marrow.

At that time, there was the daughter of a householder on a high tower who saw from afar the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita first piercing his own arm to draw blood and then intending to break his bone to extract the marrow. She immediately thought to herself:
"For what reason does this son of good family thus inflict such suffering upon his body?"
"I ought to go there and inquire as to the reason.
Having formed this thought, the merchant's daughter immediately descended from the high tower to where the Bodhisattva was and addressed him with these words: "Noble son!..."
"For what reason do you inflict such suffering upon yourself?
What do you intend to do with this blood and marrow?
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva replied:
“O virtuous woman!

You should know that I am currently destitute and possess no wealth or treasures. I shall sell my blood and marrow to this brahmin; with the price obtained, I shall purchase incense and flowers to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.”
The daughter of the elder said,
"What kind of merit and benefit will there be from your making offerings of incense and flowers to that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva?
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva replied:
"O virtuous daughter of good family, you should know that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata was able to explain for my sake the Prajñāpāramitā and the gates of skillful means."

Having studied those dharmas, one is able to serve as a refuge for sentient beings; that is, one can achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, attain a golden body endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics, possess constant light and immeasurable radiance, and be equipped with great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity; the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and so forth—all inconceivable, immeasurable, and innumerable Buddha-qualities—can all be brought to full perfection, as well as all the unsurpassed treasures of the Dharma, which are then distributed and bestowed upon all sentient beings.
Therefore, desiring now to accomplish such merit as this, I shall go to make offerings to that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā and the gates of skillful means.
At that time, the daughter of the elder addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, saying: "Noble son!
What you have said is truly most rare!"

If a person, for the sake of seeking such a Dharma as this, should exhaust their life and bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in making offerings, this is what ought to be done; their merit will not be in vain, but will bring great benefit.

"Good son! My house possesses various kinds of precious jewels, such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber, and crystal, as well as clothing, bedding, banners, pennants, precious canopies, incense, flowers, lamps, and ointments. Whatever you require, I shall give it all to you; you should take these to offer to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, and do not sell yourself again to undergo such bitter suffering."

I now also wish to go with you to the place where the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmodgata resides, in order to behold and pay homage to him, to attend upon him, to rejoice in his merit, to make offerings, and to plant various roots of goodness.
When the daughter of the elder had finished speaking these words, she stood to one side.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, concealed his form as a brahmin and restored his original appearance; standing before the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, he spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent!
"Noble son! You are able to maintain a firm and profound resolve, delighting in the Dharma and seeking it with courageous diligence. Noble son!"

When the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past were practicing the bodhisattva path, their seeking of the Prajñāpāramitā was exactly like yours now, without any difference. You shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and fulfill all the dharmas of a Buddha’s merits.
"Good son! I truly do not require human hearts, blood, or marrow; I have come merely to test you.
Whatever it is that you now require, I shall grant it to you."
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva said:
"Lord of Devas!
Can you grant me *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"Good son! This is the realm of all Buddhas; it is not my realm."
"What the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, can accomplish, I cannot accomplish.
Whatever else you require, I shall offer it all to you.
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva said:

"I now have no further wish. By the power of your truthful words, O Lord Śakra, and by the power of my own vows and my own truthful words, as well as through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, the World-Honored One—if it is known by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas that I am truly non-retrogressive in my resolve for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, may this body of mine be restored to its former state."
At that time, as soon as the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita had spoken these words, his body was restored in an instant, such that not even a trace of a scar remained.
At that time, having seen these signs, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, marveled at this rarity and vanished from sight.
Then, the daughter of the elder addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, saying:
"O son of good family!
"You should now go together with me to my home, inform my parents, and request what is needed to bring back as offerings for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita said to the daughter of the elder:
"Excellent! Let us go together; now is precisely the right time."
"Then that daughter of the elder went with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita to her father’s house.
Having arrived at the house, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita stood by the side of the gate, while the daughter of the elder entered the house and said to her parents:
'Father and Mother!'"

"In my home, I possess gold, silver, precious gems, and various other things; I pray that you will grant me a small portion of these, as well as permission for five hundred maidservants whom I provide for to follow me. I shall go together with a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Sadāprarudita to make offerings to a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Dharmodgata."

Moreover, that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata is able to expound the profound Dharma for us; having heard that Dharma, we shall immediately be able to accomplish all the merits, benefits, and virtues of the Buddha-dharmas. Therefore, Father and Mother, we pray that you grant us your permission.
At that time, her parents said to the girl:
"Regarding the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita whom you have mentioned, where is he now? The girl replied:
"He is now outside the gate.

Parents, you should know that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva possesses a profound resolve, delights in the Dharma, and is courageous and firm. Desiring to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and to extensively deliver all sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death, he has gone to offer worship to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata. In order to seek the *prajñāpāramitā*, he has sold his own body and is crying out at a loud voice within this city:
'Who will buy me?'"
Thus he cried out three times, but there was no one to buy it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita remained there weeping in sorrow and distress.

At that moment, from atop a high tower, I saw a brahmin approach the Bodhisattva; after they had conversed with one another, the Bodhisattva immediately took a sharp knife in his hand and pierced his right arm, drawing blood, and further intended to cut his right thigh, break the bone, and extract the marrow.
At that time, having seen this matter, I immediately thought to myself:
"Why is this good man thus inflicting such suffering upon his own body?"
"I should go there and inquire about the reason for this.
Having thought thus, I went immediately. I asked him:
"For what reason do you undergo such torment?
For what purpose do you wish to take this blood and marrow?
He replied to me, saying:

"I wish to purchase various incenses and flowers to go and make offerings to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata; however, because I am poor and lack wealth and treasures, I have shed my own blood and marrow to sell them to this brahmin. With the price obtained, I shall purchase incense and flowers to offer to the Bodhisattva."
"Father and Mother!
Having heard what he said, I deeply praised it and further asked him:
'If you now make such offerings to that Bodhisattva, what kind of merit and benefit will there be?'"
He replied to me, saying:
"Because of making offerings to that bodhisattva, one may hear from him the Prajñāpāramitā and the gates of skillful means (upāyamukha).
Having studied these dharmas, one is then able to accomplish the inconceivable, immeasurable, and innumerable qualities of a Buddha."
Having heard these words, my heart was filled with joy, and I said to him:
"Noble son! To practice such difficult austerities for the sake of seeking the Dharma is truly rare and marvelous!"

"You need not now afflict your body with such suffering. My home possesses gold, silver, precious jewels, and all manner of things; I shall give you whatever you desire. Furthermore, I also wish to go together with you to the place where the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmodgata dwells, so that we may behold and pay homage to him, attend upon him, and joyfully make offerings."
I spoke again, saying:

"For now, let us go together with you to my father’s house; having informed my parents, we shall request wealth and treasures to take with you both to offer as an act of worship to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata."
He replied: "Excellent! You may go."
"Now is precisely the right time.
Parents! For this reason, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita has come here together with me.

Therefore, if my parents wish to enable me to accomplish all supreme dharmas of merit, please grant me permission for the various kinds of wealth, treasures, female attendants, and so forth that I desire; do not create further obstacles.
At that time, the parents said to their daughter:
"The young man of whom you speak is truly most rare!

For the sake of seeking the Dharma, he practices what is difficult to practice, desiring to accomplish the inconceivable qualities of a Buddha’s merit and wishing to bring great benefit to all sentient beings."
This causal condition is the most supreme undertaking in all the worlds.

Now, listen as we grant you leave to go; whatever you desire, you may do as you please. We, too, wish to go to where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata resides, in order to behold him, pay our respects, attend upon him, and joyfully make offerings to him.
At that time, for the sake of making offerings to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, the daughter of the elder said to her parents:
"I also do not dare to obstruct another's merit; if you, my parents, wish to go, you may do as you please."

At that time, the daughter of the elder immediately prepared five hundred chariots, adorned them with various jewels, and had five hundred handmaidens each adorn their bodies. Each maiden mounted one chariot, and all the gold, silver, precious gems, clothing, bedding, banners, pennants, jeweled canopies, incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, and various other items were loaded onto a single chariot.
At that time, the daughter of the elder rode in a single carriage together with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita; her parents and kinsmen also rode in precious carriages.
Thus adorned and surrounded by a retinue, she departed from her residence and traveled eastward to the place where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata was staying.

Having traveled in this manner for five hundred yojanas, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita and the daughter of the elder saw from afar a city. That city had sevenfold walls and was surrounded on all sides by rows of trees made of the seven precious substances. It was twelve yojanas in length and breadth, vast and pure, with five hundred streets and lanes connected everywhere. Its bridges and ferries were level, upright, secure, and prosperous; it was teeming with people and exceedingly delightful.

In a crowded area within that city, there was a great Dharma throne, lofty, vast, and exquisitely beautiful, adorned with various jewels. From afar, they saw the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata seated upon the throne, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of gods, humans, and the fourfold assembly, who paid him respectful homage as they listened to his preaching of the Dharma.

Having seen this, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita felt a sense of jubilation and leaped for joy with great delight, like a bhikṣu who has attained the bliss of the third dhyāna. With single-minded concentration, respect, and reverence, he spoke to the merchant’s daughter, saying:
"This city is named Gandhavatī, and that bodhisattva is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata."
"At this time, we ought not to proceed before him by carriage.
Having spoken these words, they each descended from their carriages and proceeded forward on foot with joy, solemnity, and reverence.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma (Shi Hu), Court Profferer of the Great State, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Dharma-Transmitting Master, and Purple-Robed Subject, by Imperial Decree. Chapter Thirty: Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva, Part Three. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, accompanied by the merchant’s daughter, her handmaidens, parents, and kinsmen, surrounded by a retinue and carrying various precious jewels and offerings, entered the City of Universal Fragrance. With single-minded longing and yearning, he desired to see the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita and his companions had entered the city, they approached the place where the Bodhisattva was staying, not far from there. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita saw Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with hundreds of thousands of myriads of devaputras, scattering celestial māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, and various other exquisite celestial blossoms, as well as celestial gold and silver flowers, into the air; they also scattered powdered sandalwood and performed extensive, subtle celestial music, such that the scattered flowers remained suspended in mid-air.
Having seen this, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita immediately asked Śakra, Lord of the Devas:

"Kauśika! For what reason do you, together with countless hundreds of thousands of devaputras in the midst of space, scatter various celestial flowers and powdered sandalwood incense, and extensively perform celestial music?"
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "Good son, do you not know?
There is a dharma named Mahāprajñāpāramitā; it is the mother of all Buddhas and also the mother of all Bodhisattvas.
Those who study this dharma are able to accomplish all-knowledge and fulfill all the dharmas of a Buddha’s merits.
"You should now know this!

At the place where the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmodgata expounds the Dharma, there is a separate seven-jeweled terrace, lofty, vast, exquisite, and adorned with various ornaments. A net of genuine jewels is interlaced and draped over it. Within that terrace is a bed made of the seven treasures, and upon that bed is placed a casket of the seven treasures. Inside the casket, the true Dharma of this Mahāprajñāpāramitā is inscribed upon golden plates. It is surrounded on all sides by various precious gems. At the four corners of the terrace, four silver incense burners are placed, burning black aloeswood incense as an offering to the true Dharma of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā."
"For this reason, we gods have scattered flowers from the midst of the sky as an offering.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "Kauśika!..."

As you have said, this True Dharma of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā—the mother of all Buddhas and the mother of Bodhisattvas—is subtle, profound, supreme, and most rare; can you, by means of skillful expedients, demonstrate it to me?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:

“Good son! That sublime Dharma of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā is within a casket of the seven precious jewels; it has been sealed with the seals of the seven precious jewels by that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmodgata. I have no means by which I could show it to you.”

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, together with the merchant’s daughter and the others, proceeded further until they arrived at the place where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata was.

Thereupon, they divided the gold, silver, rare treasures, clothing, bedding, banners, pennants, precious canopies, incense, flowers, lamps, and ointments they possessed into two portions. First, they took one portion and together made offerings to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā; next, they took the other portion and likewise together made offerings to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
Having made this offering, he further scattered various exquisite flowers of wonderful colors and fragrances toward the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.

By the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, the flowers thus scattered remained suspended in the air above the Bodhisattva, transforming into various wonderful pavilions of precious gems. Within these pavilions, there naturally appeared necklaces of pearls, interspersed and hanging down in profusion.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita and the merchant’s daughter, having seen these signs, both thought to themselves:
'Excellent! These signs are truly rare.'"

If even the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Dharmodgata, while currently dwelling on the bodhisattva stages, possesses such supernatural powers and majestic virtue, how much more so after he has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; his various merits will be beyond all measure and calculation.

At that time, having formed this thought, the daughter of the elder increased her reverence, respect, and affection for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata; likewise, the five hundred female attendants also each increased their reverence, respect, and affection.
At that time, the daughter of the elder and her five hundred female attendants all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and they all spoke these words:
"By the causal conditions of these roots of goodness, may we attain Buddhahood in a future age."

When he was a bodhisattva, he likewise cherished and revered the *prajñāpāramitā* no differently than the bodhisattva mahāsattva Dharmodgata; he extensively proclaimed the *prajñāpāramitā* for others and accomplished the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, all exactly as the bodhisattva mahāsattva Dharmodgata does today, without any difference.
Having spoken these words, the daughter of the elder and her five hundred female attendants immediately prostrated themselves, placing their heads at the feet of the Bodhisattva.
Having paid homage, they joined their palms and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita had completed the aforementioned acts of worship, he immediately prostrated with his head at the feet of the Bodhisattva.
Having paid homage, he circumambulated him, offering various praises, and stood with palms joined, gazing up at him with joy.
He addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, saying: "O Great Being!
You should know that I have come here because of wholesome causes and conditions."
"Originally, for the sake of seeking the Prajñāpāramitā, I was contemplating skillful means within a secluded forest when a voice in the sky addressed me, saying:
'You should travel eastward to seek the Prajñāpāramitā.'"
Following the instructions as given, I immediately traveled toward the east. Not long after traveling eastward, I again thought to myself:
"Why did I not previously ask that voice in the sky how far I should travel to the east?"
"In what direction and from whom did you hear the Prajñāpāramitā?
At that time, I was filled with grief and wept; I remained in that very place for seven days and nights.
At that time, while I was grieving and weeping, I suddenly saw the form of a Tathāgata standing before me and speaking these words:
"O son of good family!
From here, traveling east for five hundred yojanas, there is a city named Saugandhikā. There dwells a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Dharmodgata.
You should go there, and you will be able to hear the Prajñāpāramitā.
Having heard these words, my heart was filled with great joy; I immediately focused my mind one-pointedly upon that Great Being right there, contemplating the Prajñāpāramitā.

At that time, dwelling in the perception of non-reliance upon all phenomena, I immediately entered immeasurable and innumerable gateways of samādhi. Within those samādhis, I beheld the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds in the ten directions, each expounding the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
All these Tathāgatas praised me, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!"
"Because of your pursuit of the causes and conditions of the *prajñāpāramitā*, you shall gain entry into the various gates of *samādhi*.
Then, after all the Tathāgatas had thus provided me with instruction, benefit, and joy through various means, and had comforted me, they suddenly vanished from sight.
At that time, having emerged from samādhi, I could no longer see the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
My heart was filled with anguish, and I thought to myself:
"From where did those Tathāgatas just now come?"
"Where has he gone? I further reflected:

"That Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata has deeply planted roots of goodness under previous Buddhas; he has mastered the Prajñāpāramitā and possesses all skillful means. I shall go to him to hear and receive the Prajñāpāramitā and to inquire about this meaning."
"For this reason, I have now come here to behold and pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
My heart is filled with joy and I am deeply gratified, just as a bhikṣu experiences the bliss of the third dhyāna."
"O Mahāsattva!
Just as I saw the Tathāgata within my samādhi, I did not know from where he came,
nor to where he went."
“I only pray that the Great Being will instruct me, so that I may always behold the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Chapter 31: The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: “Good son!
The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
Why is this? True Suchness is immovable, and True Suchness is the Tathāgata.
The unarisen dharma has neither coming nor going; the unarisen dharma is itself the Tathāgata.
The limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) has neither coming nor going; the limit of reality is itself the Tathāgata.
Emptiness neither comes nor goes; emptiness is itself the Tathāgata.
The undefiled dharma neither comes nor goes; the undefiled dharma is itself the Tathāgata.
Quiescent extinction has neither coming nor going; quiescent extinction is itself the Tathāgata.
Space has neither coming nor going; space is itself the Tathāgata.
O son of good family!
Apart from such dharmas as these, there is no separate dharma that can be called the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, what is meant by the "Tathatā (Suchness) of the Tathāgata"?
It is the Tathatā of all dharmas; they are all one and the same Tathatā. This Suchness is without discrimination, without duality, and without even threefold distinction.

"Good son! It is like the end of spring and the beginning of summer, when at midday a shimmering mirage arises. If at that time someone were to seek water therein, what do you think: from where would that water come?"
Did it come from the eastern ocean?
Or did it come from the southern, western, or northern oceans?
Its departure was likewise.
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva said:
"In that mirage, not even water can be found; how much less could there be any coming or going?
It is merely what is falsely perceived by the ignorant and the witless."
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata said: "Good son,
all Tathāgatas are likewise thus."

If a person is attached to forms and sounds, and gives rise to discrimination regarding the Tathāgatas as coming or going, one should know that such a person is foolish, lacking wisdom, and perceives what is illusory.
Why is this? The Tathāgata is the Dharma-body; he is not a physical body that can be seen. Good son!
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) neither comes nor goes; all Tathāgatas are likewise without coming or going.

Furthermore, it is like the elephant corps, cavalry, chariot corps, and infantry created by a magician through illusion; because these four types of troops are produced by illusion, they neither come nor go.
All Tathāgatas are likewise thus: they neither come nor go.
Furthermore, it is as if someone, within a dream, might see one Buddha, two Buddhas, three, four, five, or even hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.
"Good son! From where do those Buddhas come?
To where do they go?"
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva said: "O Mahāsattva!
That which is seen in a dream is unreal and lacks any determinate nature; within such phenomena, how could there be any coming or going?"
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata said:
"All Tathāgatas are likewise so.
As the Buddha has taught, all phenomena are like dreams."

Because some people cannot understand all phenomena as they truly are—like dreams—they instead cling to and discriminate among the Buddhas and Tathāgatas in terms of physical forms, sounds, speech, and names, conceptualizing them as either coming or going.

"Good son! If, within these dharmas, one does not know false conceptualization as it truly is, you should know that such persons are called foolish ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*). They receive bodies of birth and death and transmigrate through the various realms of existence; they remain far removed from the *prajñāpāramitā* and far removed from all Buddha-dharmas."

Good son! If a person understands in accordance with reality that all phenomena are like dreams, as the Buddha has taught, then within these phenomena there is no phenomenon whatsoever that comes or goes; therefore, there is nothing to differentiate.

To understand, as it truly is, that all Tathāgatas neither come nor go, and are neither born nor extinguished—to know thus is to see the Dharma, and is to know the Dharma. Such a person is close to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, does not receive in vain the faithful offerings of the land, and is able to serve as a great field of merit for the world.

Good son! Furthermore, it is like the great ocean that produces various kinds of jewels; these jewels do not come from the east, nor do they come from the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or from above or below. Rather, they are the collective retribution brought about by the meritorious deeds performed by all sentient beings.
Therefore, the great ocean produces all manner of rare treasures; each of these treasures arises from causes and conditions, nor does it arise without causes and conditions.
When causes and conditions harmonize, they exist; when causes and conditions disperse and cease, they no longer exist.
Existence does not come from the ten directions, nor does non-existence go to the ten directions.

The bodies of all Tathāgatas are likewise: they do not come from the ten directions, nor do they go to the ten directions; they are produced solely through the conjunction of causes and conditions, yet they do not abide within the phenomena of causes and conditions, nor are they produced without causes and conditions.
When causes and conditions harmonize and combine, there is arising; when causes and conditions disperse, there is cessation.
Arising does not come from the ten directions, and cessation does not go to the ten directions.

Good son! It is also like a *vīṇā* lute which has strings, a sounding board, and a bridge. If a person strikes it with their hand and produces sound, that sound comes from nowhere: it does not come from the strings, nor from the sounding board, nor from the bridge, nor from the hand. It exists only through the conjunction of causes and conditions; when these causes and conditions disperse and cease, there is no sound. Once the sound has ceased, it likewise goes nowhere.
Good son! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are also like this.

They arise in accordance with reality from all corresponding roots of goodness and various causes and conditions; they are not born from a single cause, a single condition, or a single root of goodness, nor are they born without causes and conditions.
Through the convergence of conditions they arise, yet in arising there is no coming; through the dispersal of conditions they cease, yet in ceasing there is no going.
Son of good family!

You should thus understand, in accordance with reality, that all Buddhas and Tathāgatas neither come nor go. If you know that the Buddhas neither come nor go, you will abide in the non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena.

One who knows thus possesses the skillful means of practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and shall certainly attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

“At that time, when the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmodgata was thus teaching the Dharma of the coming and going of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways, manifesting eighteen signs: namely, it quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked equally everywhere; it roared, roared everywhere, and roared equally everywhere; it thundered, thundered everywhere, and thundered equally everywhere; it surged, surged everywhere, and surged equally everywhere; it crashed, crashed everywhere, and crashed equally everywhere; it struck, struck everywhere, and struck equally everywhere.”

After manifesting these eighteen signs, all the palaces of Māra were obscured and no longer appeared; various extraordinary flowers bloomed out of season, and all the flowering and fruit-bearing trees upon the great earth leaned toward the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.

Śakra, Lord of the Devas, the Four Great Kings, and the hosts of devaputras of the desire realm rained down exquisite celestial flowers from the midst of the sky, scattering and offering them to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata; they also scattered various celestial flowers over the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva!
It is because of you that we have today, in the presence of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, heard this most supreme and profound True Dharma.
"Today we have obtained a great and excellent benefit; this is the most rare and marvelous thing in the world.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, saying:
"By what causes and conditions has the great earth trembled and these various signs appeared?"
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata said:
"Good son! It was precisely because I have just explained to you that all Buddhas and Tathāgatas possess a dharma that neither comes nor goes that such a sign appeared."

“At that time, eight thousand people attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); eighty thousand nayutas of people resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; and sixty-four thousand people became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.”
At that time, having heard this Dharma, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita was filled with great joy and exultation, and he spoke these words:

“Today I have attained the most supreme benefit; for the sake of seeking the Prajñāpāramitā, I have been able to hear from my spiritual friend regarding the teaching of all Tathāgatas that there is no coming or going.”
"I have now attained such perfected roots of goodness that I am certain not to regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having spoken these words, he was filled with even greater joy; leaping into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees, he reflected from mid-air:
"From where shall I now obtain exquisite incense and flowers to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata?"
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, immediately offered celestial māndārava flowers to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita.
The Lord of Devas spoke these words:
"Good son! You should take these exquisite flowers and offer them as an act of worship to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata."
"I shall now assist you in accomplishing the benefit of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, having accepted the flowers offered by Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately scattered them as an offering toward the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
